News.title: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride
News.content:
First, Burnham inherited the broad deal that's likely to be signed. The UK and EU were originally meant to mint a new and, they hope, improved agreement back in May, then in July, and well, political upheavals mean one thing for getting things done â delay.

But that means the outlines of a new agreement have been clear for many months, an approach based on "closer alignment" as Sir Keir Starmer proclaimed to us at the start of the year.

So if the prime minister hails agreement, spare a thought for those who started the work to get it this far many months ago.

One source familiar with the negotiations told me, "They are 90% there", with agreements designed to make life easier for food producers, a deal on emissions trading which could help manufacturers, and new arrangements for youth visas (although it's understood there is still haggling over putting a cap on the numbers).

An EU source close to the process said: "The bone of contention is a cap â we proposed 150,000, the UK proposed 50,000 â but we would expect to reach a compromise", even though it has been "very tense" on both sides.

A last-minute call from the EU to cut tuition fees for its students is expected to be parked for now with more months of discussion to come. Another fine tradition - agree what you can, but file some tough stuff away for future chat.

There are dilemmas too on the EU's so-called "Made in Europe" plans â draft laws to protect its industries from being hammered by Chinese competition. The purpose is clear â to help the economy grow, with the prime minister quoting figures that suggest closer ties to the EU without going back in could add 0.4 percent to GDP.

But as the tabloid-friendly row over salty snacks illustrates, making it easier to do business with the bloc doesn't come without a cost, and a political awkwardness.

News.title: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza
News.content:
Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help.

Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter.

Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil.

Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation.

Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season.

Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate.

"We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help."

The Hamas-run government in Gaza said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. A spokesperson said the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs" had caused injuries, some of which were critical.

Veitch also said there were fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents available in the Gaza strip due to UN budget cuts.

"We have to be much more choosy about where we're going to be supporting," he said.

"But unfortunately, heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help."

Israel has said it restricts the entry of items into Gaza that could be used for military purposes.

Maryam Odeh, 34, who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah, told AFP news agency: "We no longer know how to protect our children.

"My children ask me where we will sleep tonight, and I have no answer."

Khaled al-Najjar, 41, told AFP: "We fear for our children not only from the flooding of the tents, but also from the cold and the widespread diseases."

News.title: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event
News.content:
We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails.

In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.

An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications".

However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".

The Cabinet Office said: "The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid's 75-year history."

Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.

At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour.

The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.

The response from the government was that while copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.

As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused.

"If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."

While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.

I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.

It felt like an omen.

News.title: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed
News.content:
"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."

That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.

Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.

Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act.

The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.

None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.

News.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
News.content:
We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.

He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.

The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.

Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".

He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.

But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.

Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.

These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.

Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.

He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".

Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.

This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.

"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.

It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.

"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.

But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.

"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.

And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.

He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.

Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.

"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."

With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.

More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.

It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.

Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.

News.title: Dolly Parton's manager drops lawsuit against her nephew
News.content:
The manager of the late country music star Dolly Parton has dropped a lawsuit against her nephew.

The civil case was filed by the company that manages Parton's business interests less than a month after her death.

It included allegations of threats, intimidation and coercion against Bryan Seaver, the relative who publicly confirmed Parton had died in August. A temporary restraining order was also sought.

Seaver, who previously served as Parton's head of security, denied the allegations.

In a statement to the BBC's US partner, CBS News, Seaver's attorneys said he was "grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the family can grieve peacefully".

Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns the security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services (SAPS).

It provided security to Parton, who died of cancer aged 80, for the final 20 years of her life.

Weeks after Seaver confirmed her death, both he and his company were dismissed by She's Alive, which manages Parton's estate.

Danny Nozell, Parton's longtime manager and the head of She's Alive, filed for a temporary restraining order against Seaver and his company, which was granted by a judge.

In court filings, he accused Seaver of "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", after demanding payment from the estate.

The documents included messages in which he allegedly threatened to damage Parton's brand and business interests if his demands were not met.

The filings also alleged that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.

Seaver denied threatening the estate and in a statement published by TMZ at the time, he said he was a "career soldier and military contractor" but insisted he had simply been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".

News.title: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attack
News.content:
Two men and a boy have been arrested after a teenager was injured in an attack involving a sword near two schools in Gloucester.

St Peter's High School and Willow Primary Academy, in Tuffley, were put into lockdown after the incident at 08:50 GMT on Friday.

Police said a 17-year-old suffered a wound "believed to have been caused by the sword".

A 19-year-old was arrested overnight on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. An 18-year-old was held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. Meanwhile another 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
News.content:
A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".

It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".

Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.

There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.

In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.

The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.

However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.

On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.

"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.

Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

News.title: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure that victims in rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.

His comments come after Metropolitan Police boss Sir Mark Rowley told the BBC that what he heard reported from Russell Brand's trial came very close to "victim blaming".

The government needs to "constantly look" at how rape trials are conducted to better support alleged victims in court, the prime minister told Times Radio, although BBC News understands there are no plans to change the law around rape trials.

Actor and comedian Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault after a four-week trial in London.

During an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, it was put to Sir Mark that Brand's defence barrister Ian Winter KC "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark replied: "I think what I've heard reported heads towards, it's getting very close to victim blaming, which is something we've thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don't do."

He said he would support a call from the Victims' Commissioner for a legal duty that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark explained.

In a Times Radio interview on Saturday, Burnham said he would "look closely" at the police chief's comments.

He said the government needed to look at how to "make sure they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court".

"[I'm] always prepared to make changes," he said. "We need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape, we need to get the conviction rate up.

"All of this is part of our broader agenda as a government combatting violence against women and girls."

Pressed on whether this might lead to a change in the law, the prime minister replied: "I wouldn't rule anything out... I will study what's happened here in great detail."

Brand, who has starred in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall, will be sentenced on Monday and is expected to face substantial jail time.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault after the jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody.

It has since been revealed that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Met said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Sir Mark told BBC Breakfast he "wouldn't be surprised if many more came forward".

In the wake of Brand's trial, Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said rape trials must be conducted "in a way that challenges myths and misconceptions about sexual violence".

In a social media post, Waxman wrote that "victims need confidence that the justice process is fair and based on evidence, not myths and false assumptions about rape and trauma".

Speaking to the Today programme on Saturday, director and founder of the Centre for Women's Justice Harriet Wistrich agreed that juries need to understand "underlying behaviours" without "running to judgement" over how a victim behaved in a particular way.

But former Conservative MP Anna Soubry, who has now returned to her work as a barrister where she often defends rape and sexual offence cases in the Crown court, told the BBC "people are being misled" by Sir Mark's comments.

"Every single judge in those cases must give, and does give, a very firm direction to the jury on exactly these points," she said.

As a result, she said she was " really disappointed" in the police chief and stressed "we've got to trust our juries" who are able to have an understanding of the nature of sexual offences.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

News.title: We thought mum abandoned us - then we discovered she'd been murdered
News.content:
"We didn't have anyone to support us really in our lives. We struggled growing up," added Mehmet.

They were unaware that their mother had been beaten to death by her partner before hiding her body in the cellar of their home for about a year before disposing of her remains in household waste bins.

The court heard Dunkley had maintained his account that Lashley had disappeared for decades, despite being spoken to by police multiple times.

He said she had left her youngest child, who was not Dunkley's son, alone in their flat. Dunkley took the nine-month-old to social services and he was later adopted.

Judge Chambers said the "most significant aggravating factor" in the case was that Dunkley had killed the mother of a baby, who she had still been breastfeeding.

Mehmet said Dunkley killed his mother "in such a horrible way and then lied to us for 27 years", and that learning about her death had made him feel guilty about the resentment he had felt in the past.

"I feel bad in a way now that I felt that way towards mum," he said.

News.title: Evacuations in Liverpool city centre after car crash causes gas leak
News.content:
A gas leak caused by a car crashing into a restaurant in Liverpool city centre has led to road closures and the evacuation of neighbouring buildings.

The incident happened at about 12:30 GMT on North John Street when a Peugeot car hit the window of Tiger Rock Restaurant, Merseyside Police said.

The driver stayed at the scene and there is no indication that this was a deliberate act, the force said.

Three people who had been in the restaurant at the time of the crash were assessed for minor injuries, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

A spokesman said the impact caused a gas leak so a cordon has been put in place by firefighters and the police, with a structural engineer and a gas engineer due to attend.

Neighbouring buildings have been evacuated as a precaution and road closures are in place at the junction of Dale Street and North John Street, and also the junction of North John Street and Lord Street.

Buses have also been temporarily diverted with all Wirral Metro services terminating at Whitechapel, and starting their return journey from Sir Thomas Street.

News.title: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
News.content:
"The Claimant, playing a dead soldier, was lying on the port side of a ship which had been lit up by gas powered flame bars to simulate it being on fire," according to documents he filed at London's High Court.

"He was positioned only a few feet away from the gas line. Without warning, there was a gas explosion that caught the Claimant and blew him forwards.

"He saw 20 foot tall flames and felt immense heat. His costume caught fire. He was immediately aware that strips of skin had peeled from his arms.

"He panicked and ran, falling over a few times before escaping the flames. Bottles of water were thrown on him by colleagues, he was undressed and clingfilm was applied to his burns."

The legal claim said he suffered "flash burns" to 15% of his body, plus injuries to both knees and his right wrist, and was flown by helicopter to hospital in Marrakesh.

"He remained in excruciating pain. Treatment there was limited," Sarsfield's claim said. He was repatriated to the UK four days later, where his wounds were "treated appropriately" in hospital.

"Formerly a man of considerable physical prowess, the Claimant suffered considerable physical de-conditioning," with limitations to his mobility, and also suffered psychological symptoms, his claim said.

It added: "He has sustained significant scarring that is permanent and which is hypersensitive. He needs to keep out of the sun."

August Street Films' legal defence said "no admissions are made as to the alleged injuries sustained by the Claimant".

The company is a subsidiary of film studio Paramount, which said several people were hurt in the accident.

A Paramount spokesperson said in 2023: "While filming a planned stunt sequence on the set of the Gladiator sequel, an accident occurred during which several crew members experienced non-life-threatening injuries.

"The safety and full medical services teams on-site were able to act quickly so that those who were impacted immediately received necessary care. They are all in stable condition and continue to receive treatment.

"The well-being of the cast and crew is of the utmost importance to us, and we have strict health and safety procedures in place on all our productions. We will continue monitoring the situation and taking all necessary precautions as we resume production."

Sarsfield, August Street Films and Paramount declined to comment further.

News.title: Third person arrested after car damaged by gunshots
News.content:
A third person has been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.

South Wales Police said a vehicle on the A48 in Morriston, Swansea, sustained damage "consistent with a firearms discharge" on Friday and one person was left with minor injuries.

A 41-year-old man, from Llansamlet, and a 16-year-old boy, also from Llansamlet, were arrested in the aftermath on Friday and remain in custody.

On Saturday police said a 29-year-old man from Swansea had also now been arrested on suspicion of affray and possessing an offensive weapon.

Police continue to investigate and are appealing for witnesses and anyone with footage of the incident to come forward.

Ch Supt Stephen Jones, of South Wales Police, said the force believed that the "individuals involved are likely to be known to one another."

"Incidents such as this are rare but we appreciate they cause significant concern within local communities," he said.

The force said it was not currently aware of any wider threat to the public.

Jones said: "A visible policing presence will remain in the area as officers continue their enquiries and provide reassurance to local residents.

"I would like to urge anyone who does have information to make contact."

South Wales Police said it was also aware of rumours and speculation circulating on social media in relation to this incident, and asks the public not to share unverified information.

Residents were told to avoid the area and events, including a local firework display due to take place on Friday, were cancelled.

Video circulating online shows police officers next to a stationary car that appeared to have been struck by a shotgun blast on Clase Road near an Asda superstore.

A National Police Air Service helicopter was circling the area but has since returned to base.

South Wales Police said all road closures put in place following the incident had been lifted.

Anyone who witnessed the incident, or who has information or footage that could assist the investigation, is asked to contact South Wales Police via its major incident public portal.

News.title: Baxters fish soup cans recalled over fears they could 'swell and rupture'
News.content:
Customers who bought cans of a fish soup manufactured by Baxters have been urged to dispose of them in outside bins over fears the tins could burst.

The firm has recalled its Chef Selections Cullen Skink soup, a smoked haddock chowder, due to a manufacturing fault which may cause it to spoil and cans to "swell and potentially rupture", according to the Food Standards Agency (FSA)., external

If spoilt, the soup may have an "unpleasant odour and flavour", the FSA said.

The company, based in the north east of Scotland, said the issue may affect the 400g cans with batch code L07XC and an April 2029 best before date.

Shoppers who bought the soup in England, Wales and Scotland have been told not to eat it, and to instead dispose of it without opening it.

"Carefully place the full can in a bag and dispose of it in an external bin," the FSA told customers.

People seeking a replacement are told to contact Baxters customer care team at ccuk@baxters.com.

Founded in Fochabers in Moray in 1868, Baxters remains one of Scotland's best-known food manufacturers.

It remains a privately-owned family business and is now run by fourth-generation family member Audrey Baxter.

News.title: Beach homes face demolition months after being sold
News.content:
A property investor and a woman planning for her retirement have been told their homes are at risk of falling into the sea just months after they purchased them.

The two properties are part of a collection of former fishermen's cottages in the hamlet of Newport, south of Hemsby, Norfolk.

The houses, which were both bought in the last three months, are among nine properties in the area deemed to be at risk of coastal erosion.

Great Yarmouth Borough Council has advised the homeowners to leave their properties for their own safety.

News.title: AI in property listings is false advertising, house-hunters say
News.content:
Property buyers and renters say the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in listings appearing on sites like Rightmove is "false advertising" and wastes time for all involved.

Jessica Otterwell, who is hunting for a flat in Brighton, East Sussex, told the BBC: "It's like if you went to buy a car because the picture was of a brand-new Mercedes and you turned up and it was a Skoda with one wheel."

An estate agent in Sussex said it could cost up for Â£50,000 to stage a property with furniture, while another in Surrey added: "Technology should help people, not deceive them."

Rightmove, a portal website which pulls in listings from other estate agents, and does not sell or rent properties directly, said AI-generated imagery was allowed on the site if it was clearly labelled.

The BBC has seen some property listings in which the images have been watermarked "Virtually staged" or "Artificially enhanced", but many others have not been disclosed.

The practice has been dubbed by some as "housefishing".

News.title: Five European leaders call for closer ties with Britain ahead of crucial EU summit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Five European leaders have called for closer ties with Britain ahead of a crucial EU-UK summit.

In a letter to Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa, the leaders of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark, said stronger commitments on clean energy would be beneficial to both sides.

Andy Burnham will meet Ms Von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and Mr Costa, who leads the European Council, on 20 November at the summit in Brussels.

The prime minister will push for deals to cut costs and red tape for British farmers and businesses, support industry and boost growth.

In a letter seen by the Guardian, the five leaders describe the UK as a “close partner in the energy transition”, adding that Britain’s integration into the EU’s internal electricity market was “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea area and transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world”.

They add: “We call on you and the UK to agree during the summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations.”

open image in gallery Five European leaders have called for closer ties with Britain ( AP )

Leaked draft documents prepared ahead of the summit reveal that the EU is demanding financial contributions from the UK in exchange for access to its single market for electricity.

The papers, seen by Sky News, show that the EU expects an “appropriate level of financial contribution towards reducing economic and social disparities between the regions of the EU”.

It says both the UK and Brussels hope to “conclude these negotiations swiftly” so Britain can access the market “as soon as possible”.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham will meet EU leaders in Brussels at the summit in November ( AFP/Getty )

The EU is also requesting that the UK scrap plans to deport European offenders under recent Home Office rules that permit foreign nationals to be removed once sentenced.

A British government source stated that the UK will not agree to the EU’s demands.

The EU’s former Brexit negotiator, Michel Barnier, has meanwhile warned the prime minister that he will not be able to rejoin its single market “à la carte”, adding: “There is no cherry picking.”

The comment came after Mr Burnham said rejoining the EU’s internal market is among options he could pursue when reworking the UK’s relationship with the bloc.

Speaking on the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, Mr Barnier said: “There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms [movement of goods, services, capital and people] are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market.”

News.title: Former federal prosecutor set to probe whether Trump officials misled court in golf course case
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A federal judge announced Saturday that she intends to appoint a former top federal prosecutor from President Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether government officials and attorneys deliberately misled her during a lawsuit challenging a high-profile Washington construction project involving the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.

Jessie Liu, who previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethical standards or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the litigation, which was initiated in February by two golfers and the DC Preservation League.

The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park land on Nov. 15 to construct a "World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course, requiring the administration to give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" of the course while the lawsuit remains active.

Reyes is offering both sides an opportunity to be heard regarding her plan to name Liu as special master in the dispute. The parties must submit their responses in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the case is scheduled to take place.

Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to determine whether federal officials lied about the full extent of the renovation plans across months of court hearings. She is also seeking to clarify if they were truthful about various actions taken, including the cutting of hundreds of trees early last month. Having previously rejected multiple motions from plaintiffs asking her to intervene because she trusted government attorneys, Reyes formally announced an investigation into the government's conduct during an Oct. 30 hearing.

open image in gallery Donald Trump ( Reuters )

In her former role as the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw several matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller as part of his investigation into potential ties between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated Liu to serve as associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking job in the Justice Department.

Liu ultimately withdrew from consideration after facing opposition from members of the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee over her past membership in a legal association that supported abortion rights. She later resigned from that organization, explaining that it endorsed left-leaning positions, and is currently a partner at her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP.

David Super, a professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, observed that a judge launching a formal investigation into the conduct of trial participants "can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court."

Super noted that the step also reflects "of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues."

Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing following several Truth Social posts by Trump indicating there were active plans for the golf course, with construction slated to start Nov. 15. Trump stated that the park would remain closed for 15 months while the work was carried out.

The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic across multiple subsequent court sessions when administration officials were unable to confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually questioned whom she could trust, leading the Department of Justice to file notice on Oct. 28 acknowledging that the redevelopment plans were real.

News.title: Tottenham to submit formal complaint over Jayden Bogle decision
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tottenham Hotspur will submit a formal complaint to Pro Ref over the decision not to dismiss defender Jayden Bogle during the 1-0 defeat to Leeds at Elland Road.

It is understood Tottenham believe Bogle should have been sent off and will write to refereeing body Pro Ref to seek an explanation as to why the incident did not result in a red card.

Bogle lunged into a tackle on Spurs forward Mathys Tel and landed on Tel’s ankle with his left foot. The on-field decision from referee John Brooks was to award a foul to Spurs but issue no cards of further punishment to Bogle.

The game was paused as Tel received treatment on the pitch and the Video Assistant Referee looked in detail at the incident. The decision from the VAR arrived after a four-minte review with Tony Harrington opting against calling Brooks to the pitch-side monitor to review the challenge himself.

The challenge was deemed “reckless” but the match continued with Bogle left unpunished and Tel eventually forced off due to lingering affects on his Achilles.

The incident came just a week after Crystal Palace's Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for a similar challenge in Spurs' win over the Eagles. Later in the game, Tottenham’s Pedro Porro wa shown a yellow card for a challenge similar to Bogle’s which infuriated manager Roberto de Zerbi.

open image in gallery Mathys Tel had to be subbed off due to a lingering niggle following Jayden Bogle's tackle ( PA )

"I have big confidence in the referee. Nothing changes if he goes to the monitor," said De Zerbi. "If they didn't take the right decision I don't know. We have to keep the eyes on the performance where can improve.

"I was surprised on the yellow card for Pedro Porro because it was clear. The potential red card, I couldn't say. We have full confidence in the referee and VAR. I cannot say nothing more."

News.content:

Formula 1 returns to Brazil and the famous Interlagos circuit for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, round 20 of the 2026 season.

Kimi Antonelli became F1’s youngest-ever world champion as his podium last time out in Mexico City gave the 20-year-old Italian an unassailable lead in the championship race with four rounds remaining.

Max Verstappen continued his excellent run of form with a third victory in four races and now the Red Bull driver has leapt up to second in the leaderboard, two points clear of third-placed Lewis Hamilton and 11 points ahead of fourth-placed George Russell.

Hamilton was furious with his Ferrari team after seeing a win fall away in Mexico City following an early tangle with teammate Charles Leclerc. Hamilton is a three-time winner at the Interlagos circuit, the venue where he memorably won his first title in 2008.

Follow live action from the Sao Paulo Grand Prix with The Independent.

News.title: London Bridge Tube station evacuated and closed over fire alert
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

London Bridge underground station was closed as authorities responded to a fire alert on Saturday evening.

Members of the public were evacuated from the building during the incident at around 5.30pm.

In a post on the Transport for London accessibility account, a statement read: “London Bridge station - This station is closed while we respond to a fire alert. Tickets will be accepted on London Buses.”

The station has since re-opened.

open image in gallery People crowded around the entrance of London Bridge ( Paul Farrell )

“London Bridge station - the station has now re-opened,” read a TfL account announcing the new on social media shortly after.

Pictures from the scene show a crowd of people huddled outside the entrance of the tube station while TfL staff looked into the incident.

London Bridge is one of the busiest transport stations with over 53 million entries every year, according to data by the Office for Rail and Road figures from 2024 - 2025. It is the capital’s oldest railway station and was opened in December 1836.

It was part of a £1bn development between 2013 and 2018 and is situated on Tooley Street and St Thomas Street. Both trains and tube lines operate from the station.

The Independent has contacted British Transport Police for comment.

News.title: Nato considers anti-tank barriers along Russian border as Putin rearms
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Finland is looking to Ukraine’s defence experience as the country seeks to fortify a 1,340km border with Russia.

Finland’s army commander, Lieutenant General Pasi Välimäki, said Kyiv’s “extensive defense lines” and anti-tank obstacles have helped to slow down Russia’s attacks.

“Conditions in Finland are more challenging,” General Pasi Välimäki told Bloomberg.

“If we build fortifications and dig anti-tank ditches or obstacles as deep as those in Ukraine, how long does it take before our environment turns them into artificial ponds?”

The lieutenant also stressed that Russia has already started to rebuild its military and weapons stockpile, with the likes of T-90 tanks and BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles delivered to storage facilities.

open image in gallery Finland is looking to Ukraine ’s defence experience to bolster its border with Russia ( AFP/Getty )

While Finland is unable to prevent Moscow from rearming, Välimäki said they are aiming to create a “barrier” so that Russia cannot move any further towards Finland, or an alliance.

It comes as both Finland and Norway broke convention to speak directly to Vladimir Putin last week, sparking fury from European leaders.

Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere held “frank and substantive” talks with the Russian president in a bid to influence the Kremlin’s position as the conflict in Ukraine approaches the start of its fifth year.

But the move attracted criticism from their Nordic counterparts including Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, as they urged Europe’s leaders to “stick together” on Ukraine.

open image in gallery Finland and Norway broke convention to speak directly to Vladimir Putin this week ( AFP/Getty )

In a joint statement, Stoere said he and Stubb had spoken to Putin for about 90 minutes, and linked the initiative to planned peace discussions between Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in Abu Dhabi next month. The discussions will be their first since February.

They said they had then spoken to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed the call had been coordinated with Kyiv, calling it “the right approach”.

“We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process,” he said, adding that he also hoped a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky could “pave the way to other steps in the peace process”.

“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said. “We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact ⁠on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.”

Stoere said he and ​Stubb had “stressed ⁠the importance of de-escalation,” and that both had voiced strong support for Ukraine.

But Frederiksen hit out at the call, saying she saw no signs that Russia wanted peace, adding: “I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo.”

News.title: De Zerbi blames players rather than referee for worrying defeat
News.content:
After victories against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace, this was a blow for De Zerbi after looking to move into the European places. Leeds had not scored in 298 minutes of football, nor had they won in five previous matches, yet the Tottenham manager could barely recognise the players who had won three matches in a row.

De Zerbi had warned his team they would face a hostile atmosphere at Elland Road, but instead of rising to the challenge, Spurs were passive until it was too late.

“We didn’t win any duels, we didn’t win any one-to-ones, there was space to play and we didn’t take the right position,” De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show personality, we didn’t show what we are or who we are. It is part of the journey for sure. It can be normal in football but we have to be honest, if you are not honest the future is not good. If you analyse our behaviour we can become a top team.

“We worked very hard this week. We spoke all the days about the intensity, the type of game we would have found in this stadium and the atmosphere, it was not a surprise for us. Sometimes it can happen that we didn’t play the kind of game we want.”

De Zerbi’s honesty shines a light on the amount of work that still needs to be done at Spurs. Even after three straight wins, he has refused to get carried away despite fans looking upwards towards the European places.

Neither did the Italian want to blame the officials for failing to send off Bogle. Brooks has history with Spurs, sending off Xavi Simons against Liverpool last season. Here, he booked De Zerbi for his protests after Bogle’s heavy challenge that forced Mathys Tel off through injury.

News.title: Odegaard winner spares officials from another VAR row
News.content:
Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Brutal truth is Scotland never looked like beating All Blacks
News.content:
“They [New Zealand] are playing some excellent rugby right now and it is our first game of the season, which is always the toughest challenge for us too. It is a different New Zealand team. It is a team that is playing much more ambitious rugby. They are informed, they are cohesive. They played a lot of Test matches over the summer. We are going to have to find ways to win, find ways to stay in the fight because they will have a lot of possession too.”

New Zealand won all three of their home fixtures back in July in the first half of the Nations Championship, beating France, Italy and Ireland to claim a maximum 15 points. They faced Australia in two Bledisloe Cup fixtures last month, with the All Blacks easing to victory in both matches, scoring 93 points. They will go on to face Wales and England after this game. The All Blacks have travelled to the northern hemisphere without captain Ardie Savea, who is sidelined with a shoulder injury.

“Scotland are a quality side,” New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie said. “They are very well coached and have built a lot of depth over recent years. They play a very similar brand of footy to us and we know we will need to be at our best on Saturday [today]. Murrayfield is an iconic place to play so it will be a special occasion to kick off our northern tour.”

It has been an emotional week for the All Blacks as they continue to come to terms with the tragic loss of their long-time head of security Logan Cadwallader, who died at the team’s Edinburgh hotel earlier this week.

Kick-off from Murrayfield is at 2.10pm.

News.title: Feinberg-Mngomezulu leads Springboks’ nine-try obliteration of Italy
News.content:
What a difference a decade makes. In November 2016, Italy beat South Africa for the first, and so far only, time. Now the Springboks have obliterated Italy – and the roots of this victory can be traced back to that defeat 10 years ago.

That historic result sparked a major rethink in South Africa, a rethink that ultimately led to Rassie Erasmus replacing Allister Coetzee as head coach in early 2018. Erasmus has overseen a remarkable transformation of the Boks since: from an embarrassing loss in Italy to back-to-back world champions.

This win in Turin was built on what Erasmus’s Boks are known for: a potently powerful set-piece and a back line that can deliver mesmerising moments. The one disappointment for their head coach will be how they failed to match the intensity and ruthlessness of their first-half performance in the second 40 minutes.

“It’s almost impossible to put 80 minutes together at 100 per cent,” he said afterwards. “But when you win 66-7, I don’t think you can start nitpicking problems in the second half. That said, we have to play much better than this if we want to be competitive against France and Ireland.”

The Boks were 45-0 up at the break having scored six tries. The majority came off the back of their driving line-out, which they were able to launch to great effect inside Italy’s 22. Morne van den Berg, Malcolm Marx (two) and Siya Kolisi were all beneficiaries of the power of their maul in the first half. Damian Willemse also enjoyed an easy run-in when Jasper Wiese released him into space, but the stand-out finish came from Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu inside 10 minutes.

The 24-year-old fly-half is undoubtedly one of the most exciting players in world rugby and he showed his full repertoire here: deft hands, pinpoint vision and metronomic kicking. The opening try was special, too: his dummy carved out the space for him to break through Italy and he then had the pace to beat any chasing defenders to the corner, where he acrobatically finished one-handed.

News.title: Ireland send out ominous warning with second-gear walloping of Argentina
News.content:
Is it time to fire up the emerald green bandwagon? Not quite yet. But this was not a bad start to Ireland’s autumn; a 42-12 walloping of Los Pumas with Andy Farrell’s team still nowhere near their best. That should be highly encouraging for those of an Irish persuasion.

A year out from the World Cups of 2015, 2019 and 2023, Ireland had enjoyed banner seasons, eyeing up global glory. They never made it past the quarter-finals.

The build-up this time has been tougher going – the Aviva, unusually for this time of year – was not even full for this Nations Championship encounter. But perhaps Ireland will be better for it. They had far too much on a crisp Friday night in Dublin for an Argentina team who were missing a few of their stars, notably Bath’s Santiago Carreras and Lyon prop Thomas Gallo, but still packing 750 caps’ worth of Test experience in their starting XV.

Farrell was missing a few big names himself. Caelan Doris and Jack Conan were out injured, with the Englishman opting to hand Sean Jansen and Nick Timoney starts in the back row. Farrell also chose to start Craig Casey rather than Jamison Gibson-Park – arguably their best player of the last 18 months – at scrum-half, with Sam Prendergast starting again at 10 given Jack Crowley’s absence.

All in all there was a slightly experimental feel to proceedings, making Argentina potentially dangerous visitors. But Ireland had far too much in reserve. Hugo Keenan grabbed a hat-trick and took the player of the match award. Robert Baloucoune was consistently excellent. Mack Hansen’s return on the wing was hugely welcome. Tominey stood out in the back row.

Farrell said he was delighted with the result, if not the entire performance, making special mention of the likes of Keenan, Hansen, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, all of whom were returning from long injury lay-offs.

“The game’s never going to be perfect. But if you look at the bigger picture, to win 42-12 against a really good side in Argentina, I don’t think too many teams have done that,” Farrell said. “You have to be pleased.”

Asked whether he was happier with the 42 points scored or the meagre 12 conceded, Farrell added that it was probably the latter: “We want to be known for our defence. It shows our mentality.”

Los Pumas scored the first try of the game, Mateo Carreras getting the jump on Casey in the corner to field a Tomás Albornoz crossfield kick.

News.title: ‘Air Caluori’ puts on show as England A offer exciting glimpse into future
News.content:
England A 59 Argentina XV 24

Noah Caluori and Luke Northmore both scored twice as England A produced an emphatic victory over Argentina XV at the Rec.

On a night when England’s back line showcased plenty of attacking flair and free-flowing rugby, the hosts ran in nine tries to shrug off a dogged Argentina outfit.

Bath’s Max Ojomoh shone bright on his own turf and combined effortlessly with Northmore in a midfield partnership which showed plenty of promise for the future.

A young and inexperienced touring Argentina side hung tough in a see-sawing first half which yielded seven tries, but England found another gear after the break, with Jack Kenningham and Jamie Blamire among those on the scoresheet.

The hosts enjoyed a dream start when Caluori dotted down inside the opening two minutes, setting the tone for a helter-skelter first half.

News.title: Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place
News.content:
Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

News.title: A tech editor’s guide to finding genuine Black Friday discounts
News.content:
The Black Friday shopping season is here. The world’s biggest technology brands, including Amazon, Samsung, Apple and Sony, are all expected to drop their prices, with British retailers such as John Lewis, Currys and Argos throwing their hats in the ring as we speed towards the new year.

While you might already have your eye on a gadget or two in the hope they drop in price during the sales, it’s important to shop wisely – and, crucially, manage expectations.

As Telegraph Recommended’s tech editor, who has been covering the Black Friday sales for well over a decade, I have picked up a number of must-know tips.

Whether that’s buying last year’s iPhone for less than the latest model, or accepting the sad truth that game consoles won’t be discounted ahead of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch, here’s everything you need to know – including early discounts.

FRANKIE RAYMOND says spearheading Cray Wanderers to a stunning win over Stockport would be the highlight of his career – despite already shining in one of the FA Cup’s biggest upsets.

The midfielder, 33, played a key role as non-league minnows Boreham Wood beat Bournemouth in 2022.



And Raymond has set his sights on another huge shock as seventh-tier Cray host League One promotion chasers Stockport at Flamingo Park on Sunday.

Wanderers had never reached the first round of the FA Cup in their 166-year history before a nail-biting penalty shootout triumph over Bedford Town last month.



Raymond reckons beating Stockport in front of a sell-out crowd would be the pinnacle.

The Cray skipper told SunSport: “It was a huge achievement to win at Bournemouth, but I think this would mean a little bit more to me.



“I’m a local boy and I’ve got a real connection to the club. As the captain, I see what this FA Cup run means to everyone.

“Achieving an upset would mean an awful lot to me and I’ve already been lucky through my career.

“I’ve played Everton twice in the FA Cup and beaten Bournemouth. These occasions don’t come around often.

“These are games you’ve got to cherish and we’ve got a really confident bunch.”

Sports.title: Spanish football pays emotional tribute to Jesus de Miguel after tragic striker died following collision with goalkeeper
Sports.content:
Next

SPANISH football paid an emotional tribute to Jesus de Miguel as LaLiga returned for the first time since the striker’s tragic death.

Tenerife star De Miguel died aged 30 on Tuesday following an accidental collision during his side’s LaLiga 2 match against Andorra the previous evening.



Spanish football was plunged into a state of mourning following De Miguel’s death.

Both Tenerife and Andorra’s scheduled matches this weekend were postponed, but the rest of the slate has gone ahead.



Earlier today, Malaga hosted Racing Santander at La Rosaleda.

Ahead of the contest, both sides made sure to pay their respects to De Miguel.

Players from each team walked onto the pitch wearing T-shirts with De Miguel’s No9 on the back, as well as the message “Siempre en nuestro recuerdo” – meaning “Always in our memory” in English.

This poignant message was also broadcast on the big screens, as the packed crowd rose to applaud the sentiment.

The match referee carried a wreath of flowers onto the pitch before laying it down onto the centre circle as players lined up for a period of silence.

On TV coverage of the game, a QR code was broadcast directing viewers to a crowdfunding site made to support De Miguel’s family.



The match was stopped in the ninth minute as players, officials and supporters took part in a minute’s applause for De Miguel.

“Always in our memory” again appeared on TV screens, as well as the QR code.

De Miguel’s death was deemed to be down to “accidental chest trauma” by a post-mortem.



The late forward had collided with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during the closing stages of Monday’s match.

Owono was sent off for his challenge, before the match was abandoned.

The goalkeeper, 25, was left devastated by what happened.

He subsequently released a statement, which read: “These are being the most difficult days of my life.

“I am struggling to find the words, and it is very hard for me to process anything that has happened.



“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I am thinking of him, his family, and all the people who loved him.

“I know there will be many matters to address, and I will face whatever comes with complete respect.

“But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything other than Jesus and the grief we are experiencing.

“Rest in peace, Jesus.”

The Spanish Footballers’ Association (AFE) has pledged to support Owono through counselling.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Athletic report that a source close to a team-mate of the goalkeeper said: “Owono is destroyed, locked in his house and disconnected from the world.

“Right now, he doesn’t even know who he is.”

Sports.title: Burnley’s drop into Championship goes from bad to worse as they blow 4-1 lead to somehow lose under new manager
Sports.content:

BURNLEY’S season hit a new low as Fabio Celestini watched his lose despite a three-goal lead with 28 minutes to play.

Alex Robertson’s own-goal put the Clarets 4-1 up in the 62nd minute in Cardiff.



But the Aussie midfielder went from zero to hero as he struck a 95th-minute winner with a rocket from outside the area to leave Burnley in the drop zone.

The winner sent the remaining Bluebirds fans into delirium and had viewers claiming the Championship is the greatest league in the world.



Incredibly, Cardiff were on the reverse end of a three-goal comeback on Wednesday.

Brian Barry-Murphy’s team led West Ham 3-0 at the break, but new boss Scott Parker fired up the Hammers in the dressing room and earned a huge point in his first game in charge.

After a rollercoaster week in which they scored seven goals, Cardiff sit 14th — six points off the playoffs.

Celestini has two points from three matches since replacing Nicky Hayen with Burnley at risk of suffering a double relegation.

Marcus Edwards fired in a fine second, before Colwill’s goal-bound effort bounced in off Ollie Tanner.

Sports.title: ‘Horrendous feeling’ – James Trafford reveals how bad it got at Man City and ended up ‘ringing people and venting’
Sports.content:
Next

JAMES TRAFFORD has opened up on his hellish return to Manchester City in 2025.

The 24-year-old was brought back to the club after two excellent seasons with Burnley, prompting City to activate his buy-back clause and match Newcastle’s £31 million bid.



But after starting the first three games of the season, Pep Guardiola went out and signed Gianluigi Donnarumma for £26m. Trafford would only start one more Premier League game for the club.

The four-time England international moved to Leeds for £40m in the summer and sans a bad error in their 2-0 loss to Bournemouth last week, he has impressed at Elland Road.



Speaking on Football Daily’s The Football Interview, Trafford reflected on how difficult life got for him at the Etihad Stadium after losing the place he returned to the club to take.

He said: “What a horrendous, horrendous feeling. Not playing.

“You are ringing a lot of people and just venting. Like most people, you have a [bad] day at work and you ring someone up.

“I ring my dad, I ring my mum, I ring my missus, I ring my mates. I like ringing my mates and we can just have a good talk about it all. It’s quite funny.

“I had to play regularly this season for my own mental wellbeing. You just lose yourself not playing.

“Maybe I’m different, I don’t know, but the feeling of not playing every week, it felt horrendous.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“I just had to play every week this season for that mental feel-good and to keep progressing with my career and edging me closer to achieving the dreams I want to achieve.”

Despite playing second fiddle to Donnarumma, Trafford did win both the Carabao Cup and FA Cup that season and started both finals.

He didn’t like spending so much time on the bench, but Trafford still sees the benefit of returning to the club he turned professional with.

He said: “Going into any season, I always have the highest of hopes and always the belief that it will go the best way it could.

“Unfortunately, we didn’t win all four trophies. It didn’t go how I expected it to go, but it happens.



“In the moment, I just tried to make the best of it as I could. Looking back, I don’t think it was a disappointing season in the end because I learned so much, I improved so much and I won two trophies in one year.

“There were moments when I was very down, regretting things and feeling disappointed, but looking back, I’m very thankful for the experience. What an incredible year.”
