World.title: Carlota de Limón: The Mexican cocktail that transported me to my mother’s kitchen
World.content:
“You have to try one of these; it’s like a refreshing key lime pie,” a hotel guest at the bar said. I walked over to the friendly group, all with the same drink in hand. The cocktail in front of them resembled a blended piña colada that was pale yellow and frothy on top, garnished with a thin lime wedge on the rim.

My friend and I were staying at the Dreams Estrella del Mar in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, for a few days to check out the hotel and all its amenities. After the nightly show, we stopped by the bar for a drink and tasted what would ultimately be the most memorable part of the trip.

The cocktail was tangy from the lemon, sweet from the sugar, and instantly took me to something very familiar. The creamy texture and the balance of tart and sweet also felt familiar, as if I had tasted this combination many times before.

Then it hit me: It was a dessert my mom used to make growing up, and one I’ve always requested when I’m home. It was a favorite of mine that she called “lemon dessert,” which I know now as a Carlota de Limón.

Back in my mother’s kitchen

Carlota de Limón is a Mexican icebox cake made with lemon juice, Galletas María (sweet, thin vanilla cookies), and a creamy mixture of evaporated and condensed milk. Layered and chilled until set, it has the perfect balance between sweet and tangy.

It was one of my favorite desserts growing up. I remember eating it by the spoonful, freshly made and the day after, as well as the feeling of disappointment when it was gone. It wasn’t reserved for special occasions, and my mom made it regularly whether we were having dessert at home or sharing a meal with guests. It was a dish that was made on a whim, ingredients almost always on hand, and one that didn’t last long.

In other words, it was always a hit.

My mother’s kitchen was where our family came together and where some of our deepest conversations happened. While water boiled for pasta or soup simmered in spices, we would all gather around the island, almost like magnets pulling us closer, filling the space with conversation, laughter and connectedness. That feeling is still there today when I visit my parents, especially around the holidays or special occasions.

An unexpected connection

At the hotel, I pulled up a bar stool and watched the bartender make another drink. Curious about its inspiration, I struck up a conversation with him. He was 23 and working his first hotel bartending job, where he had been experimenting with flavors and creating cocktails, something he found to be a fun, creative outlet.

When I described the dessert the cocktail reminded me of, he recognized the Carlota de Limón, a favorite of his, too. He had been experimenting with ingredients to create the drink, combining Licor 43, the vanilla and spice notes echoing the María cookies, and the fresh lemon juice, sugar and heavy cream to match the creamy layer. He would then shake it vigorously with ice until the mixture turned frothy and cold, adding a simple lime wedge as the finishing touch.

What began as an experiment in flavors had unexpectedly recreated something familiar to me. The bartender didn’t know my personal backstory of the dessert, but his experimentation with a new cocktail and my memories of my mother’s kitchen had led us to the same place.

Why flavors stay with us

Research from the National Library of Medicine has a name for the way a familiar smell or taste can bring back a personal memory: the Proust effect, named after the French writer Marcel Proust. The theory is that taste and smell can trigger autobiographical memories, leading to powerful emotions. Research on the brain’s olfactory pathways also shows direct connections between smell processing and the regions involved in emotion and memory, which makes sense given my strong and positive response to the citrus cocktail.

To me, Carlota de Limón was more than just a dessert; it was something my mother made regularly, in a kitchen where conversations and laughter occurred. The flavor was familiar, but so was everything I associated with it.

When I returned home, I found myself thinking less about the resort’s beautiful pools, manicured grounds or nightly shows, and more about that cocktail. A drink I’d encountered on vacation that had brought back a dessert so familiar that I hadn’t thought much about what it meant to me until that moment.

On the drive home from the airport, my husband asked how the trip went. My answer was simple: “Do we have any lemons? I have a drink in mind.”

Sandra Lee is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: My family always travels during Día de Muertos. Here’s what we’ve enjoyed most
World.content:
There are certain magical aspects of living in Mexico that simply cannot be replicated elsewhere — its foods, traditions and seasons. And because of Mexico’s vast geography and cultural topography, many of those elements can be heightened by being in the right place at the right time.

In that regard, nothing compares to Día de Muertos: A time of year in which colors are blooming, communities are celebrating and honoring loved ones, and regional gastronomy, customs and superstitions are on display for everyone to be collectively immersed in.

Beyond the obvious, increasing importance of the Mesoamerican holiday in Mexico for so many native families and local households, Día de Muertos means something especially personal for me and my family since it marks our anniversary of having moved to Mexico from California. The holiday always reminds me of arriving in Mexico after having gained dual citizenship and being received by festive parades, open-armed friends and relatives, and getting a dose of Mexico’s fullest, most complex flavors that have come to define what we most enjoy about living on this side of the border.

Building our own annual tradition

My wife’s and my own appreciation for Día de Muertos extends further back, years before we had fully relocated to Mexico. In 2019, we visited my mom, who is Mexican-born and was living on my abuelo’s ranch in Oaxaca at the time. We spent a month traveling the state of Oaxaca with her. The highlight? A full week of Día de Muertos in Oaxaca City.

I’ll never forget when we arrived, hopped off the bus, dropped our things off and went into the loud, colorful streets as Oaxaqueños had already kicked off their days-long celebration in the middle of the afternoon. A man wearing a Spider-Man mask saw us standing among the crowd, and as we soon found out would be a common occurrence and part of the local hospitality, he offered to pour out a shot of mezcal from the bottle in his hand.

As an outsider, there is no warmer welcome on the planet than someone picking you out of the masses on the street and pouring you mezcal. It’s a spirit and energy that would come to embody every Día de Muertos holiday we’ve experienced — the sense of connection and togetherness.

Since then, we’ve turned it into our own tradition to celebrate the holiday in different parts of Mexico as often as we can.

The regional nuances of Día de Muertos

My wife recently shared a visual map with me that outlines the different kinds of pan de muerto that are prepared throughout Mexico, based on each state’s history and gastronomic influences. Her point, besides nudging me to pick up another round of pan de muerto for our house, was that Mexico offers more to try than we know, especially whenever Día de Muertos rolls around.

It’s true. Everywhere we’ve been during this season has always presented a new way through which to experience and understand the multidimensionality of how the holiday is celebrated and revered.

Nearby, in the town of Naolinco, Veracruz, and its surrounding mountain communities, the festival is largely centered on the cempasúchil. This year, the community of San Pablo Coapan welcomed thousands of visitors for its fifth annual Festival del Cempasúchil, in which the local cempasúchil farms open to the public with a festival-like array of activities, food and Instagrammable photo ops.

The flower fields are decorated with playful calaveras that are decorated in Veracruzano style, ranging from a 25-foot-tall Jarocho skeleton to a human-sized fútbolero in the afterlife wearing a Tiburones Rojos soccer uniform from the 1990s (a team that no longer exists but certainly evokes memories for anyone who recalls the historic Veracruz team and grew up watching Liga MX).

In the pueblo of Naolinco proper, just a few miles up the mountain, Día de Muertos is celebrated with “La Cantada” (or a townwide serenade), where locals go around singing from the cemeteries to the streets throughout the night.

Major cities and regional rituals

Of course, there are the more globally popular and large-scale interpretations of Día de Muertos that can be seen in Oaxaca or Mexico City. In both cases, the holiday draws countless international and domestic visitors who join in on the fun and traditions as local families honor their deceased relatives with a mix of humility and bombast.

In both Oaxaca and Mexico City, expect massive gatherings of happy-go-lucky tourists and locals, as you’ll have to shuffle your way around the crowds and generally pay higher prices. The celebrations are bigger, louder and, to a degree, more capably geared toward tourism than other locales. I’d say for starters, both Oaxaca’s capital and Mexico City are a comfortable entry point into Mexico’s sprawling multiverse of Día de Muertos, as they provide broadly appealing and easy-to-navigate celebrations, both of which my family has enjoyed and experienced ourselves multiple times.

Of course, we still have a bunch of places to visit on our wishlist that I’ve been told about by my Mexican family members and other travelers. In the Huasteca jungles, “Xantolo” brings the holiday to life with “La Viejada,” a regional masked dance in which townspeople dress up as elders (similar to Veracruz’s “El Viejo del Año Nuevo” custom at the end of every year) to remember their relatives.

1 of 17

Indigenous customs from Huasteca to Campeche

In parts of Michoacán, there is a lake procession where the Purépecha fishermen use torches to light their path across the water and celebrate with all-night vigils.

Choo Ba’ak, a bone-washing ritual that happens every year in the Campeche pueblo of Pomuch, is part of Hanal Pixán (the Maya Day of the Dead) and offers an idiosyncratic version of the holiday unlike the contemporary mainstream version that is usually portrayed.

National Geographic described the ceremony as such: “…families wash the tombs and clean the bones of their deceased. After the cleaning they keep the ossuaries, or the box where the bones are deposited, open so the skulls and bones receive sun and air, as dictated by tradition. Relatives also arrange, paint and adorn the ossuaries and cover them with an embroidered white tablecloth bearing the name of the deceased.”

In Huaquechula, Puebla, unique altars — three to four stories tall, resembling a pyramid — are on display inside homes, with each layer of the altar representing a different aspect of life and death (the earth, the heavens and a celestial summit). The elaborate designs are typically defined by white cloth and marigolds.

As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me, you’d need more than a few lifetimes to truly experience all that Mexico has to offer regionally for Día de Muertos.

Our highlights from this year in the mountains of Puebla

The Pueblo Mágico of Cuetzalan del Progreso is tucked away in the northernmost edge of the state of Puebla, high up in the Sierra Norte mountains.

Unlike the majority of Puebla, which is commonly known for its arid plateaus and Talavera pottery in its state capital and surrounding areas, northern Puebla offers a microclimate and culture of its own that more closely resembles the humid, tropical and high-altitude Indigenous communities of Papantla in northern Veracruz, which is located just a few miles away on the other side of the mountain.

It’s not what one might think of when thinking of Puebla. And yet, it’s where regional customs for Día de Muertos are flourishing. We drove roughly four hours north of Xalapa (or about five hours northeast from Mexico City) to experience it for ourselves this year.

We weren’t disappointed, to say the least.

The town’s architecture alone is worth the winding mountain curves that one must navigate to reach the small, ages-old village that is — because of its elevated location in the mountains — famously drenched in drizzly mist and rainfall. The narrow alleys and steep, cobblestone paths (which all lead to the gorgeous Parroquia de San Francisco de Asís and its Totonac voladores, who perform their flying ritual on a sky-high wooden pole at the center of the plaza) resemble a miniature version of Guanajuato’s capital city, without the overcrowded tourism and with a hyper-local texture.

Flying globos de Cantoya into the night

I was told by a couple of young locals that families don’t commonly celebrate Día de Muertos by visiting the graveyards overnight (which is the tradition elsewhere). Instead, they light “globos de Cantoya” (miniature hot-air balloons made from paper and other materials) and send them off into the night.

From groups of high schoolers to older professionals who’ve mastered the craft, the town gathers on Día de Muertos weekend, as everyone takes turns setting up and sending off hundreds of their custom, artisanal balloons. The balloons — and their makers — vary in style, decoration and success (often, the small balloons will self-combust in flames and come burning back to earth, which can sometimes cause fires in the area). But generally, it’s a safe and spectacular tradition to witness in person.

The tradition, as it was explained to me in the pueblo, is meant to represent a path back to the heavens for the souls who are visiting their altars to enjoy the ofrendas laid out. Each globe, as it ascends brightly and colorfully into the night sky, is meant to guide family members back to the spiritual realm.

In recent years, Cuetzalan has turned the tradition into a legitimate state-funded festival, known locally as “El Vuelo del Quetzal” (The Flight of the Quetzal), and officially as Festival Internacional de Globos Artísticos de Papel. Surprisingly, the festival is only in its second year of formal operation, which helps it retain a charmingly niche, DIY feeling.

Local flavors and looking ahead

During the day, it is all preceded by local dances, voladores, Catrina costume contests and the general ambiance of a Pueblo Mágico worth its salt: excellent food, tianguis and a dense number of historic stairways and nooks to explore.

Among the standouts in town, you cannot skip TAOL, which is led by Chef Adriana Márquez and offers elevated, accessible takes on local dishes, including tlayoyos, chilpozontle, itacate, pipián, coffee and more. It’s the kind of chic eatery that would draw lines out the door in Mexico City, but since it’s hidden behind an unassuming stone exterior in Cuetzalan, it is able to offer ample space and friendly prices for what I would consider among the best cuisine I’ve tasted this year.

Paired with Día de Muertos activities and the hordes of costumed kids making their rounds on Halloween night to ask for their calaverita at local shops, which my son participated in, a few nights in Cuetzalan is a slept-on destination for late October and early November.

Though we elected to stay home last year to dedicate our time and resources to building and decorating an altar inside our home — with the help of my mom, who supplied many photos of our relatives — we’ve enjoyed going on the road to see how others embrace the spirit of the tradition.

I’m already thinking about where we might end up next year and what it will impart.

World.title: Why Tuesday’s US midterm results are a historic opportunity for Mexico-US relations: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Most of us intently watched Tuesday night’s midterm election results in the United States, regardless of political affiliation. As the MND team is committed to remaining apolitical, I will not weigh in on my personal thoughts on the results. I will, however, comment on what they mean for Mexico and for Mexico-U.S. relations.

It’s important to understand that the hardline approach of the Trump administration over the past two years against both Mexican immigrants and Mexico effectively silenced leaders on both sides of the border. Mexico was constantly on the defensive against the U.S. on tariffs, cartels, deportations, the rights of Mexican citizens abroad and many other topics. Mexican Americans, regardless of status, watched with anxiety as their communities came under threat from aggressive ICE raids. For many people and for Mexico in general, it was a time to keep your head down and stay quiet. The focus became on surviving the storm rather than thriving, leading or growing.

But the midterm election results have dramatically changed that dynamic.

First of all, I am happy for Mexican Americans. They will hopefully no longer have to fear the heavy-handed tactics often deployed by members of ICE. I recently wrote about the death of the 18th Mexican-American in ICE custody here: Yet another Mexican national dies in the custody of ICE: A perspective from our CEO.

People living in the United States — either legally or illegally — shouldn’t have to fear for their lives at the hands of the government. The data shows that the raids have often gone far beyond focusing on criminals, as the administration suggested it would do. Too many good people have been demonized by ICE as the agency has become increasingly extremist.

I am also happy for Mexico. The country has been the brunt of countless threats by the Trump administration on everything from tariffs to immigration to drug policy and cartels — despite historic cooperation from the Sheinbaum administration on many of these issues. Businesses on both sides of the border have had to deal with near-constant tariff threats, which oftentimes defy standard logic and strategic rationale for the North American region. Both Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly claimed that Mexico is run by the cartels, that President Sheinbaum is “afraid of the cartels,” and threatened to take unilateral action in the country. Hopefully, the unprecedented cooperation will continue and the unhelpful threats will diminish.

I am happy for the states of California and Texas, which both elected Mexican American governors. These two states — the largest and most economically prosperous in the United States — now account for more than half of the people of Mexican origin in the United States. Mexican Americans represent 40% of the total population in those states, which, if they were stand-alone counties, would be the fifth- and eighth-largest in the world in terms of GDP. Children of Mexican immigrants to the U.S. now lead both states. The newly elected lieutenant governor of Nevada is also of Mexican heritage.

Mexican Americans stood up, voted, and were heard — loudly and clearly. Their collective action presents a tremendous opportunity for Mexico. Let me give two examples:

1. I recently wrote about the huge, untapped opportunity that the Mexican diaspora in the U.S. represents for Mexico. The engagement of Indian American businesspeople with India stands in stark contrast to the lack of engagement of many Mexican American businesspeople with Mexico. Post-election, the timing is perfect for this to change. The opportunity for Mexican American businesses to further connect with Mexico to find talent, suppliers or customers is massive and could unleash economic growth in both countries.

2. It’s time for Mexico and the U.S. to think BIG on binational projects and initiatives. If not at the national level, most certainly at the state level. Some great examples already exist or are in process. In California, think of the Tijuana airport, which actually straddles the border into California. The airport has experienced phenomenal growth and is a perfect example of how the two countries can work strategically to develop closer ties. In Texas, think of the newly-opened second railway between Laredo and Nuevo Laredo or the proposed expansion of the World Trade Bridge from eight to 18 lanes. Think of the soon-to-be-opened Pharr project adding a four-lane bridge in Reynosa, or the Colombia-Solidarity highway projects to better connect Nuevo León and Laredo. Or even consider the Green Corridors planned project for an autonomous system to transport cargo from Monterrey to Laredo.

It’s a historic time for real leadership — strategic, long-term, big thinking that can foster engagement and economic prosperity between the two countries. Far too much time has been lost dividing, threatening and silencing bilateral collaboration and cooperation. The current circumstances offer an opportunity to take the relationship to a whole new level. Leaders on both sides of the border, stand up! The time is now.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico City’s Quintonil named best restaurant in Latin America
World.content:
Quintonil, a contemporary Mexican restaurant in Mexico City, was recognized as the best restaurant in Latin America and the fourth best globally in the 2026 edition of The World’s 50 Best Restaurants, presented Wednesday at the Municipal Theatre of Lima, Perú.

Led by married couple Chef Jorge Vallejo and restaurateur Alejandra Flores, Quintonil was the only Mexican representative among the top 50 in the ranking.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The 50 Best Restaurants (@theworlds50best)

“With a reputation for weaving fresh, local ingredients and traditional Mexican flavours and techniques into modern preparations, [Quintonil] has cemented its place as a Mexico City classic,” 50 Best said.

Asador Etxebarri, a Basque restaurant in Atxondo, Spain, was ranked best in the world.

Despite securing a place in the top five, Quintonil dropped one spot in the rankings, falling from third to fourth place this year.

Founded in 2012 by Vallejo and Flores, Quintonil has built its concept around Mexican fresh local produce and a contemporary interpretation of traditional flavors and techniques. Many of its ingredients are sourced from an urban garden just 30 meters away from the restaurant.

Located in the high-end neighborhood of Polanco, the restaurant is named after an edible wild plant belonging to the amaranth family, widely used in traditional Mexican cuisine and featured in some of the dishes and drinks served there.

The power duo brings complementary expertise to Quintonil: While Vallejo leads the kitchen, Flores oversees the service experience in the dining room.

“Quintonil is the setting for chef Jorge Vallejo’s boundary-pushing Mexican cuisine and his wife Alejandra Flores’ exceptional hospitality,” 50 Best said.

50 Best highlighted dishes including roasted duck with coconut manchamanteles mole (a fruit and chile sauce) and a beetroot reduction, wild mushroom chileatole soup with cacahuazintle (a traditional corn variety) and beans, and ice cream made with honey from stingless melipona bees, served with papaya and lavender marmalade.

The tasting menu costs around 4,900 pesos (US $233) featuring four pairing options that include wines from around the world, Mexican wines, a selection of terroir-driven wines and rare finds, and a non-alcoholic option.

It also features a cocktail menu incorporating Mexican ingredients.

The recognition from 50 Best adds to Quintonil’s list of accolades, which includes two Michelin stars, a distinction it shares with only one other restaurant in Mexico: Pujol, also located in Mexico City.

With reports from El País

World.title: Mexico City ponders 9-year prison terms for poisoners of animals in publc spaces
World.content:
Mexico City lawmakers are seeking tougher penalties for poisoning animals — including up to nine years in prison under one proposal — after four dogs were recently killed by toxic meat allegedly placed as bait in the Condesa neighborhood.

Labor Party lawmaker Diana Barragán introduced the measure Thursday, seeking to explicitly recognize poisoning as a serious form of animal abuse under the capital’s penal code.

The push follows criminal proceedings against Salvador “N,” who is accused of leaving poisoned pieces of sausage and other meat in and around the capital’s Parque España.

The 58-year-old was arrested near the park around 6:20 a.m. Oct. 30 and formally charged the following day. A judge ordered him held pending trial on animal abuse and cruelty charges.

Barragán’s proposal would allow sentences of up to five years when poisoning injures an animal and three to nine years when it causes death, according to the text posted on the Mexico City Congress website.

The measure would explicitly add poisoning as an aggravating circumstance, increasing existing penalties rather than creating a separate offense. It would cover toxic substances, contaminated food and other chemical or biological agents.

Barragán argued that existing provisions leave legal gaps by not explicitly addressing poisoning. She also warned that toxic bait in parks, gardens and sidewalks endangers children, families and other passersby.

Two other initiatives introduced Wednesday would strengthen penalties and restrict convicted abusers’ access to animals.

Citizens’ Movement (MC) lawmaker Luisa Fernanda Ledesma Alpízar proposed increasing prison terms and fines by up to two-thirds for placing multiple poisoned baits or committing repeated attacks.

In addition, judges could temporarily bar convicted offenders from acquiring, adopting or caring for animals after release. Restrictions would be recorded in an animal abuser registry that shelters and other organizations could consult.

Separately, Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) lawmaker Tania Nanette Larios Pérez proposed four to eight years in prison for killing animals or endangering their lives or health through poison, harmful chemicals, concealed sharp objects or adulterated bait.

The local proposals — which now await committee review — follow a separate animal welfare initiative, known as the “Pay de Limón” bill, that activists presented to the Mexican Senate last year.

As for Salvador’s case, the judge gave investigators two months to complete their investigation. He remains at Mexico City’s North Prison and has not been convicted.

Prosecutors allege he left contaminated food in Parque España and nearby streets from Oct. 26 through 28. Pills containing methomyl, a highly toxic insecticide, were allegedly concealed inside meat and sausages.

Police initially detained Salvador for resisting arrest. They had stopped him because he resembled someone shown in images circulated on social media, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors had received seven complaints from owners of affected animals. Four dogs died, while three others remained under treatment, the newspaper El Heraldo de México reported Thursday, citing senior prosecutor Jorge Emilio Iruegas Álvarez.

Authorities previously recovered 14 pieces of suspected poisoned meat in Parque España and surrounding streets.

Prosecutors were also examining whether the bait endangered park visitors, including children, and could warrant additional charges, Iruegas said.

Investigators were still examining Salvador’s reported claim that he had acted in retaliation for an alleged dog attack on his son.

With reports from El Sol de México, El Heraldo de México, El Informador and Excélsior

World.title: Meta launches its Muse AI agent in Mexico, a first for the Latin American market
World.content:
Muse, Meta’s artificial intelligence (AI) agent, has arrived in Mexico, the first country in Latin America to receive it.

In a LinkedIn post, Meta México Country Manager Marco Casarin explained what its AI agent can provide users:

“It doesn’t just answer questions: you tell it what you want to achieve, it figures out how to do it, creates the plan, and moves forward on its own. It takes tasks off your plate, accompanies you, organizes you, and keeps you focused.”

🚨 MUSE LAUNCH ALERT 🚨 muse just touched down in mexico 🇲🇽

órale, ya llegó 🌮 https://t.co/Z1dZMx8yvj — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) November 5, 2026

And just what is an AI agent?

According to SAS, a global software company, AI agents are “systems powered by AI that perform complex tasks or make informed decisions with varying human involvement.”

AI agents “surpass traditional chatbots and large language models by integrating data and advanced analytics tools to be more adaptable and capable of complex reasoning across industries.”

Casarin said that Muse can connect to your email, calendar, messages and Instagram, describing its ability to connect to other apps and services, always under the user’s control, as one of its standout features.

The first Muse connectors in Mexico will be in the retail, credit and lending categories, as well as in the travel, car rental, entertainment and food delivery industries. Some of the brands mentioned by Casarin are: Cinépolis, Coppel, Despegar, Kavak, Liverpool and Rappi.

Users will be able to access the products and services of these brands, “allowing you to buy movie tickets, find your next car, plan your holiday trip, and find the best deals for everyday purchases,” Casarin wrote. “No more jumping from app to app, no more opening 10 tabs. Decide your goal, ask Muse for it, and enjoy.”

Equally important, according to Casarin, is that the user is always in control. “You decide what it can access,” he said. “You authorize every action before it happens, and you see everything it does and everything it plans to do.”

In Mexico, Muse is already available in Spanish for users over 18 years old through iOS, Android, and muse.ai. it will soon be compatible with AI glasses, and you’ll even be able to interact with Muse via WhatsApp.

Fair warning: The convenience of an AI agent comes with the price of sharing more details about your life and, once AI agents obtain users’ information, there’s no taking back the data shared.

And as Fast Company magazine points out, Meta’s controversial history with user data makes its promises about privacy a hard sell.

With reports from El Universal, Milenio and Infobae

World.title: Detained Mexican judge faces extradition to US over $2 million bribe to free alleged Canadian drug trafficker
World.content:
District Judge Luis Benítez Alcántara, arrested in Colombia on Nov. 1 on charges of accepting a US $2 million bribe from drug traffickers, could face up to 15 years in prison for each of the nine charges the United States seeks to bring against him.

Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, is accused of taking the bribe to release a suspected drug trafficker who was facing charges in an investigation into a billion-dollar drug trafficking ring, U.S. officials said Thursday.

Benítez is the first Mexican federal judge indicted by the United States, which has already requested his extradition from Colombia to face charges in the U.S.

“Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States,” U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

The bribery case in question involved Andrew Clark, 36, a Canadian drug trafficker and second-in-command to Ryan James Wedding, 44, a former Olympic snowboarder for Canada who led one of the biggest, most notorious and violent transnational criminal organizations.

Clark was arrested in Mexico in October 2024 on U.S. drug trafficking, murder and attempted murder charges in which Wedding was also named. U.S. officials formally requested his extradition in November 2024.

Benítez was presiding over the extradition proceedings when — after accepting the US $2 million bribe payment — he issued rulings that directly facilitated Clark’s release from custody in February 2025, according to U.S. officials.

Clark was re-arrested days later and subsequently extradited to the U.S. where he faces nine charges of distributing and possessing cocaine, methamphetamine, engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise, homicide related to a criminal enterprise, attempted homicide related to a criminal enterprise, and drug trafficking offenses.

Since Benítez accepted money in exchange for releasing Clark, he is considered an accomplice.

As a result, the judge faces a nine-count U.S. grand jury indictment charging him with being an accessory after the fact. The U.S. Department of Justice also accuses him of being an accomplice in drug trafficking and homicide.

If convicted, Benítez would face a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison on each count.

“Mr. Benítez will be held accountable,” Blanche said. “The Department of Justice will continue to identify and dismantle transnational criminal organizations that threaten the security of the American people.”

The judge had a career spanning more than two decades within Mexico’s Federal Judiciary, but his record of decisions is tainted. For example, he released the only defendant in the Pegasus spying case against journalists.

The arrest of Benítez is the latest chapter in the U.S. investigation into the multinational drug trafficking network allegedly run by Wedding, who was apprehended in Mexico earlier this year. He was then flown to California, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and drug charges.

In a related incident, Édgar Aarón Vázquez, the leader of the New Empire Cartel and accused by the U.S. of protecting Wedding in Mexico, was killed on Thursday during a confrontation with police in the State of Mexico.

Vázquez is also believed to have been the intellectual author of the July 2024 murder of Milton Morales, a top Mexico City security official.

With reports by The Associated Press, Reuters, Proceso and Reforma

World.title: Guyana Opposition Presses Oil Budget on Food
World.content:
File photo, February 2015. Central Georgetown and the Demerara River waterfront, Guyana, seen from the air. Photo: amanderson2, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

GUYANA · ECONOMY

Published Saturday, 7 November, 1:30 p.m. ET · Source: Guyana Bureau of Statistics, statements by opposition MPs

An opposition lawmaker says Guyana’s record oil-funded budgets are not lowering what households pay for food, transport and electricity. Sharma Solomon, who speaks for the opposition APNU coalition on natural resources, demands proof that the spending has cut food prices.

Official data show food prices 3.8% higher in September than a year earlier. The opposition cites projected oil revenue of about US$6.5 billion this year.

Key Facts The claim MP Sharma Solomon says record oil budgets have not eased grocery, transport or power costs.

The data Georgetown food prices were 3.8% higher in September than a year earlier.

Inflation Overall prices rose 3.4% in 12 months; transport and communication rose 4.2%.

The ask Solomon wants the government to publish how much food prices have fallen.

What the Opposition Says

Sharma Solomon, an opposition member of parliament for the APNU coalition (A Partnership for National Unity), says the government’s record oil-funded budgets have not eased the cost of living. He says the average working-class Guyanese cannot pay a grocery bill with talk of economic growth.

He asks the government to explain why food prices stay high despite the spending, and to say by how much they have fallen. He also asks what share of oil revenue is committed to a long-term programme to cut food costs.

Solomon says the government points to a G$100,000 cash grant (Guyanese dollars, about US$480), farm subsidies, removed taxes and stable electricity tariffs. He argues that production has not risen and that savings from tax relief do not reach households.

File photo: a street market in Georgetown, Guyana.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Official Price Data Show

Guyana’s Bureau of Statistics reports that prices in Georgetown were 3.4% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier. Food prices were 3.8% higher, and transport and communication costs 4.2% higher.

The same release shows food prices down 0.3% from August. They remain 3.8% above last year’s level.

The Oil Money Behind the Debate

Guyana’s oil comes from offshore fields run by a consortium led by ExxonMobil, the US oil major. Solomon says output averages about one million barrels a day and cites projected oil revenue of about US$6.5 billion this year.

The 2026 budget is G$1.558 trillion, about US$7.5 billion at the Bank of Guyana’s official rate of about G$208.5 per US$. The government presented it in January and parliament passed it in February.

In Plain English APNU is one of Guyana’s opposition groups, and the governing party is the PPP/C led by President Irfaan Ali. The Bureau of Statistics measures prices in the capital, Georgetown, and the cash grant is a one-off payment to adults.

What It Means for You

For investors in US-listed oil companies, Guyana is a major source of production growth. Public debate over who benefits can shape future contract and tax terms.

Readers who track Guyana can follow the Bureau of Statistics’ monthly price index for Georgetown. Dollar figures in this article use the Bank of Guyana’s official rate of about G$208.5 per US$.

What Is Not Known

Solomon cites a 6.7% rise in food prices from the government’s mid-year report, a figure we could not reconcile with the Bureau’s 3.8% for September. We also found no official electricity or transport tariff data to test his claims on those costs.

We have not seen the government answer his questions in public. We will update this article if it does.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the Guyana opposition say?

How fast are prices rising in Guyana?

The Bureau of Statistics says Georgetown prices rose 3.4% in the year to September, with food up 3.8% and transport and communication up 4.2%.

File photo. The command building of the Metropolitan Police of Bogotá, Colombia, December 2017. Photo: EEIM, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Published Saturday, 7 November, 1:25 p.m. ET · Source: Indepaz, Toro municipal government, Valle del Cauca police commander

Three women were found dead inside a home in Toro, a town in the Valle del Cauca department of southwest Colombia, on Friday 6 November. Armed men attacked them, local authorities say.

Indepaz, a Colombian research group that tracks killings of this kind, counted it as the 104th massacre of 2026. It came less than 24 hours after another attack in the same town that killed two people.

What We Know

Three women were found dead inside a home in Toro on Friday 6 November after armed men attacked them. Local authorities are investigating.

Preliminary information indicates that the three belonged to one family. Police have not said how many attackers took part, how they got in or why they came.

Hours earlier, on Thursday 5 November, two people were killed and a third wounded in an attack on the road to Toro. It is not confirmed whether the two events are linked.

The Official Response

Local authorities held an extraordinary security council with the police, the army and the municipal government after the killing. Colonel Amaury Aguilera, commander of the Valle del Cauca police department, said a special team of investigators has been assigned.

Toro’s mayor, Jhon Fredy Valencia, announced a reward of up to 10 million Colombian pesos (about US$3,100) for information leading to those responsible. Toro has had five people killed in less than 24 hours.

Why Indepaz Counts This as a Massacre

Indepaz, the Institute of Studies for Development and Peace, a Colombian research group, records any killing of three or more people in one attack as a massacre. It listed this case as the 104th massacre in Colombia in 2026.

The institute says Toro faces risk from disputes over territorial control and illegal economies, including drug trafficking and street-level drug sales. It names the Adán Izquierdo front of the Isaías Pardo bloc, a dissident armed group, as well as Los Flacos and local gangs as present in the area.

What It Means for You

Valle del Cauca is the department of Cali, one of Colombia’s largest cities, in the southwest of the country. Travellers should check their government’s travel advice before visiting rural areas.

Indepaz’s running count of massacres is one gauge of violence in Colombia. The institute lists drug trafficking among the disputes behind the risk in Toro.

What Is Not Known

Police have not announced a motive, a suspect or the number of attackers. They have also not confirmed whether the attack was linked to the one on Thursday.

Police have not confirmed how the victims were related. We will update this article when prosecutors release findings.

World.title: Venezuela Quake Victims Blocked From Loans
World.content:
A shopping street in the Sabana Grande area of Caracas at night, in an undated photo. It does not show the October price data. Photo: QuinteroP / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

VENEZUELA · QUAKE RECOVERY

Published Saturday, 7 November, 1:10 p.m. ET · Source: Presidential Habitability Commission database, Venezuela’s Economy and Finance Ministry, statements by residents

Venezuelans who lost their homes in the June earthquakes say a faulty QR code is blocking the state-backed loans meant to rehouse them. The code, issued after building inspections, is meant to prove a home collapsed, and banks require that proof.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Latin America story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Owners from 38 housing complexes say the code shows wrong names, wrong addresses or the wrong damage level. Their home loans, part of the government’s “Venezuela Renace” plan, stall as a result.

Key Facts The problem Quake victims say their QR records show wrong names, addresses or damage levels.

The scale Owners from 38 complexes report errors; a news outlet counted at least 118 buildings affected.

The stakes Banks require proof that a home collapsed before they approve a Venezuela Renace loan.

The loan The state pays 80% of homes up to US$70,000 and 50% from US$70,000 to US$100,000.

Power Index Venezuela ranks 12th of 14 in Venezuela ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 29.4 points (November 2026 edition).

How the Code Blocks Credit

The Presidential Habitability Commission, the body that inspected buildings after the quakes, records each building’s label in a QR code that banks read. To qualify, an owner needs proof that the home collapsed, and the code is meant to carry it.

Raquel Herrera told reporters she lost her husband and sister when her building near Puerto Viejo, in La Guaira state, fell. She says the code lists her building under a different name and in another parish, so her documents do not match and her loan file stalls.

File photo: the skyline of Caracas with the Ávila mountain behind it.

One Building, Two Labels

Owners of Abejita II, an apartment building in Caraballeda, a coastal town in La Guaira state, say a first inspection classed it as collapsed. A second inspection kept a red label, but they say the code now records only light damage.

Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Without a collapse record, they say, they cannot apply for the credit, and the building is unsafe to return to. Residents of other buildings on the coast describe the same limbo and ask for new inspections.

How Many Are Affected

Owners from 38 residential complexes told a Venezuelan news outlet that the code shows duplicated entries, wrong addresses or labels that do not match the building. The outlet’s review counted at least 118 buildings on the central coast with conflicting records.

The same outlet’s reading of the commission’s online database put the total at 999 collapsed buildings in La Guaira state as of 3 November. The database also includes houses, shops and public buildings, so it is not a count of apartment blocks.

Similar complaints appeared earlier. A regional radio station reported in September about wrong QR records and system failures at Banavih, the state housing bank.

What the Credit Offers

Venezuela’s Economy and Finance Ministry named three state banks first to take applications under the “Venezuela Renace” plan: Banco de Venezuela, Banco Digital de los Trabajadores (a state bank for workers) and Banco del Tesoro. It said more banks would join, and that banks must answer within five working days.

For homes priced up to US$70,000 the state pays 80% and the buyer finances the rest. For homes from US$70,000 to US$100,000 the state pays 50%, and the loan term is up to 25 years.

What It Means for You

For aid groups, insurers and investors tracking Venezuela’s reconstruction, the flaw shows that money can be ready while paperwork is not. The loan requires a certificate that the building collapsed.

Owners can look up whether their building is listed as collapsed in the commission’s public database before they visit a bank. The database is open to the public at habitable.gob.ve.

What Is Not Known

We have not seen the commission publish how many records it has corrected or a date for new inspections. We also do not know whether the errors come from the census, the inspections or the database.

We have not seen the government say whether it will relax the collapse-certificate rule. We will update this article when officials respond.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Venezuela Renace plan?

It is a state programme that helps families who lost their homes in the 24 June earthquakes buy a new home. Public banks take applications and the state subsidises the price.

What goes wrong with the QR code?

Owners say it shows duplicated entries, wrong building names or addresses, or the wrong damage level. Banks then reject loan files because the code and the documents disagree.

How big is the housing loss?

A news outlet’s reading of the commission’s database put the total at 999 collapsed buildings in La Guaira state on 3 November. It includes houses, shops and public buildings.

World.title: Brazil Rate-Cut Plan Draws Currency Warning
World.content:
File photo. The Palácio do Planalto, the presidential office in Brasília, 2020. Photo: Senado Federal, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Published Saturday, 7 November, 1:05 p.m. ET · Source: Banco Central do Brasil (Brazil’s central bank), public statements by the economists

A Brazilian economist has warned that cutting the benchmark interest rate in half could push the real into a currency crisis. Paulo Gala, an economist and professor at the Getúlio Vargas Foundation (FGV), a leading Brazilian university and think tank, made the case in a video summarised on Saturday 7 November.

He answers André Lara Resende, a former central bank director and one of the designers of the 1994 Real Plan, which ended Brazil’s hyperinflation. Gala agrees with the goal of a lower rate but not with the method.

Key Facts The rate The central bank’s rate committee, Copom, held the Selic, Brazil’s benchmark rate, at 13.75% on 4 November.

The plan Lara Resende proposes cutting the rate roughly in half, to about 7% to 7.5%.

The warning Gala says capital flight could drain reserves, now US$367.9 billion, within weeks.

The bill Gala puts annual interest costs near R$1 trillion (about US$182 billion), almost 10% of GDP.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 74.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction platform, gives 88.5% to no Selic change in December (7 November, 12:35 p.m. ET).

Where the Rate Stands

Brazil’s central bank held its benchmark rate, the Selic, at 13.75% on Wednesday 4 November. The decision by its rate-setting committee, known as Copom, was unanimous and ended a run of five cuts.

The Selic therefore stands at 13.75%. Gala’s example starts from 14%, a slightly older level.

The Plan Gala Is Answering

André Lara Resende, a former central bank director, has proposed cutting the Selic by roughly half, to about 7% to 7.5%, on a gradual path. He argues that Brazil’s foreign-currency reserves are large enough to cushion any fall of the real along the way.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The central bank reported reserves of US$367.9 billion on 5 November. Our earlier articles covered the idea and reactions among President Lula’s allies.

Why Gala Says a Forced Cut Backfires

Gala argues that Brazil pays about R$1 trillion a year in interest on its public debt (about US$182 billion at R$5.50 per US$), nearly 10% of the economy. By comparison, he says, the primary deficit, which excludes interest, has ranged between R$50 billion and R$100 billion (about US$9 billion to US$18 billion).

Almost R$5 trillion (about US$907 billion) of domestic debt falls due within twelve months, he says, so the state depends on investors renewing it willingly. If the government forces yields down and investors judge the risk too high, he warns, they would sell and buy dollars.

He argues that heavy daily currency trading means a defence of the real could burn through reserves in weeks. A weaker real would then raise the cost of fuel, food and other inputs.

What Gala Proposes Instead

Gala shares the goal of a lower Selic and says nobody disputes it. His answer is fiscal moderation, not the austerity of Joaquim Levy, Brazil’s finance minister in 2015, or of Argentina’s president Javier Milei.

“Nobody here is defending a squeeze on the population,” Gala says. He calls instead for “fiscal moderation and strategic intelligence.”

What Prediction Markets Say

Bettors see no immediate change. Polymarket, a prediction platform, gives 88.5% to no change in Brazil’s rate at the December meeting, with US$64,048 traded, and a 5.7% chance of a quarter-point cut (7 November, 12:35 p.m. ET).

For the January meeting the same platform gives 58.0% to no change and 16.7% to a quarter-point cut, with US$13,017 traded. The March market gives 57.5% to no change, with US$10,457 traded.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

Nothing in the central bank’s 4 November decision adopts the plan, so holders of Brazilian bonds and the real face no new rule today. Finance Minister Dario Durigan has said the government is not studying a rate cut by decree.

The next official signal is the Copom minutes, due on Tuesday 10 November, which will show how the committee weighed the pause. The central bank’s reference rate for the real was R$5.50 per US$ on Friday 6 November.

What Is Not Known

We could not open Gala’s video itself, so his figures come from a summary of it and are his claims, not verified data. We have not seen the government or the central bank adopt Lara Resende’s plan.

More: Brazil news in English; Brazil Rate Cap Idea Wins Some Lula Allies; Brazil Denies Plan to Cap Interest Rates.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Selic?

The Selic is Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, set by the central bank’s committee, Copom. It stands at 13.75% after the 4 November meeting.

What does André Lara Resende propose?

He proposes lowering the Selic gradually by roughly half, to about 7% to 7.5%, and using foreign-currency reserves to cushion any fall of the real.

Why does Paulo Gala object?

Gala argues that forcing rates down would make investors sell government debt and buy dollars. He warns that this could drain the central bank’s reserves in weeks.

World.title: Democratic Win Hits Oil and Defence Stocks
World.content:
MARKETS · US MIDTERMS

Published Saturday, 7 November, 1:00 p.m. ET · Source: closing prices of the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, 3 to 6 November 2026

Wall Street had a rough week after Democrats won Congress. Between the close on election day, Tuesday 3 November, and the close on Friday 6 November, defence, oil and artificial-intelligence stocks fell while hospital operators rose.

The biggest losers outside the United States were Latin American oil companies listed in New York. Petrobras fell 12.1% and Argentina’s YPF 13.7%.

Key Facts Defence US defence contractors fell: Lockheed Martin 11.3%, RTX 7.0%, General Dynamics 5.5%, Northrop Grumman 4.6%.

Energy US oil major Exxon fell 6.5%; Brazil’s Petrobras lost 12.1% and Argentina’s YPF 13.7%.

Market A fund tracking the S&P 500, the main US stock index, fell 2.5%.

Basis Changes compare closing prices on Tuesday 3 and Friday 6 November 2026.

Defence and Oil Take the Hit

Lockheed Martin fell 11.3%, RTX (a US missile and jet-engine maker) 7.0%, General Dynamics 5.5% and Northrop Grumman 4.6% between the close on election day and the close on Friday. Exxon Mobil lost 6.5% and the refiner Phillips 66 lost 9.6%.

One reading is that investors expect a Democratic Congress to spend less on the military and to press for lower energy prices. That is a market judgment, not a statement from any company, and the wider market also fell over the same three sessions.

Archive photo: traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.

Latin American Oil Shares Fell Harder

Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, fell 12.1% in New York trading, from US$21.08 to US$18.53 a share. YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil company, fell 13.7%, from US$44.81 to US$38.66.

Ecopetrol, Colombia’s state-controlled oil company, fell 6.0%, from US$16.54 to US$15.55. A fund that tracks US energy companies fell 7.6%, so Petrobras and YPF fell by more than the US sector.

Vale, Brazil’s iron-ore miner, moved the other way and rose 5.6%, from US$10.98 to US$11.59. We have no evidence of why, and the gap shows the oil moves were not a general sell-off of Latin American shares.

Tech Stocks Slide

Nvidia, the leading maker of artificial-intelligence chips, fell 9.7%, and Tesla fell 10.1%. Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns the social network Truth Social, lost 32.9%, from US$5.95 to US$3.99.

No company has tied its decline to the election. The wider market also fell over the same days, as the S&P 500 fund’s loss shows.

Hospitals and Homebuilders Gain

HCA Healthcare rose 6.9%, Tenet Healthcare 6.2% and Universal Health Services 10.4%. Investors appear to bet that a Democratic Congress will restore or expand funding for programmes such as Medicaid, the public health insurance for low-income Americans.

An exchange-traded fund that holds US homebuilders, which tracks companies exposed to housing, rose 3.2%. A fund that tracks the S&P 500, the main index of large US companies, fell 2.5% over the same three sessions.

What It Means for You

Investors who hold Latin American oil shares through US-listed receipts, known as ADRs, saw the sharpest losses of the week. The move shows how closely these shares follow US politics and energy prices.

The next test is the US inflation report for October, scheduled for Tuesday 10 November at 8:30 a.m. ET. Our reports cover the political side, including what the midterms mean for Argentina’s debt and what comes next in Washington.

What Is Not Known

No company has tied its share price to the election, so every explanation here is an interpretation. It is also unclear how much of the fall will last once the new Congress takes office and sets its agenda.

Which stocks fell after the Democratic win?

Between 3 and 6 November, Lockheed Martin fell 11.3%, Exxon Mobil 6.5%, Nvidia 9.7% and Tesla 10.1%. Petrobras and YPF fell 12.1% and 13.7%.

Which stocks rose?

Hospital operators rose: HCA 6.9%, Tenet 6.2% and Universal Health Services 10.4%. A homebuilder fund also rose 3.2%.

Did the election cause the moves?

No company has said so, and the wider market also fell over the same days. Investors’ expectations about a Democratic Congress are one plausible reason.

World.title: Gunman Kills 6 in Kraków’s Main Square
World.content:
Europe Intelligence Brief — Monday, June 8, 2026.

POLAND · SECURITY

Published Saturday, 7 November, 1:00 p.m. ET · Source: Małopolska Police, Poland’s Interior Ministry, Prime Minister’s Office

A gunman drove a car into Kraków’s Main Square on Saturday afternoon and fired on people at random, Polish police say. Six people have died and more than a dozen are wounded.

Police shot the suspect, a Polish citizen, and he is in hospital. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the shooting an attack.

Key Facts What A gunman fired on people in Kraków’s Main Square at about 3 p.m. (9 a.m. ET).

Toll Police say six people are dead, four women and two men, and more than a dozen are wounded.

Suspect A Polish citizen in his twenties was shot by police, detained and taken to hospital.

Police Two officers are wounded, one in very serious condition, Poland’s Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński says.

As of 7 November, about 6:30 p.m. Kraków time (12:30 p.m. ET)

What Happened on Saturday

Police in the Małopolska region around Kraków say a man drove a car into the Main Square at about 3 p.m. and began shooting at random people. Officers shot him and detained him at the junction of Stradomska and Dietla streets.

A police spokeswoman said the suspect fired a military-type long gun and wore camouflage and a bulletproof vest. Police have not said how many shots were fired or how long the attack lasted.

Poland’s Interior Minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said two police officers were wounded. One has a gunshot wound, and the other is in very serious condition after being hit three times.

Police also dismissed unverified reports that two attackers were involved. At this point the only known suspect is the man in custody.

In Plain English Rynek Główny, the Main Market Square, is the medieval heart of Kraków and one of the largest town squares in Europe. Małopolska is the Polish province around the city, and its police lead the response.

File photo: the Warsaw skyline with the Palace of Culture and Science, in Poland’s capital.

The Toll Rose Through the Afternoon

Police first reported five dead and more than a dozen wounded. Later in the evening they said a sixth victim had died: four women and two men.

Poland’s Response

Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the shooting an attack and said police are examining its background and every circumstance. He praised the officers who stopped the gunman and appealed to politicians of all parties not to play politics with the tragedy.

Bartosz Grodecki, head of the National Security Bureau, the presidential security office, was due in Kraków as security chiefs met. We will add further official statements as they come.

What It Means for Travellers and US Readers

Kraków is a popular stop for visitors from the United States and across Europe, and the square was busy on a Saturday afternoon. Anyone in the city should follow instructions from Polish police and rely on official channels for updates.

Travellers with plans to visit Kraków should check the travel advice of their own government before they go. Poland is a member of NATO and the European Union.

What Is Not Known

Police have not named the suspect or announced a motive, and it is not yet clear whether he acted alone. The final death toll may still change, because it rose from five to six within hours.

The nationalities of the dead and the wounded have not been published, and officials have not said how the gunman obtained his weapon. We will rewrite this article as officials confirm more.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Kraków?

On Saturday 7 November at about 3 p.m., a man drove a car into Kraków’s Main Square and shot at people, police say. Officers shot and detained him.

How many people died?

Police said later on Saturday that six people had died, four women and two men, and more than a dozen were wounded. The toll rose from five earlier in the afternoon.

Is it safe to visit Kraków?

Police have detained the only known suspect. Travellers should follow police instructions and check their own government’s travel advice.

World.title: Ghana Central Bank Says Gold Loss Is Paper
World.content:
Office towers and traffic at a junction in Accra, the capital of Ghana. photo. Office towers and traffic in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Photo: Synth85, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

GHANA · CENTRAL BANK

Ghana’s central bank told Parliament that a loss of GH¢17.5 billion (about US$1.5 billion at today’s rate) on its gold-buying programme is an accounting entry, not cash that left the country, according to press reports of the hearing. Paul Bleboo, the Bank of Ghana’s head of gold management, told a committee of Ghana’s Parliament that oversees economic policy on Friday 6 November 2026 that the rise of the cedi, Ghana’s currency, in 2025 created the gap.

For anyone holding Ghanaian debt or trading the cedi, the question is how much of that cost is real. The bank’s audited accounts show a separate, net figure for gold deals.

Key Facts — What At a parliamentary hearing the bank called a GH¢17.5 billion (about US$1.5 billion at today’s rate) gold shortfall an accounting loss.

— Why The cedi rose 40.7% against the US dollar in 2025; the bank links the gold loss to that rise.

— Audited The 2025 accounts show a separate GH¢9.05 billion (about US$780 million at today’s rate) net loss on gold deals.

— Open The audited accounts carry no GH¢17.5 billion gold line, and the Governor’s written statement omits it.

— Next The bank’s rate-setting panel meets 16 to 18 November; the rate stood at 14.0% in September.

What the Bank of Ghana Told Parliament

Mr Bleboo said gold is bought locally at the market exchange rate but recorded at the bank’s own, lower rate. He called the result “an accounting loss and not a real loss” that covers “a chunk of the total cost” of the 2025 programme.

As an illustration, he described gold bought when a dollar costs about GH¢15 and converted after the cedi has moved to about GH¢12. He presented this as a hypothetical, not as a named deal.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Audited Accounts Show

The bank’s audited 2025 accounts record a net loss on gold deals of GH¢9.05 billion (about US$780 million at today’s rate). Of that, GH¢8.85 billion came from Gold for Reserves, the programme that buys gold to turn it into foreign currency, and a net GH¢203 million from Gold for Oil, a scheme that sold gold to help pay for fuel imports and ended in March 2025.

In 2025 the bank bought 2,914,305 fine ounces (a standard gold weight) of doré gold, which is unrefined gold bars, and sold 2,895,426 ounces. The annual report says the gold is sold within the shortest possible time and is not held for price gains.

Note 13 of the annual report says the Gold for Reserves figure includes GH¢7.99 billion (about US$690 million) of realised fair-value gains moved over from other comprehensive income, a line for value changes that skip the profit statement. Other comprehensive income as a whole shows a GH¢19.32 billion (about US$1.66 billion) loss, and the bank’s loss for the year was GH¢15.63 billion (about US$1.34 billion).

Central Accra seen from above, with an office tower on the skyline.

How the Cedi’s Rise Enters the Story

The Governor of the Bank of Ghana, Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, told the same committee that the cedi gained 40.7% against the dollar in 2025, though his written statement does not link the rise to gold losses. On the bank’s account, when the cedi rises, a dollar from a gold sale is worth fewer cedis than the cedis the bank paid miners for the gold.

Mahamudu Bawumia, Ghana’s former vice-president, and other opposition leaders say the programme cost the bank about US$1.7 billion, citing the International Monetary Fund (IMF) 2025 assessment. We covered that claim and the call for an inquiry in our earlier report on the Ghana gold programme loss.

Who Pays From Here

Dr Asiama said moving the cost of domestic gold purchases to the Ghana Gold Board, known as GoldBod, the state gold buyer, should ease the burden on the bank’s balance sheet. The row over GoldBod’s leadership is covered in our report on the opposition’s call for its chief to go.

The cedi has since fallen 7.9% in the first half of 2026 and 9.5% by 18 September, the Governor said. See our report on Ghana’s 6% growth and its reserves and the cedi’s gains on gold sales.

What It Means for You

For holders of Ghanaian bonds or cedi exposure, the audited accounts, not the hearing, are the numbers to anchor on. The Monetary Policy Committee, the bank’s rate-setting panel, meets from 16 to 18 November, after holding the rate at 14.0% in May, July and September.

What Is Not Known

The GH¢17.5 billion figure comes from the hearing; it is not in the Governor’s written statement or the annual report, so how it relates to the GH¢9.05 billion net loss is open. Mr Bleboo described it as “a chunk” of the total cost, so the full cost of the programme is also open.

It is also unsettled how much of the exchange-rate cost the public ultimately bears, a point opposition leaders dispute. Further figures may come from the bank or from any parliamentary inquiry.

Sources: Bank of Ghana, Governor’s statement to Parliament’s Committee on Economy and Development, 6 November 2026; Bank of Ghana, 2025 Annual Report and Financial Statements; committee hearing of 6 November 2026. US$ conversions at GH¢11.65 per dollar, the market close of 6 November 2026, applied to all 2025 figures. More Ghana news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Ghana’s central bank lose money on gold?

Its audited 2025 accounts show a net loss of GH¢9.05 billion (about US$780 million) on gold deals. The bank told Parliament the larger GH¢17.5 billion (about US$1.5 billion at today’s rate) figure is a book loss caused by exchange rates, not cash that left Ghana.

What is a book loss?

A book loss is a drop in value that appears in the accounts without money physically leaving. Here it comes from recording the gold at the bank’s own lower rate rather than the higher market rate paid for it.

Does the opposition accept that explanation?

No. Opposition leaders, citing the International Monetary Fund’s 2025 assessment, say the programme cost the bank about US$1.7 billion.
