World.title: Red Tide Spreads in Costa Rica’s Gulf of Nicoya and Cooking Won’t Make Shellfish Safe
World.content:
If you plan to order oysters, mussels or pianguas anywhere around the Gulf of Nicoya, ask where they came from first. Costa Rica’s National Animal Health Service (SENASA) has widened the zones where selling and eating these shellfish is banned because of a toxic red tide. The new restrictions cover shellfish harvested on the western shore of the gulf between Playa Blanca and Punta Curú.

They also cover the coastal strip from the mouth of the Jesús María River to the sugar dock at Punta Morales. This is not a new alert. Red tide restrictions have been in place in the gulf since June 12, according to researchers at the National University (UNA), and the restricted zones have grown as lab tests find toxins at new points.

SENASA based this latest expansion on the recommendation of an interagency commission that includes UNA’s Marine Phytoplankton Laboratory. The ban applies to bivalves, the two-shelled mollusks such as oysters, mussels and pianguas. They feed by filtering seawater, so when toxic algae bloom, the toxins build up in their flesh.

The hard part is that you cannot tell a contaminated shellfish from a safe one. UNA specialists say the toxins do not change how the shellfish look, smell or taste. Cooking does not destroy them either, so a well-cooked plate is no safer than a raw one. The algae involved can produce paralytic, diarrheic, amnesic and neurotoxic toxins, according to UNA. The species identified as the source of the paralytic toxins in the gulf is Pyrodinium bahamense.

SENASA has warned in earlier advisories that eating contaminated bivalves can cause anything from digestive problems to neurological effects and, in severe cases, death. If you feel tingling or numbness around your mouth, nausea or dizziness after eating shellfish, get medical care right away and tell the doctor what you ate.

UNA experts say the current event may be linked to El Niño. Warmer seas and a more layered, stratified water column can favor the growth of Pyrodinium bahamense. The species also has a dormant stage in seabed sediments that works like a bank of seeds. Those cysts need to be stirred back up by ocean processes tied to winds and tides before they germinate, and UNA says that part of the cycle still needs study.

The same warm-water conditions are already weighing on the gulf’s coastal communities, where El Niño has left fishermen with catches too small to pay for fuel. Until the restrictions lift, buy shellfish only from sellers who can tell you exactly where it was harvested. At restaurants and ceviche stands, ask about the source. If no one can give you a clear answer, skip the oysters, mussels and pianguas.

The measure covers bivalve mollusks only. Authorities continue to monitor the algal blooms and have redrawn the restricted zones each time new test results come in.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Grynspan Wins 12 of 15 Votes in Eighth UN Secretary-General Poll
World.content:
Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan widened her lead in the race to become the next UN secretary-general on Thursday, winning 12 “encourage” votes from the 15-member Security Council in its eighth informal straw poll, according to leaked results reported by the UN-focused news site PassBlue.

Grynspan also received three “discourage” votes. In the seventh poll on Oct. 30, she had 11 “encourage” and four “discourage” votes, so Thursday’s result added one supporter and removed one objection. Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, stayed in second place with nine “encourage,” four “discourage” and two “no opinion” votes, unchanged from the previous round. Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett received eight, five and two, cutting her “discourage” count from six.

The newest entrant, Türkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioğlu, secretary general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe and a former foreign minister, drew three “encourage,” eight “discourage” and four “no opinion” votes in his first poll. The United Arab Emirates’ Lana Nusseibeh received seven, six and two, according to the same tally.

Further back, Uganda’s Olara Otunnu received four “encourage” votes and Ecuador’s María Fernanda Espinosa three. Ivonne A-Baki, also from Ecuador, received one “encourage” vote against 14 “discourage.”

Council members again used ballots of the same color, which hides whether any “discourage” votes came from the five permanent members that hold a veto: the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom. PassBlue reported widespread speculation that the United States has consistently discouraged Grynspan and that Russia may have joined it this time.

The only color-coded poll so far, held Oct. 16, showed Grynspan, Grossi and Rodrigues Birkett each with two “discourage” votes from permanent members. An outside expert told PassBlue that China may be pushing to keep the polls undifferentiated to give the Latin American candidates more time to build support. To be recommended to the General Assembly, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favor in the Council and no veto from a permanent member. The 193-member General Assembly then makes the appointment.

Time is short since Secretary-General António Guterres’s second term ends Dec. 31 and the Council’s president for November, Latvian Ambassador Sanita Pavļuta-Deslandes, warned this week that the window to agree on a candidate is closing. No date has been set for the next straw poll, and it is not yet known whether it will be color-coded.

Sinirlioğlu was scheduled to hold a public dialogue with the General Assembly on Friday and an informal meeting with Council members on Monday. President Laura Fernández asked for support for Grynspan’s candidacy this week at the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid. Grynspan was Costa Rica’s second vice president from 1994 to 1998, led the Ibero-American General Secretariat from 2014 to 2021 and has headed UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) since 2021. Costa Rica formally nominated her on March 3.

If she is chosen, she would be the first woman to lead the United Nations since its founding in 1945, and the first Central American.

World.title: Five Costa Rica Regions on Yellow Alert as Saturday Rain Hits Soaked Ground
World.content:
If you live in or are traveling through the Central Valley, the Pacific coast or the Northern Zone, you are now under a yellow alert for rain. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) raised five regions from green to yellow yesterday, and the National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects another wet day today on ground that can barely take more water.

The regions on yellow alert are the North Pacific, Central Pacific, South Pacific, Central Valley and Huetar Norte, which covers the Northern Zone. The Caribbean stays on green. That is a step up from yesterday morning, when the whole country was still on green alert even as the chance of a tropical depression was fading.

Why the upgrade? It comes down to soil. CNE president Alejandro Picado said the low-pressure system off the Pacific coast kept pushing showers and storms ashore from Thursday night. Soils on the Pacific slope are now 80% to 95% saturated, according to the commission. When the ground is that full, rain runs straight into rivers, ditches and drains instead of soaking in.

The numbers from Thursday night into yesterday show how fast it adds up. The IMN recorded 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) across Guanacaste and Puntarenas in 12 hours. Hojancha took 111 mm (4.4 inches) and Barú 56 mm (2.2 inches). Yesterday morning, local emergency crews handled incidents in San Carlos, Fraijanes, Poás, Alajuela and Sarapiquí, mostly overflowing sewers. The CNE said no one had to be evacuated.

For today, the IMN said the low near the Pacific coasts of northern Costa Rica and Nicaragua will keep the atmosphere unstable. Expect rain from early morning along the Pacific coast. In the afternoon, showers and thunderstorms spread to several regions, including the Caribbean and the Northern Zone. The Central Valley should get scattered rain, with occasional thunder in the east.

Guanacaste is the area to watch this weekend. The IMN warned that rain along the Pacific coast can come in bursts of 30 to 60 mm (1.2 to 2.4 inches) within six hours, especially in the North Pacific. Isolated gusts can reach 80 km/h (50 mph), which is enough to bring down branches, signs and power lines.

It will stay cool in the capital. The IMN forecast a high of 24.7 C (76 F) and a low of 18.5 C (65 F) in San José today. Liberia should reach about 33 C (91 F), and Quepos about 28 C (82 F).

The storm system itself is weakening. In yesterday’s outlook, the U.S. National Hurricane Center cut the odds of a tropical depression to 30% over both the next 48 hours and the next seven days. That is down from 40% on Thursday night and from the 60% chance it carried earlier in the week. The center said conditions will turn increasingly hostile over the weekend, but warned the system can still bring heavy rain to parts of Central America.

So what should you do? Plan outdoor time for the morning, when storms have been weaker. Never drive or walk through a flooded street, river or ravine, because you cannot judge depth or current until you are in it. On mountain roads, slow down for fog, fallen trees and small landslides, which are more likely when hillsides are this wet.

On the coast, the risk is on the water too. The CNE asked small fishing boats and tourism operators to watch sea conditions closely. That follows several days of rough surf on the Pacific beaches. If a boat tour or surf lesson is in your plans, ask the operator about conditions before you go.

Yellow alert means local emergency committees are active and ready to respond, not that a disaster is under way. Forecasts for systems like this can change quickly, so anyone with weekend plans should check the latest IMN update before heading out and call 911 in an emergency.

World.title: Costa Rica Removes Don Pepe Figueres Monument After Protest Vandalism
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Culture and Youth removed the bronze monument to former President José Figueres Ferrer from San José’s Plaza de la Democracia on Friday morning, less than four weeks before the country marks the anniversary of the army abolition Figueres declared in 1948.

Culture Minister Jorge Rodríguez Vives ordered the temporary removal after the sculpture was defaced during demonstrations in recent weeks. A crew from the state power company CNFL lifted the figures by crane, and the pieces were taken to the National Museum’s José Fabio Góngora facility in Pavas, where specialists will clean and restore them.

Rodríguez described the decision as difficult but necessary to protect the ensemble from further damage. He acknowledged freedom of expression and peaceful protest as pillars of Costa Rican democracy but said exercising those rights cannot come at the expense of the nation’s heritage.

The minister said he expects those responsible to cover the cost of restoration, subject to the findings of the competent authorities, adding that damage to national heritage should not go without consequences. He also said the figures will not return to the plaza until there are guarantees they will not be vandalized again. The ministry characterized the removal as a temporary conservation measure, not a surrender of public space to vandalism.

The National Museum, which administers the plaza, has filed criminal complaints with the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and the San José prosecutor’s office. According to the museum’s preliminary technical assessment, the latest incident left graffiti, spray paint and scratches on the bronze figures themselves, whereas damage in October mainly affected the monument’s base.

The museum has warned it cannot guarantee a full return to the sculpture’s original condition, because the paint penetrated surfaces already worn by age. Specialists expect the work to take several weeks. Rodríguez put the cost of the initial cleaning alone at about 1 million colones (roughly $2,000). The ministry said the total cost will be determined once its technical and economic assessment is complete, and it has not announced a date for the monument’s return.

The damage occurred during protests against budget cuts to public education and university funding. The most recent incident followed a student demonstration in the plaza on the night of Monday, Nov. 2. María Ortega Zamora, president of the student federation at the State Distance University (UNED), said four hooded people dressed in black arrived around 1 a.m. and began defacing the monument. She denied that students were responsible.

The removal drew a sharp response from the National Liberation Party (PLN), which Figueres founded in 1951. Álvaro Ramírez, head of the PLN’s legislative caucus, likened the move to a dictator’s playbook, writing on social media that it erased memory, disrespected history and removed symbols of the country’s democracy.

Ramírez argued that a nation’s historical memory cannot be treated as an obstacle and that defending it is part of defending democracy. He said the PLN will demand that the restored statues be returned to the Plaza de la Democracia as testimony to Costa Rica’s history.

The dispute adds to tensions between President Laura Fernández’s administration and opposition parties, including the PLN, as the education budget protests continue. The ensemble, by Costa Rican sculptor Marisel Jiménez Rittner, was unveiled on April 28, 1998. Its four bronze elements depict Figueres, a girl with a violin symbolizing culture, a boy with a book representing education, and a sledgehammer recalling the abolition of the army.

This is not the first time the monument has left the plaza. It was moved to the National Museum’s gardens in 2008 during a renovation of the square, and its original sledgehammer had been stolen. After restoration by museum specialists and the sculptor, it was reinstalled in December 2016, when the space was renamed Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército.

The plaza sits beside the National Museum, the former Bellavista barracks where Figueres declared the army abolished on Dec. 1, 1948. Army Abolition Day commemorations have traditionally included a floral offering at the monument, and it remains unclear whether the figures will be back in place for this year’s ceremony.

Figueres, popularly known as Don Pepe, led Costa Rica three times and remains one of the defining figures of its modern history, closely tied to the institutions, social reforms and unarmed democracy that shaped the country’s identity.

World.title: A Proposed 15% Tax Would Reach Costa Rica Residents’ Foreign Dividends and Interest
World.content:
Costa Rica residents who earn interest, dividends, rent or capital gains outside the country would pay a 15% tax on that income under a bill the government has sent to the Legislative Assembly, a change tax specialists say would break with the country’s long-standing territorial tax system.

The bill, presented by the Finance Ministry on Sept. 22, would tax five types of passive income earned abroad by Costa Rican tax residents: interest, dividends, royalties, rent and capital gains. It would apply to individuals as well as companies, trusts, investment funds and other structures that are tax residents in Costa Rica.

The proposal sets no minimum threshold. Daniel Pelecano, director of tax and legal services at Grant Thornton, said that means small and large investors would be taxed on the same terms. Costa Rica has generally taxed income based on where it is generated rather than where the earner lives. A 2023 reform, Law 10.381, taxed some foreign passive income, but only for certain entities in multinational groups that failed to meet economic-substance requirements.

The new bill would repeal those limits and make tax residency the deciding factor for passive income. It keeps the territorial rule for active income, such as earnings from work or a business. In the bill’s statement of reasons, the Finance Ministry argues that the 2023 rules reached very few taxpayers. It also says residents receiving the same foreign dividends or interest are treated differently depending on whether they belong to a multinational group.

The ministry says the bill takes into account tax already paid or withheld abroad in order to avoid double taxation. Tax specialists say the mechanism works as a deduction rather than a direct credit, with the foreign tax subtracted from the income before Costa Rica applies its own rate.

Tax lawyer Gabriel Zamora Baudrit illustrated the effect with $100 in US dividends that have already had $30 withheld. Costa Rica would apply its 15% rate to the remaining $70, collecting $10.50 and bringing the combined tax burden to 40.5%. Under a direct credit capped at the Costa Rican amount, the $30 already paid would exceed Costa Rica’s $15 charge, leaving nothing more to pay. Zamora said the bill’s formula falls short of that standard and amounts to a new tax on residents’ foreign passive income, not simply a 15% rate.

Companies that already pay corporate income tax would follow a different route. Rather than paying the flat 15%, they would add the foreign passive income to their taxable profits, which are taxed at rates of up to 30%. Marianela Masís, director of tax and legal services at PwC Costa Rica, said the bill is not a full worldwide income tax because it is limited to certain passive income. She said those most affected would be tax residents who now receive passive income from abroad and fall outside the special regime for multinational groups.

Specialists said retirees who live on returns from investments abroad could fall within the bill’s scope. How pension funds would be treated remains one of several open questions, along with the double-taxation formula, the lack of a threshold and how far the exception to territoriality should reach.

Central Bank President Róger Madrigal said in October that the tax could discourage residents from investing abroad, depending on how foreign tax rates compare with local ones. He said dollars brought back into the country would only affect the exchange rate if they were converted into colones and that the local financial system was deep enough to absorb any inflow.

The bill has only begun its passage through the Assembly, and its text could change. Tax specialists say it would need 38 votes if lawmakers classify it as a new tax, or 29 if it is treated as a reform of existing law. The Finance Ministry has not published an estimate of how much the tax would raise. The proposal comes as the government confronts a revenue shortfall that has already forced cuts across the 2027 budget.

World.title: Local Elections Drove Costa Rica’s CPTPP Reversal, Sources Say
World.content:
Concerns about the 2028 municipal elections helped drive Costa Rica’s decision to abandon its bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), according to four people linked to the accession process who spoke to local reporters on condition of anonymity. The government has not responded to their accounts.

President Laura Fernández announced on Oct. 28 that she would shelve the accession and dismissed Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos the same day. The previous administration of Rodrigo Chaves had announced, days before the current government took office, that it had concluded negotiations on the substantive terms of Costa Rica’s entry.

The CPTPP has been in force since 2018 and has 12 members: Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Brunei, Chile, Mexico, Canada, Peru, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia and the United Kingdom.

The sources’ accounts center on an Oct. 9 meeting at Casa Presidencial, where the president and Chaves, now Minister of Finance and of the Presidency, convened 46 organizations to review the agreement. One attendee said about 40 municipalities in agricultural areas, along with other business groups, opposed the deal.

That attendee said pushing ahead could have jeopardized those municipalities’ ties to the ruling Pueblo Soberano party. Attendees said Chaves defended the agreement at the meeting on free-market grounds. At the same meeting, the president asked Trejos to organize working groups with productive sectors and set Nov. 23 as the deadline to decide whether to sign the accession protocol, according to the sources. Some of them described the meeting as a formality, arguing the decision had already been made.

Agricultural groups protested outside Casa Presidencial on Oct. 9, and several organizations marched against the agreement on Nov. 3. Chaves publicly backed the reversal on Oct. 29. In a government video, he said he fully supported the president’s decision and noted that he had authorized the Foreign Trade Ministry to begin negotiations, citing access to a market of about 600 million consumers.

The sources also described friction over how the deal was handled. One said the government’s new approach included criticism of the way the Foreign Trade Ministry negotiated and of its failure to share information with business chambers. Trejos reportedly sought permission from the bloc’s 12 members to make the negotiated protocol public. According to the sources, that permission was not granted, and the text has not been released.

Costa Rica already has trade agreements with six CPTPP members: Mexico, Canada, Peru, Chile, Singapore and the United Kingdom. One source said the main additional benefit of membership would have been access to the Japanese market. The Presidency had not answered questions about the accounts submitted by local reporters on Nov. 3. The government has not publicly explained the reasons for the reversal beyond the president’s Oct. 28 announcement.

The bloc’s ministerial meeting in Vietnam, scheduled for Nov. 23 to 27, would have been Costa Rica’s first as a participant. With the accession shelved, the country’s existing bilateral agreements remain its main framework for trade with the Asia-Pacific region.

World.title: Your $1,000 Now Buys 46,810 Fewer Colones Than in January
World.content:
The US dollar slipped again in Costa Rica this week, leaving anyone who earns in dollars and spends in colones with noticeably less buying power than at the start of the year. The average rate on Monex, the Central Bank’s wholesale foreign exchange market, closed at 450.26 colones on Thursday, Nov. 5, according to Central Bank data. That was down from 453.81 on Oct. 26 and the lowest daily average since at least that date.

The Central Bank’s reference rate for Friday, Nov. 6, stood at 453.34 colones to sell dollars and 448.27 to buy them. A day earlier, the reference rate was 454.41 to sell and 449.63 to buy. The longer view shows the scale of the shift. On Jan. 2, the Monex average was 497.07 colones, which means Thursday’s close was 46.81 colones lower, a drop of about 9.4% since the start of 2026.

In practical terms, $1,000 converted at the Monex average on Jan. 2 would have brought 497,070 colones. At Thursday’s average, the same amount brings 450,260 colones, a difference of 46,810 colones, or about $104 at current rates. The decline cuts both ways. People paid in dollars and spending in colones, from exporters and tourism businesses to retirees receiving pensions from abroad, lose purchasing power as the rate falls, while households that earn colones and owe dollar-denominated rent or loans pay less to cover them.

The weak dollar has already squeezed some sectors that sell to foreigners, including medical tourism, where revenue measured in colones has fallen. The Monex average first dropped below 450 colones on July 17, when it reached 449.95, at the time the lowest level since the market opened in 2006. The Central Bank described the Costa Rica’s dollar surplus as extraordinary earlier this year and has bought dollars in the market to limit sharper falls.

The broader picture is one of abundant dollars, with the Costa Rica’s dollar supply hitting a record two decades after the end of scheduled devaluations. Monex is the wholesale market where banks and other authorized institutions trade dollars with one another, so its average does not match the price at a bank window. Banks and exchange houses set their own buying and selling prices around the Central Bank’s reference rate, which is published every business day.

World.title: 5,000 Shareholders, No Dividends and a Court Order for Hospital CIMA’s Top Executive
World.content:
A civil court in San José has ordered Clifton Neal Orme, the legal representative of Hospital CIMA, to appear in person and testify in a case brought by minority shareholders who say they have spent years trying to recover their investment in one of Costa Rica’s best-known private hospitals.

The order, issued Oct. 20 by the Second Collegiate Civil Court of First Instance is part of a pre-trial evidence proceeding. That type of proceeding gathers testimony and documents before a full lawsuit is filed, and the court has made no finding of wrongdoing. Neal must personally answer the shareholders’ questions as a party to the case and identify and produce any documents put to him.

He must also present an account of his administration, including a detailed list of the company’s assets and liabilities for 2025. The company, registered as Hospital San José S.A., must hand over a certified copy of the minutes of its Feb. 23, 2026, shareholders’ meeting and its financial statements for 2025.

The court warned that if Neal fails to appear without justification, refuses to answer or responds evasively, it may apply article 42.2 of the Civil Procedure Code. Under certain conditions, that provision allows a judge to treat the facts raised in the questioning as true. A hearing set for Oct. 29 was called off because the court had not yet appointed an English interpreter for Neal, who does not speak Spanish. The hospital must deposit 92,660 colones (about $204) to cover four hours of interpretation, and the court will set a new date once the case file is ready.

The proceeding was filed by shareholder Francisco Castro, who holds 17,336 shares. Panacea JSG S.A., a company represented by 79-year-old investor José Jop, joined as an interested party with 528,748 shares, or about 1.91% of the hospital’s capital.

The court rejected the shareholders’ request for a court-appointed expert to audit the company. Their combined stake of about 1.92% falls short of the 10% that article 26 of the Commercial Code requires for that measure, the court ruled, though it granted their other requests for financial and corporate records. Hospital CIMA’s legal representation said the company will comply with whatever the court requires of it through the proper legal channels. Because the matter is ongoing, it said it would not comment on specific proceedings or on the documents requested.

The case is the latest chapter in a long-running dispute between the hospital and its small investors. Sebastián Vargas, the attorney representing Jop, has said the company has more than 5,000 individual and corporate shareholders, some of whom say they have gone more than two decades without a dividend or a way to sell their stakes.

According to audited financial statements cited in local press reports, the company posted cumulative losses of more than 16.9 billion colones (about $37 million at current exchange rates) between 2019 and 2024. Hospital San José S.A. also appears among the large taxpayers that reported losses or zero taxable income to the Finance Ministry for four consecutive fiscal years, from 2021 through 2024.

The same statements show the balance owed to the hospital by International Hospital Corporation (IHC), a Dallas, Texas-based company related to the controlling shareholder, rose from $11.9 million in 2023 to $13.3 million in 2024. IHC designed and built the hospital, which opened in Escazú in 2000 and has long served the country’s medical tourism market.

Only one minority shareholder is known to have won a case against the hospital. In 2023, a court granted physician Manfred Freer the right to withdraw from the company and be paid for his shares, plus dividends, interest and costs, after finding the hospital had recorded profits in two consecutive periods without distributing them. The Supreme Court’s First Chamber upheld that ruling on April 10, 2025.

During that case, the hospital argued that withholding profits reflected a shareholder agreement to reinvest in its operations and maintain quality of care. A court-ordered appraisal later valued each of Freer’s shares at $6.32, against the $1 per share the hospital had maintained. The dispute has also reached the criminal courts. In December 2025, the hospital and Neal filed a criminal complaint for alleged extortion against Jop and Vargas after Jop raised options for recovering his money, including going to the press.

The Pavas Criminal Court dismissed that complaint, and the Specialized Criminal Court for Organized Crime upheld the dismissal on Sept. 30, 2026. Public registry records list Neal as vice president of Hospital San José S.A. and Gary Brent Wood as its president. No new date has been set for Neal’s testimony. Evidence gathered in pre-trial proceedings of this kind is typically used to decide whether to file a full civil lawsuit.

World.title: Belize to lodge formal protest following aggressive acts of intimidation by Guatemalan Armed Forces in Sarstoon
World.content:
Belize to lodge formal protest following aggressive acts of intimidation by Guatemalan Armed Forces in Sarstoon

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed that this morning, a Belize Defence Force (BDF) patrol conducting a routine patrol around Sarstoon Island was aggressively approached by two Guatemalan Armed Forces (GAF) vessels that had crossed into Belizean waters, in an evident attempt at intimidation.

“The BDF patrol acted with professionalism and restraint and returned safely to the Sarstoon Forward Operating Base after concluding its patrol. The Sarstoon Forward Operating Base has since been reinforced by additional BDF and Belize Coast Guard vessels,” the Ministry said.

The Government of Belize condemned the acts of aggression and the incursion into Belizean waters.

“Under the 1859 Treaty, the boundary is the mid-channel of the Sarstoon River, and Sarstoon Island lies within Belize’s sovereign territory. With Guatemala’s claim pending before the International Court of Justice, both countries are obliged to refrain from any action that may aggravate the dispute,” the Ministry added.

Belize will lodge a formal protest with the Government of Guatemala and report the incident to the Organization of American States.

The Government commended the BDF for its discipline and composure and calls on Guatemala to respect Belize’s sovereignty and refrain from further provocation.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted that Belize remains committed to the peaceful resolution of the dispute.

World.title: One Scholarship, A Lifetime of impact: My Rotary story
World.content:
One Scholarship, A Lifetime of impact: My Rotary story

By Zoila Palma: November is Rotary Foundation Month, a time to celebrate the power of giving and the extraordinary impact that contributions can make in transforming lives.

For me, Rotary Foundation Month is especially meaningful because I am living proof that Rotary’s investment in education transforms lives.

My name is Zoila Palma. Today, I am a journalist and website administrator with Breaking Belize News and Manager of Palma’s Lumber and Supplies. But before these titles, I was a young girl from Santa Elena, Cayo, whose educational journey was forever impacted by the Rotary Club of San Ignacio.

In 2003, my parents had only recently started Palma’s Lumber and Supplies. It was a small backyard operation, and like many young families building a business, they were working hard to establish themselves.

I had just started First Form at St. Ignatius High School when, during my first week of classes, I was called to the principal’s office. I was informed that I needed to bring my parents to school the following day.

I remember sitting in the principal’s office with my parents when the news was delivered. A representative of Rotary informed us that I had been awarded a four-year high school scholarship based on my Primary School Examination (PSE) results and academic merit.

I will never forget that moment. The first cheque, issued in my name, covered the refund of my first-year school expenses. It was a significant moment for my family and an opportunity that we were incredibly grateful for.

For the next four years, I worked hard, determined to make the Rotary Club of San Ignacio proud and demonstrate that their investment in my education was worthwhile. I also remember attending a breakfast at the San Ignacio Hotel with other scholarship recipients.

In 2007, I proudly graduated as the Valedictorian of St. Ignatius High School. At my commencement exercise, I gave glory to God and expressed my gratitude to my parents and the Rotary Club of San Ignacio for believing in me and supporting my education.

That scholarship did not end with my high school graduation. It helped lay the foundation for the opportunities that followed.

A journey of learning and representing Belize

Over the years, my work in journalism has opened doors to professional development, international exposure and opportunities to engage with media professionals, diplomats and institutions.

Some of these milestones include:

2018

-Became a proud alumna of the U.S. Department of State’s prestigious International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP), participating in Building Digital Literacy and Media Responsibility in Democracies in the Digital Age. The experience provided an opportunity to engage with international media professionals and explore the importance of digital literacy, responsible journalism and media accountability in strengthening democracies.

– Participated in a media tour of The Hague, Netherlands, under “From Fear to Facts: Demystifying the ICJ”, exploring the International Court of Justice and its role.

– Participated in the Guatemala leg of the “Demystifying the ICJ” initiative.

2019

– Participated in a Digital Media Press Group exploring Taiwan’s political and economic development.

– Engaged with the International Center for Journalists (ICFJ) and the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) in Jamaica through professional development on organized crime and corruption reporting.

– Delivered a presentation on “Digital Media for the 21st Century” at Sacred Heart College.

– Covered Decision Day and the ICJ referendum, an important moment in Belize’s national history.

2020

– Participated in the United States Department of State Foreign Press Centers programme, “Elections 2020: A Virtual Reporting Tour of the United States and the American Electoral Process”, gaining insight into the American electoral process.

2021

– Conducted a sit-down interview with then U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Keith Gilges at the U.S. Embassy in Belmopan.

2024

– Was recognized by St. Ignatius High School in its Natius Alumni Spotlight on Success feature.

“Zoila Maria Palma, a beacon of journalistic integrity and community activism from Santa Elena, Cayo, has carved a notable path since her valedictorian graduation from St. Ignatius High School in 2007,” St Ignatius High School wrote.

2025

– Participated in the REVISA programme in Panama, which focuses on combating misinformation, enhancing digital security and strengthening data literacy among journalists across Latin America and the Caribbean.

– Was featured by Special Envoy for Development Rosanna Briceño under the Women and the Media category. The recognition highlighted my work in journalism, commitment to truth and dedication to amplifying voices and informing communities.

Beyond these opportunities, I have been featured during International Women’s Day celebrations, including a 2020 feature by young entrepreneur and photographer Mary Robinson.

Giving back and creating lasting impact

Today, I continue to serve my community through journalism, advocacy and engagement with young people.

When I look back, I think about that young First Former who was called to the principal’s office in 2003. I think about my parents, who were building a small business from their backyard, and the opportunity that changed everything.

I am grateful for the doors that have opened since then, but I have never forgotten where the journey began.

To the Rotary Club of San Ignacio and everyone who contributes to The Rotary Foundation, thank you. Thank you for believing in young people, investing in education and creating opportunities that extend far beyond the initial act of giving.

As we celebrate Rotary Foundation Month, I hope my story reminds us that a scholarship is more than financial assistance. It is an investment in the future of our youths, in their family and in the community they will one day serve.

One opportunity can change a life. And one life, in turn, can make a difference in many others.

World.title: PG Garifuna Council says it got just $2,000 for November celebrations
World.content:
PG Garifuna Council says it got just $2,000 for November celebrations

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Punta Gorda branch of the National Garifuna Council says it will have to scale back parts of its Garifuna Settlement Day celebrations after receiving only $2,000 for this year’s November festivities.

In a social media post, the National Garifuna Council Peini/Punta Gorda Branch acknowledged receiving the $2,000 from the National Garifuna Council. The branch said the money came out of a $60,000 donation the council received from the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) last month.

The branch said it understands that the National Garifuna Council also receives an annual subvention of $60,000, from which the PG branch is usually given $2,900 each year for the November celebrations.

“Unfortunately, NOTHING was received by us this year,” the branch said.

With just a one time allocation of $2,000 out of what it described as a total of $120,000, the branch said some aspects of its celebrations will be significantly curtailed.

Still, the branch said it remains hopeful that other activities will go ahead as normal, and closed its post by wishing everyone a happy Garifuna Settlement Day.

The National Garifuna Council has not publicly responded.

World.title: Belize delegation hosts Diaspora Reception in Taiwan
World.content:
Belize delegation hosts Diaspora Reception in Taiwan

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations, in collaboration with the Embassy of Belize in Taiwan, hosted “An Evening with the Diaspora” during the Belize delegation’s visit to Taiwan for the Taiwan International Travel Fair.

The welcome reception brought together members of the Belizean diaspora, visiting delegates, government representatives, business leaders and local stakeholders for an evening of networking and engagement.

The event provided an opportunity for Belizeans living abroad to connect with government officials and other representatives.

The gathering also aimed to strengthen relationships with the diaspora while encouraging investment, new partnerships, cultural exchange and collaboration.

World.title: World debt hits record US$365 trillion. Here’s how much Belize owes
World.content:
World debt hits record US$365 trillion. Here’s how much Belize owes

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The world is deeper in debt than ever before.

According to the Institute of International Finance (IIF), total global debt, including what governments, households and companies owe, reached a record US$365 trillion in the first half of 2026. That works out to roughly US$44,000 for every person on the planet.

Global debt climbed by about US$10 trillion in the first six months of the year alone, driven largely by borrowing in emerging markets. Over the past decade, it has jumped about 60%, up from US$228 trillion.

So where does Belize stand?

Public sector debt was BZ$4.65 billion (about US$2.33 billion) at the end of July 2026, or 65.3% of output. Speaking at a Caribbean ministerial meeting in Bangkok in October, Prime Minister John Briceño said public debt reached 66.4% of output in August 2026.

With a population of a little over 400,000, that means Belize’s public debt works out to roughly BZ$11,000, or about US$5,500, for every Belizean.

Most of it is owed abroad. In his budget presentation earlier this year, the PM said about 64% of the public debt is owed to lenders outside Belize, while the balance of BDZ$1.692 billion or 36 per cent is debt denominated in Belize dollars owed to local lenders and to the Central Bank.

World.title: Panton: Next UDP government will have zero tolerance for abuse of power
World.content:
Panton: Next UDP government will have zero tolerance for abuse of power

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Opposition Leader Tracy Panton says the viral video of a San Pedro police officer shoving a gun into a man’s mouth shows why accountability in law enforcement can no longer be optional.

Panton described the footage as deeply disturbing and pledged that a future UDP government would take a hard line.

“The next UDP government will institute a ZERO TOLERANCE POLICY for abuse of power by ANY public official, particularly those entrusted with enforcing the law and protecting our people,” she said.

She said the incident demands real accountability through due process, adding that holding those in authority responsible is key to rebuilding public trust.

“There can be no green light for unprofessional behaviour or abuse of power. Law enforcement is not above the law,” Panton said.

She also stressed that citizen security depends on a partnership built on respect, professionalism and trust between police and communities.

The police department has suspended the officer, a member of the GI3 unit, and opened criminal and internal investigations. A second officer is also being investigated.

The incident comes at a tense time for the department. A state of emergency is in effect in parts of the Belize and Cayo Districts, attorney Dickie Bradley has warned police against unlawful detentions, and Panton has repeatedly called for Commissioner Dr. Richard Rosado to resign over what she describes as a failure to discipline rogue officers.

World.title: International News: Mexican Judge arrested over alleged $2 million bribe to release Canadian drug trafficker
World.content:
International News: Mexican Judge arrested over alleged $2 million bribe to release Canadian drug trafficker

By Zoila Palma: A Mexican federal judge has been arrested and charged with allegedly accepting US$2 million in bribes to secure the release of a suspected Canadian drug trafficker from custody, according to U.S. authorities.

The judge, identified as Luiz Benítez Alcántara, was overseeing extradition proceedings involving Canadian national Andrew Clark in 2024.

According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Benítez allegedly accepted the payments in exchange for releasing Clark, who was wanted in the United States over his alleged involvement in a major international drug trafficking operation.

Clark was accused of helping manage a billion-dollar drug network reportedly led by former Canadian Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, CBS reports.

Benítez, 49, was arrested in Colombia on Sunday and is facing a nine-count indictment charging him with being an accessory after the fact. U.S. officials said they intend to request his extradition from Colombia.

Clark was reportedly rearrested days after his release and transferred to the United States, where he faces drug trafficking and murder charges.

The arrest is part of a wider U.S. investigation into Wedding’s alleged criminal network, which authorities accuse of transporting cocaine from Colombia through Mexico into the United States and Canada and orchestrating several killings.

Wedding, who competed in the 2002 Winter Olympics, was arrested in Mexico earlier this year and transferred to California, where he pleaded not guilty to the charges. Dozens of people have also been arrested in connection with the alleged operation.

World.title: NWC customers miss out on $50m
World.content:
SOME National Water Commission (NWC) customers missed out on hundreds of dollars in compensation as the utility paid only $23.76 million of the $73.78 million potentially available for breaches of its Guranteed Standards during the 2025–2026 financial year.

The shortfall of approximately $50 million is outlined in the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) 2025–2026 Annual Report, tabled in Parliament on Tuesday.

The report shows that the NWC committed 14,817 breaches of its Guaranteed Standards during the period April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026.

But the utility paid just 32 per cent of the potential compensation its customers should have received.

Among the reasons cited for the non-payment were customers failing to submit the required claim forms and NWC receiving relief from the Guaranteed Standards following Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

The OUR excused the utility from meeting certain service requirements between October 24 and December 31, 2025, because of the disruption caused by the Category 5 storm.

This meant the utility could avoid paying compensation for breaches covered by that relief during the period.

The report also disclosed that, in March 2026, the NWC requested a further six months of relief, beginning January 1, 2026. At the end of the reporting period, that request was still under review, with the OUR indicating that a decision would be issued in the next financial year.

The Guaranteed Standards are service requirements that utility providers are expected to meet. Where a provider breaches an applicable standard, affected customers may qualify for compensation, subject to the relevant conditions and procedures.

The NWC’s compensation figures form part of wider concerns about customer service and unresolved complaints recorded by the OUR during the financial year.

The OUR said it received 3,558 contacts from consumers about utility services during the period, of which 1,168 related to the NWC. These included complaints, enquiries, and other matters brought to its attention.

At March 31, 2026, the NWC also accounted for 251 of the 625 complaints that remained open across all utility providers, representing 40 per cent of the outstanding cases.

The report found that billing disputes and service interruptions were the leading reasons consumers contacted the OUR, accounting for 48 per cent and 18 per cent of all contacts, respectively.

The regulator also noted that it had secured approximately $21.34 million for customers through investigations of appeals and complaints during the financial year.

The NWC accounted for the largest share, paying approximately $9.45 million for consumers, or 44 per cent of the total. The OUR said it would continue reviewing the NWC’s request for additional relief in the following financial year.

The utility recently applied for a 51 per cent tariff increase which is to be considered by the OUR.

World.title: Labourities riding westJLP forgoes customary public rally at National Arena for scaled-down conference in MoBay
World.content:
The sea of green at the public session of the JLP’s 2023 annual conference which will not be repeated this year as only delegates will be invited to the conference to be held in Montego Bay, St James. Karl McLarty

NO National Arena spectacle, no sea of supporters bussed from across the island, no grand public rally.

The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) will again scale back its 2026 annual conference, opting for a delegates-only business meeting in Montego Bay on November 15.

JLP Deputy Leader Desmond McKenzie, who announced the decision at a media conference at the party’s headquarters on Belmont Road in New Kingston on Friday, said the party recognised that although thousands of Jamaicans had received assistance through the Government’s response in the wake of Hurricane Melissa one year ago, much more needs to be done.

“In that vein of recognising the moment and the mood of a section of the country, in respect of our annual conference we have chosen to forgo the usual spectacle which we have had at the National Arena in Kingston,” said McKenzie.

He said the annual conference will be held at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James, beginning at approximately 10 am, with about 6,000 delegates expected to attend.

The decision means there will be no customary mass public meeting, with the party saying it wants to show solidarity with Jamaicans who are still struggling more than a year after the Category 5 storm, particularly those in western Jamaica which was among the areas hardest hit.

According to McKenzie, the decision to scale down the conference was based on a recommendation from the party’s officers, which was approved by its central executive, with the conference instead taking the form of a business session to address internal party matters, political issues, and its role in the recovery effort.

McKenzie explained that prime minister and Party Leader Dr Andrew Holness is expected to address the conference at approximately 1:30 pm, with his speech to be open to the media and broadcast live.

But, McKenzie underscored that the rest of the conference’s business will take place behind closed doors, with attendance restricted to party delegates.

Meanwhile, JLP Deputy General Secretary Dr Andrew Wheatley told Friday’s media briefing that the party’s constitution requires it to hold an annual conference, which is traditionally a business meeting involving delegates.

He said the large public gathering usually associated with the event is a separate public session. Wheatley said the party had chosen to hold the business meeting in Montego Bay to engage stakeholders and workers in western Jamaica who were affected by the hurricane. “We want to empathise with the people, those affected by Hurricane Melissa, especially those in western Jamaica. So we wanted to forego the celebratory aspect of our annual conference and deal with a private business session that will afford us the opportunity to programme political activities, do a self-assessment as to where we are as a political party, and engage the most important members of the party — the delegates of the party — as we…take decisions for not only the betterment of the Jamaican Labour Party but, by extension, the people of Jamaica,” Wheatley said. He also urged delegates to participate actively as the party prepares for the next local government elections. Leadership changes will also be on the agenda, with the private session expected to include elections for the party leader and deputy leaders. Wheatley said the party understood that supporters would miss the usual opportunity to gather and celebrate its achievements, but argued that the circumstances required a different approach. JLP Chairman Robert Montague defended the decision, saying the party had a responsibility to identify with Jamaicans who were still dealing with the effects of the hurricane. He rejected suggestions that the JLP was copying the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP), which held the public session of its 88th annual conference at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, on Sunday, September 20, after moving the event from its usual venue at the National Arena in Kingston. “As a party that cares and as the national party of this country and the party that forms government, we also have a responsibility — a responsibility to those who are still suffering and who are still recovering from the hurricane. We have a responsibility to provide mature leadership to the country. [We] say, rather than jollyficate with some while some persons are struggling, let us identify with our brothers and sisters who are struggling,” he said. “You will also note that the party leader, who is prime minister, has basically put the country on notice that it is time we as a nation begin to tighten some belts, to cut some expenses in order to bring relief to those who are suffering. So, it’s a mature decision and it’s a decision if we did not take, our members and supporters would have condemned us,” Montague added.

World.title: Decide verdict on evidence, judge tells jury in Ruddock murder trial
World.content:
Family and friends of Taneka Gardner are one step closer to finding out if a jury convicts Andre Ruddock of her 2021 murder as the judge started his summation on Friday.

JUSTICE Leighton Pusey has implored the seven members of the jury in the Andre Ruddock murder trial not to arrive at a verdict based on anything they have heard outside of court, but, rather, to stick to the evidence.

Pusey began his summation to the jury on Friday morning in the Home Circuit Court, downtown Kingston, after the prosecution and defence teams finished their cases and gave their closing addresses to the jury on Thursday.

Pusey indicated from early that he would not be rushing his summation and spent a couple hours going over some of the evidence which was presented during the trial and gave the jurors instructions on how to approach their decision after some 10 witnesses testified during the trial which began in September.

Ruddock is on trial for murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of Taneka Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in St James.

Gardner was killed in what is said to have been a human-sacrifice ritual and it is alleged that Ruddock cut her throat on instructions from the now-deceased Pastor Dr Kevin Smith.

“Despite the fact that Mr Ruddock is here, he is presumed innocent. What this means is that you can’t take into consideration anything else that you may have heard or know of him, or anything that might be in terms of his circumstances. The only thing you look at is what has been said in court.

“And what has been said in court must be sufficient to satisfy you that he is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt before you can come to a verdict of guilt. In other words, he doesn’t have to prove to you that he didn’t do anything,” Pusey told the jurors.

“He doesn’t have to prove to you that he is a good person. He doesn’t have to prove to you that he is a nice person or not. That does not matter. He is innocent like any other citizen in the country from anywhere else. And therefore, you cannot start a case with anything in terms of what you have heard or anything else. The only thing that you’re going to be looking at is the evidence and the evidence only,” Pusey warned.

The judge emphasised that the accused has no requirement, no need in law, to prove that he did not do anything.

“He’s been charged with murder and in law, we define murder as the unlawful killing of a person. And so, for the purposes of that definition of law, these are the things that you need to look at. You have to first come to the conclusion of whether the person was killed.

“That is why you — not just the persons who say something — but you have a post-mortem and you also have seen, heard the evidence of the person who identified the body. So if you remember, you heard from Taneka Gardner’s father and he indicated that this is his daughter and he said that he identified the body and went to the post-mortem. So therefore, you have the evidence that Taneka Gardner died,” Pusey said.

“But also, more importantly, you have the evidence of the doctor who did the post-mortem and he gave you in great detail exactly what happened to her and what caused her death. So, in this circumstance, you have clear evidence that somebody died and that person died from a cut to the throat. It was not an accidental death, or something like that. That she was killed by somebody who cut her throat.

“The one question that you need to come to in this case is whether or not that particular person who killed her is in jail. As I said, it is not necessary for us to go through and try to find out all the things that happened on that day. Who did what. Who was good and who was bad. What we are trying to determine is whether or not Andre Ruddock was the person who killed Taneka Gardner,” added Pusey.

The judge is expected to complete his summation on Monday, which will pave the way for the jurors to begin their deliberation and return a verdict.

World.title: Alarm at Mount Alvernia High
World.content:
The entrance to Mount Alvernia High School in Montego Bay.

Principal points to gastro; students question food safety

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Principal of Mount Alvernia High School Kayon Whyne has sought to allay fears that there are food safety issues on the campus after a number of students became ill at the institution on Thursday, with a few having to seek medical treatment.

The all-girl school is awaiting results of a probe by the St James Health Department, but the educator suspects a stomach bug may have caused symptoms including vomiting and diarrhoea among several students, mainly from the lower grades. School was dismissed early Thursday, and only students from grades 10 to 13 were allowed to attend classes Friday.

“Monday, we will be back to normal. Some of the students would have wanted to come in on Friday but we took the decision,” Whyne told the Jamaica Observer Friday afternoon.

“They are in classrooms now, grade seven to nine are in online learning, the teachers are meeting with them,” she added.

When contacted the parish’s Chief Public Health Inspector Shericka Lewis confirmed that an investigation had been launched into the matter.

“We’ve gotten a preliminary report, not the fulsome report, we are still investigating,” she told the Observer Friday afternoon.

“We got a report yesterday and dispatched a team,” Lewis added, referring to the department’s initial response.

Lewis provided an initial assessment of the situation without identifying a possible cause.

“It was predominantly vomiting amongst several students,” she said.

Jitters have been rippling through the school and among concerned parents since Thursday as rumours swirl about what could have caused discomfort among those affected. According to an email from concerned students, some of their peers became ill after eating meals purchased at school.

“Several students reportedly experienced symptoms, including vomiting, after consuming food from the school canteen,” the message said.

“What makes this situation particularly concerning is that the reports are not limited to students who consumed cooked meals. Students who purchased other food items, including patties, have also reportedly experienced illness,” it continued.

Questions were also raised about why some students were allowed to return to school on Friday when the cause of the illness had not yet been confirmed.

“If the school has been deemed safe, students and parents deserve clarification on why certain year-groups are being advised to remain away while others are expected to continue attending,” the email said.

“Furthermore, what specific measures have been implemented to ensure that students who are still required to attend are not exposed to potential health risks,” it added.

The students insisted that they deserve to have confidence that the food purchased at school is safe.

“The school canteen is an essential part of the daily school environment, and maintaining appropriate food safety standards should never be treated as optional,” said writers of the emailed message.

The principal’s approach has been to treat the issue as gastro, a common ailment in schools and other closed environments such as cruise ships and nursing homes. According to Whyne, they issued a gastroenteritis alert to parents and classes were dismissed early Thursday as a precautionary measure.

But up to Friday she was still puzzled about what really happened to the girls in her care.

“We buy patties from two stores, so I don’t know. The students ate patties and I am telling you there are other parents who gave their children packed lunches for school and they would have experienced the same thing. We don’t know if it’s airborne or waterborne, we don’t know,” the school principal told the Observer.

“The health inspectors, they were just here and they say that it’s inconclusive but they are doing tests. I just had my lunch and no impact,” she added.

About 50 to 70 per cent of gastro outbreaks are caused by viruses. However it can also be caused by bacterial contamination of food and water, or passed from person to person. Gastro is typically spread when tiny particles of stool or vomit from an infected person get onto hands, surfaces, food, or water, and are then transferred to the mouth.

Whyne said two students were given medication intravenously (IV) but they are back home.

One parent confirmed that his ninth-grader was among those who became ill Thursday.

“A pure vomit she a vomit, them say she cannot come to school today. Well, most of the school have to stay home,” he told the Observer Friday.

He said he was monitoring his daughter’s condition to determine whether she would need medical attention.

The treatment regime for gastro involves small, frequent sips of liquid; gradual reintroduction of bland food; and rest. Medical care is recommended if there are signs of severe dehydration and an inability to keep any liquids down for 24 hours.

World.title: ‘45 years of Joy’
World.content:
Back row: (from left) Vice-principal of Siloah Primary Janice Larmond; Dr Joy Spence, Appleton Estate master blender; Principal Oneil Larmond; and Vice-Principal Cynthia Morris. Front row (from left): Head Boy Ammere Atkinson, Head Girl Emeika Williams, Marlonae Harriott, deputy head boy; and Kymarley Brown, deputy head girl; at the JOY45 Handover Ceremony at Siloah Primary School.

STUDENTS and teachers at Siloah Primary School are set to benefit from improved drinking water storage, classroom cooling, and teaching resources following a donation valued at $1.9 million, as part of Dr Joy Spence’s 45th anniversary celebrations at J Wray & Nephew Limited.

The contribution — made through the J Wray & Nephew (JWN) Foundation and Appleton Estate — included two 1,000-gallon water tanks for drinking water storage; 18 water stands with a supply of five-gallon water bottles; three smart televisions with wall mounts; 24 wall-mounted fans for six classrooms; and a water testing kit.

The water tanks will strengthen the school’s drinking water storage capacity, while the water stands and bottled water will support access throughout the school day.

The fans are intended to create more comfortable conditions for students, including those preparing for their Primary Exit Profile examinations, and the smart televisions will provide additional classroom teaching resources.

The handover continued a relationship that began five years ago during the ‘40 Years of Joy’ initiative, which introduced a breakfast feeding programme for primary schools surrounding Appleton Estate in St Elizabeth.

During her visit to Siloah Primary at that time, Spence was struck by Principal Oneil Larmond’s commitment to the school and the warmth of its students, inspiring her to continue supporting the institution.

Earlier this year, that support included a commitment to provide feminine hygiene supplies for girls in grades five and six throughout the year. This latest donation builds on that relationship by addressing practical needs that affect students’ comfort and readiness to learn.

“My passion is for education, and I always support causes for education through the foundation, through scholarships, and initiatives such as this. This donation responds to everyday needs that can make a real difference to a child’s school experience.

“Having drinking water readily available, cooler classrooms, and technology to support teaching can help students feel more comfortable and better able to concentrate on learning,” said Spence.

“As I celebrate 45 years with J Wray & Nephew, it is deeply rewarding to share that milestone in this way. Through the JWN Foundation, scholarships and initiatives such as this, I hope to continue helping young people access the support and opportunities they need to fulfil their potential,” added Spence, Appleton Estate’s master blender.

The school’s welcomed the contribution and acknowledged the continued support of Spence and the JWN Foundation.

“Total joy when Dr Joy Spence is around. We are extremely happy for her donation of water drums, water coolers, wall fans and smart televisions. This has transformed our learning environment, allowing our students and staff to work more effectively. This will enhance the performance of all our students. Special thanks to Dr Joy Spence and the JWN Foundation for always being there for our school and community,” said Larmond.

Education has been a meaningful thread throughout JOY45, which celebrates Spence’s journey from joining JWN as chief chemist in 1981 to becoming the first female master blender in the spirits industry in 1997.

Alongside the Siloah Primary contribution, an anniversary dinner at The University of the West Indies, Mona, on October 15 acknowledged scholarship recipient Cara Fraser, connecting the celebration of Spence’s achievements with opportunities for another generation.

The school handover brought that commitment into the community surrounding Appleton Estate, marking the anniversary with practical support for students and the educators guiding them.

World.title: CHASING THE DREAM
World.content:
SPEID... victory on aggregate will help not only to get to the semi-finals of the Nations League and qualify to the Gold Cup, but also helps us in World Cup ranking (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

SITTING calmly at the head table, Jamaica’s Head Coach Rudoph Speid set a tone of pragmatic realism and intense focus as he unveiled his 23-man squad to face Concacaf powerhouse Mexico in a pivotal two-legged Nations League clash, aiming to qualify for the regional showpeice — the Gold Cup.

The Jamaicans are set to host Mexico on Friday, November 14, at the National Stadium at 8:00 pm, and then travel to Mexico for the second leg on Tuesday, November 17 in Monterrey at 9.30 pm Jamaica time.

The winner of the two-legged tie will advance to the semi-final of the Nations League and by extension gain an automatic spot in the Concacaf Gold Cup.

“Victory on aggregate will help not only to get to the semi-finals of the Nations League and qualify to the Gold Cup, but also helps us in World Cup ranking for the World Cup Qualifiers in 2030. So it’s a very important game for us,” Speid pointed out during the press conference.

“What is important in this particular game, which is very significant, is that video assistant referee (VAR) will be on display,” Speid noted with a faint smile.

“They are using VAR in both games. I mean I must tell you that we have no luck with VAR so far, but let’s see,” he added.

Speid, who took charge of the Reggae Boyz in November 2025, almost one year in the hot seat, announced his 23-man team including one newcomer, Denzel Hall of Rotherham United in League Two in England.

The 25 year-old Hall, who plays right back, previously represented The Netherlands youth teams from Under-15 to Under-17 between 2015 and 2017. Hall is of Jamaican parentage.

“He was always someone that we were watching. But at this particular time, you know, there’s a real shortage of players in that position and he has done well enough to get a call-up. And we decided to call him to see what he could do. He learned his football in the Dutch League,” said Speid.

Sixteen players are returning from the last window in this 23-member squad: Andre Blake, Amal Knight, Richard King, Miguel Freckleton, Joel Latibeaudiere, Christopher Ainsworth, Kyle Ming, Ronaldo Webster, Brandon Cover, Courtney Clarke, Karoy Anderson, Kaheim Dixon, Ronaldo Cephas, Javon East, Tyreece Campbell, and Damion Lowe.

The other players are goalkeeper Jahmali Waite, Kevon Lambert, Tyrese Hall, Dwight Merrick, Warner Brown and Khori Bennett.

If goalkeeper Blake is selected for both games he will achieve 100 caps for Jamaica.

Speid explained why Leon Bailey and Dujuan Richards were not included.

“…When you come to a play-off game you have to be sure of every single person that you put in that squad because we only have 23 and if you have people that are doubtful and you bring them in you could end up with a lot less players than you really need. And I am telling you, in this particular game, players have to be fit. Mexico is no joke. It’s like playing two away games.

“So, you know, you have to look at the risk. We’re getting people that are not 100 per cent as against somebody who’s playing every single day, day in, day out and putting up very good performances,” said Speid.

The Regage Boyz enter the tie on an upward trajectory, still number one in the Caribbean, sitting sixth in the Concacaf and 69th globally. Mexico are 59 spots ahead, coming in at number 10 in the world.

Jamaica holds four hostorical victories over Mexico and Speid is under no illusions regarding the magnitude of the task ahead.

“A team that is ranked 10th in the world is no joke. We understand the type of monster we’re up against. But that is why the games are being played. They are not unbeatable. You just have to be on your best game and you need a little luck too,” he pointed out.

The players should arrive for camp between November 8 and 9.

World.title: Molynes chairman defends split with Thomas amid contract, salary dispute
World.content:
HIGGINS... football is a results business, and we’re not pleased with the results so we just made a decision (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

DESPITE a less-than-amicable situation between Molynes United and Jermaine Thomas, club’s Chairman Peter Higgins says he has a lot of respect for their former coach but felt change was necessary as they seek to move up the Legend Jamaica Premier League table.

As the Jamaica Observer revealed on Tuesday, Molynes decided to move on from Reggae Boyz Under-20 assistant coach Thomas following their 1-2 loss to Mount Pleasant Football Academy on Monday. It was the club’s sixth defeat in eight games and they are sitting in 12th on six points, one point above the relegation zone.

The Observer has learnt that Thomas, who was in the role for nearly three years, was officially dismissed on Wednesday after refusing to resign when asked to by the club’s management on Tuesday.

The Observer reported on Wednesday that Thomas is owed outstanding salary payments and would also receive more, given he had several months remaining on his contract. Reports elsewhere said that Thomas could take legal action, with the club owing nearly $1.5 million.

Speaking with the Observer on Friday, Higgins declined to confirm the details of the reports but revealed the separation was a necessary one for the club.

“We’re going through a little transition now but I don’t want to get into any personal thing about, or any he said, she said type of things,” he said. “I’m seeing the stuff in the media, and we deliberately say we’re not commenting because we think it’s a personal issue between the coach and ourselves in terms of the separation.”

“Football is a results business, and we’re not pleased with the results so we just made a decision. That’s the long and short of it.”

Higgins says while the club intends to honour its financial obligations to Thomas, that did not mean he had to remain in the position.

“I’m a banker; if my boss is not pleased with me, they can fire me any time I want, whether or not they owe me. They’re not going to say, ‘Because I owe you I can’t fire you.’ That just doesn’t sound sensible,” he said.

“We have some outstanding financial obligations, and we’ve written to the coach to say ‘This is how we plan to settle it.’ ”

Higgins, though, says the club has no personal issues with Thomas.

“I don’t believe that when these types of things happen it needs to be public,” he said. “Jermaine is a very nice guy, and I have nothing but good things to say about him; I have nothing negative I can say. But, at the end of the day it’s about the results.”

The Observer was unable to contact Thomas despite several attempts.

Under Thomas, Molynes avoided relegation in the past three seasons, with consecutive 12th-place finishes in the 2024/2025 and 2025/2026 season.

The club have already moved on and hired veteran local Anthony Patrick, who returns to the JPL after leading Racing United to the play-offs last season.

Higgins believes Patrick is the right choice to elevate Molynes, given his prior achievements locally.

“He has been a successful coach, certainly at the schoolboy level. You have seen the results; I think it speaks for itself,” said Higgins. “We have also seen his win rate both at his last club, Racing, and previously at Waterhouse. He actually worked with us before (for) a short time but he had done some work with us before.”

Although results aren’t certain, Higgins says the club now has optimism.

“We’re hoping it can turn around in the near future. We think it can.”

World.title: Former patient donates US$18,000-ultrasound machine to Hugh Wynter Institute
World.content:
From left: Nordia Barrett-Lewis; Dr John Harriot; Professor Aldrie Henry-Lee, pro vice-chancellor of The University of the West Indies; and Dr Carl Bruce pose alongside an ultrasound machine donated to the Hugh Wynter Institute for Reproductive Healthcare and Endoscopic Surgery at The UWI, Mona, during a donor appreciation ceremony.

AFTER undergoing several surgeries for reproductive health challenges, Jamaican immigration consultant and philanthropist Nordia Barrett-Lewis has given back to the institution that helped improve her quality of life.

Barrett-Lewis has donated a high-definition ultrasound machine, valued at more than US$18,000, to the Hugh Wynter Institute for Reproductive Healthcare and Endoscopic Surgery (HWI-RHES) at The University of the West Indies (The UWI), Mona.

The donation, which was formally recognised during a Donor Appreciation and Dedication Ceremony on October 29, is expected to strengthen the diagnosis and treatment of women’s reproductive health conditions while improving postgraduate training for doctors specialising in obstetrics and gynaecology.

For Barrett-Lewis, founder and chief executive officer of Barrett Immigration, the decision to give back was personal.

Having undergone several procedures, including her most recent surgery at the institute in February 2026, she said the care she received had made a significant difference in her life.

“I have had several surgeries, not all of them done here, but the last portion has been done here and it has given me a better quality of life,” she said.

Although she now resides overseas Barrett-Lewis continues to return to Jamaica for medical care. Following her surgery, she approached her doctor to find out how she could support the institute. After consultations with the medical team an ultrasound machine was identified as a priority.

“My hope is that women who are going through the process of whether having children, or simply having reproductive issues, may be able to get the quality care that they want,” she explained, adding that access to modern medical equipment is just as important as having qualified health-care professionals.

Director of the Hugh Wynter Institute, Dr John Harriott welcomed the contribution, noting that it would strengthen the institution’s ability to provide specialised reproductive health-care while addressing an important gap in medical training.

“We are very grateful for this donation of…a high-definition ultrasound. It’s part of our mission to use technologies to continue to advance women’s health care,” Harriott said.

He explained that doctors pursuing postgraduate training in obstetrics and gynaecology currently have limited exposure to the use of a gynaecological ultrasound, an area he has been working to incorporate into the training curriculum.

“In particular, this ultrasound is going to serve purposes for training residents in obstetrics and gynaecology in the field of gynaecological ultrasounds. It’s an area that is deficient in the programme right now, and this will serve as a template for introduction of that in the curriculum,” he said.

The institute is also planning a workshop with international experts in March 2027 to further strengthen training in this area.

Beyond its educational value, the machine will support early diagnosis, emergency assessments, and ultrasound-guided surgical procedures, improving the care available to women with reproductive health complications.

Harriott also used the occasion to highlight the range of services offered by the institute which he described as one of Jamaica’s best-kept secrets. These include fertility care, contraception, and advanced minimally invasive surgery — particularly for women suffering from conditions such as endometriosis.

“A lot of women in Jamaica suffer from chronic pelvic pain, secondary to endometriosis, which is quite debilitating,” he said, noting that the institute has helped improve the lives of several patients, including Barrett-Lewis.

Dr Carl Bruce, senior director of clinical services at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), said the donation would have far-reaching benefits for patient care, medical education and research — not only in Jamaica but across the Caribbean.

“First, in the area of patient care our women’s health divisions will be able to use this technology to diagnose with precision and accuracy. But, importantly, we’re able to train another generation of doctors who can use these technologies for their patients — and it’s training not only for the doctors in Jamaica but across the region,” said Bruce.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Bodo Ramelow
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X
