Die Welt spielt verrückt, doch im Präsidium des Bundestages herrscht überraschende Einigkeit. Bundestagsvizepräsident Bodo Ramelow (Die Linke) gibt im Gespräch mit Gordon Repinski einen seltenen Einblick in die überparteiliche Zusammenarbeit, auch bei Nachtschichten. Dabei wird deutlich, mit welcher Strategie das Gremium den Provokationen der AfD begegnet.

In seiner eigenen Partei brodelt es derweil gewaltig. Ramelow findet deutliche Worte zur Antisemitismus-Debatte innerhalb der Linken und kritisiert das taktische Lavieren einzelner Abgeordneter. Warum er trotzdem eine Gesinnungsprüfung ablehnt, aber klare rote Linien beim Existenzrecht Israels zieht, offenbart die tiefe Zerrissenheit seiner Partei.

Zudem verrät er, warum die Wahrnehmung der Linken im Bundestag derzeit auch von der Gruppe der „Silberlocken“ abhängt, wie sich die Silberlocken regelmäßig absprechen und warum er sich trotz aller Krisen nicht verrückt machen lässt.

Mit den Linken, aber auch der SPD und den Grünen beschäftigt sich auch der neue Podcast von POLITICO und WELT. In „Inside Links“ geht es jede Woche darum, wie in Deutschland womöglich eine neue linke Mehrheit entsteht, zu welchem Preis und wer künftig dabei möglicherweise am Regierungstisch sitzen könnte. „Inside Links“ gibt es auf den Podcast-Plattformen zu hören und zu sehen, unter anderem auch hier.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

Für alle Hauptstadt-Profis: Der Berlin Playbook-Newsletter bietet jeden Morgen die wichtigsten Themen und Einordnungen. Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren.

World.title: Merz’s conservatives poised to nominate Germany’s first woman president
World.content:
President of the Bavarian parliament Ilse Aigner arrives at the Christian Social Union party congress in Munich, on Oct. 23, 2026. | Alexandra Beier/AFP via Getty Images

BERLIN — Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner is set to become Germany’s next president, making her the country’s first woman to hold the office, according to two senior conservatives with knowledge of the matter.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) will nominate Aigner to succeed outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the officials told BILD, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. Both officials were granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters freely. Aigner’s nomination will officially be announced Monday, according to the officials.

Aigner, who previously served as agriculture minister under former German Chancellor Angela Merkel from 2008 to 2013, is currently president of the Bavarian State Parliament. She is also a member of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

World.title: Trump’s ‘big, beautiful’ European security plan isn’t convincing Europe
World.content:
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.

POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.

U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.

Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”

“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”

World.title: Wave of bomb threats target Irish media outlets and more European flights
World.content:
“We have expected a rise in hybrid threats to Ireland because of our hosting of the EU presidency, and the EPC meeting will be by far the biggest set-piece event of that presidency, so one must presume it’s no coincidence that we’re experiencing this spike in hybrid activity now,” the Irish official said.

The Irish government said the threats against media outlets were probably part of a European-wide pattern of threats that have targeted dozens of airlines this week, including Irish carriers Ryanair and Aer Lingus. Hackers also targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralized or coordinated effort,” the Irish government said in a statement. “However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

Bomb threats also targeted at least 18 European flights Friday, after at least 22 the day before, raising concerns that the hoaxes may be part of a coordinated campaign to disrupt air traffic.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Friday that the bomb threats affecting flights could be “an attempt at hybrid aggression and war in some psychological way.” He added that “it cannot be a coincidence that so many identical events occur with the same modus operandi throughout Europe.”

Luis Gallego, CEO of airline group IAG, said: “It is clear that what they [the perpetrators] are looking for is to create chaos and disruption in the different airports.”

World.title: EU capitals urge Brussels to ‘swiftly’ sign electricity deal with UK
World.content:
A group of countries are now urging the European Commission to wrap up discussions by the end of 2027, according to an EU diplomat granted anonymity to discuss internal discussions.

Proponents say the plan would unlock new renewable energy investment in the North Sea and could cut electricity prices.

But the EU says the U.K. would have to make a contribution to EU cohesion funds as the price of participating in the market — a politically difficult ask for London.

Clean energy hub

The leaders, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, write that the agreement is “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea” and to “transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa give a press conference at the end of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

“An agreement will thus enhance Europe’s energy security and contribute to a competitive economy that centres on access to clean and affordable energy,” the letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa states.

“These benefits underline the importance of swiftly concluding the ongoing negotiations. We call on you and the UK to agree during the Summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations.”

World.title: Spain and the Netherlands battle over ECB presidency
World.content:
Exiting European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde gives a press conference in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, on Oct. 29, 2026. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot are in the hunt for the top job after Christine Lagarde’s exit.

BRUSSELS — The Netherlands and Spain on Friday submitted candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, a former president of the Dutch central bank, were the only candidates to emerge after the 5 p.m. deadline, as expected.

Their candidacies are part of a larger game of musical chairs that includes France and Germany, as Europe’s four economic powerhouses negotiate how to secure their seats on the ECB’s executive board.

World.title: ‘I don’t know if it reassured or worried them’: European envoys quiz Le Pen over lunch
World.content:
The group of ambassadors from the eight countries that share a border with metropolitan France — Germany, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Monaco and Andorra — already met with conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau in September. They are planning to host meetings with the other presidential hopefuls, including far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, at their respective embassies in the coming months.

“I don’t know if it reassured or worried them,” said an adviser to Marine Le Pen who accompanied her to the lunch. “What is sure is that they can now report back to their capitals what the National Rally wants to do,” the adviser added.

Le Pen was mainly questioned about her plans to downsize the EU and on bilateral issues, as well as U.S. President Donald Trump after his seismic defeat in the midterm elections.

While in the past, the National Rally has been supportive of Trump, the party has progressively distanced itself from the U.S. president. The National Rally’s Jordan Bardella on Wednesday said his party was not affected by the result and suggested that Trump’s popularity was undermined by the war in the Middle East and its economic consequences.



Le Pen has also been campaigning for a harsher approach on migration, which would involve stricter checks at the borders, potentially impacting countries whose envoys she met on Wednesday. All of them, apart from Andorra and Monaco, are part of the Schengen free-movement area.

“There is a general interest on what would her stance be on the key issues of mutual interest and cooperation on which we are working with France,” said one diplomat from a participating country.

“It was a very frank exchange. She told them what she says everywhere and she was able to elaborate on a number of topics a little more at length than she would do on TV,” the same adviser said, adding that Le Pen regularly meets ambassadors.

World.title: Election favorite says Spain should quit as World Cup co-host if Morocco stages the final
World.content:
Feijóo noted that the 2030 World Cup was originally a Spanish-Portuguese bid, until Morocco was invited at a later stage. Despite that chronology, Moroccan officials have been pushing vigorously to stage the final, which is the world’s most prestigious sports event.

Rafael Louzán, Spain’s football chief, told POLITICO in June that he was confident either Madrid or Barcelona would host the final, despite Morocco pouring vast amounts of cash into football infrastructure.

Tensions have flared between the two countries in recent months. Spanish political parties this summer accused Morocco of stoking a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, after 80,000 people surged into the city in late July.

A Sigma Dos poll for El Mundo following the Ceuta crisis found that 84.4% of Spaniards opposed Spain continuing to co-host the World Cup with Morocco.

Leftist party Sumar, the Socialists’ junior coalition partner, said this summer that the World Cup “cannot be shared with a country that uses desperate people for its own geostrategic interests.”

The left-wing party tabled a resolution in parliament that far-right Vox backed in an unusual convergence. The text never made it to a vote because parliament was dissolved ahead of the snap election.

World.title: 'Peace is possible and we are called to build it' Pope Leo XIV says in Uruguay
World.content:
During his sixth apostolic journey, Pope Leo XIV stopped in Paysandú, in Uruguay, where he celebrated Mass in the Parque París Londres in front of more than 40,000 faithful.

 

Arriving at the exhibition area in the popemobile from the "Brigadier General Aviator Tydeo Larre Borges" International Airport, the Pontiff made his way through the cheering crowd, blessing those present. When he reached the altar, next to an image of Blessed Jacinto Vera, he centred his entire homily on the key concepts of unity and community.

"Peace is possible and we are called to build it," the pontiff said during the liturgical celebration. He then offered the multitude three symbols characteristic of Uruguayan soil to show how to safeguard and spread the Christian faith today.

The first element he evoked was the "General Artigas" bridge, a metaphor for the importance of building strong bonds and engaging in dialogue with others. The second was represented by the local palm trees, which grow together in groves and recall the communal nature of the Church. Finally, there was mate, the famous traditional drink shared at moments of encounter, highlighted as a deep emblem of familiarity and brotherhood. "An element deeply significant to your culture, around which friends or relatives gather to share," Leo XIV said.

At the end of the service, after official thanks from the bishop of Salto, Arturo Eduardo Fajardo Bustamante, the Pope presented a chalice to the local diocese.

Faithful await Pope Leone XIV AP Photo/Andrew Medichini

Leo XIV's programme in Uruguay

The packed schedule for the day continued with an intense itinerary of institutional and pastoral engagements. After the liturgy in the park, a visit to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary followed for the unveiling of a commemorative plaque and a greeting to the faithful outside the building. The Pontiff then left Paysandú for the capital, Montevideo, where the second part of his busy official agenda continued.

In the late afternoon in the capital, the Pope will meet the social community of Casavalle at the Parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe. This will be followed by an engagement with the academic and education sector at the Catholic University of Uruguay. Both moments will be a central opportunity for direct dialogue with the educational and care institutions of the South American country.

The day will conclude at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium, which the Pope will reach by travelling in the popemobile to allow once again for an encounter with the public. In the sports venue, Leo XIV will preside over a solemn prayer vigil together with thousands of young people and faithful who have travelled from all over the country for the closing event.

On Sunday, the pope is expected in Florida, about 90 kilometres from the capital Montevideo, considered the "cradle" of the nation because it is where the Declaration of Independence took place in 1825. It is also an important religious centre due to the presence of the National Shrine of the Virgen de los Treinta y Tres. In the square in front of it the Pope will celebrate Sunday Mass.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 7th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Mélenchon presents party manifesto as social unrest continues across France
World.content:
Hard left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has called on his supporters to gather in Le Bourget, just north of Paris, on Saturday, where he is set to present his party's new manifesto, "L'Avenir en commun" (The Future in Common).

 

After launching his campaign in June with a rally attended by 26,000 people outside the Basilica of Saint-Denis, he went on to hold a second major rally in Clermont-Ferrand in the Auvergne region.

That event coincided with the start of the high-school students' movement in France and was also marked by a symbolic visit to the Gergovie plateau, where the Gauls famously defeated Julius Caesar's Roman army.

His choice of venue for this latest campaign event also appears calculated.

It was in Le Bourget that François Hollande delivered his now-famous declaration during the 2012 presidential campaign: "My real opponent is the world of finance."

The statement was intended to establish his left-wing credentials before he went on, once elected, to pursue supply-side economic policies - a first for a French Socialist leader.

Nearly fifteen years later, Mélenchon is seeking to position himself as the candidate of a decisive break with the left, at a time when social unrest is spreading across the country.

Firmly in second place in the polls on around 18%, the France Unbowed (LFI) leader has picked up several endorsements in recent days.

On Thursday, most Communist and overseas-territories MPs in the National Assembly formally backed his candidacy, despite French Communist Party leader Fabien Roussel also running. The Greens, meanwhile, are expected to decide in mid-December on a possible alliance with LFI.

Despite this momentum, Mélenchon still trails well behind Marine Le Pen, who is polling at between 35% and 37%.

'Liberty, equality, solidarity'

A few hours before his rally in Le Bourget, Mélenchon unveiled his campaign poster.

It shows his portrait set against a Gergovie landscape, a backdrop that also evokes a rural France where the LFI vote remains weak, along with a reworked republican motto: "liberty, equality, solidarity."

On social media, some internet users are already comparing it with François Mitterrand's 1981 poster, which showed him in front of a Burgundy village dominated by its church, above the slogan "quiet strength."

'L'Avenir en commun'

While previous versions of the programme placed the creation of a Sixth Republic at the top of the agenda, ecological transformation has now become one of France Unbowed's main priorities.

Among its proposals, the party is proposing to replace existing administrative regions with "eco-regions" organised around the management of water resources. It also wants to enshrine stronger environmental protections in the constitution.

France Unbowed is also sticking to its commitment to a gradual phase-out of nuclear power, although the target of reaching 100% renewable energy has been pushed back from 2050 to 2060.

On the economic and social front, Mélenchon is keeping faithful to his long-standing pledges: to raise the minimum wage (SMIC) to €1,700 pcm and eventually lowering the legal retirement age to 60 for people who have paid into the pension system for 40 years.

The programme has been published without a detailed financial breakdown, but party officials stress that it is a "foundation" that will be supplemented by around 50 documents detailing the various measures.

At a press conference in mid-October, Mélenchon and Éric Coquerel, the LFI head of the National Assembly's finance committee, presented their "revised budget" for 2027 in the event of victory.

It contained roughly €100 billion in additional revenue to be generated through tax measures, as well as €80 billion in additional spending.

In foreign policy, the LFI is continuing to focus on the war in Gaza and Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. It is also proposing to suspend the association agreement between Israel and the European Union.

On Ukraine, the document calls for a ceasefire but says little about military support for Kyiv. It also advocates setting up a new European security framework that would include Russia.

A 'plan to dismantle France'

Mélenchon's manifesto has already drawn strong reactions from his opponents.

In a post on X, Le Pen, the far-right National Rally presidential candidate, hit out at what she called a "plan to dismantle France".

"It takes the process of deconstruction initiated by Emmanuel Macron since he came to power to its logical conclusion," she wrote.

Speaking near Marseille on Saturday, former prime minister Édouard Philippe, who is also running in the presidential election, criticised what he dubbed Mélenchon's "communitarian vision" and his "administered economy".

Referring to his two rivals on the far right and the hard left, the centre-right candidate said he saw "many points in common" between Le Pen and Mélenchon, notably their "hatred of European integration" and their desire to "leave NATO."

Protests continue

Mélenchon's rally comes as demonstrations continue across France.

On Thursday, nearly 200 marches took place across the country as protesters demanded an increase in the minimum wage and wages more generally, as well as measures to tackle economic insecurity, protection of public services and more resources for schools and universities.

Organisers estimated the turnout to be around 1.6 million people, while the interior ministry put the figure at 575,000 demonstrators.

World.title: Six people killed and 15 injured in shooting in Kraków, Polish authorities say
World.content:
At least six people were killed and fifteen injured, among them two police officers, after a gunman opened fire on the main square of the Polish city of Kraków.

 

These numbers were confirmed by the regional government of Małopolska on Saturday evening.

The perpetrator was shot by officers and then transported to hospital, the police stated.

A spokesperson for the local firefighters told Polsat News that the perpetrator fired a gun from a passing car.

Numerous police cars and ambulances appeared in the area around St Mary's Basilica. A helicopter from the air ambulance service was also dispatched to the site.

Poland’s Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński tweeted:

“Police officers risked their lives while intervening in Kraków. They acted immediately. Thanks to their heroic actions, the attacker was quickly apprehended.

One police officer has a gunshot wound; the condition of the second is very serious — he suffered three gunshot wounds. He is currently undergoing surgery.”

Malopolska police confirmed that the gunman is a Polish citizen and denied reports about a possible second perpetrator being sought.

The city office said that rescue services are working on the Main Square and that the police are conducting operations in several locations.

President Karol Nawrocki said his he was "deeply concerned by reports of the tragic events in central Kraków" and that his "thoughts are with the victims, those injured and their families."

Nawrocki added that the "head of the National Security Bureau is on his way to Kraków."

This is a developing story and will be updated by our journalists as soon as more information becomes available.

World.title: Spain: Baby's body found in freezer in Ourense may have been there over 20 years
World.content:
The Civil Guard is investigating after the body of a baby was found inside a chest freezer in a storage room at a block of flats in Allariz, in the Ourense province of north-west Spain.

 

According to the local newspaper La Región, the discovery was made last Monday by a woman who was going through the belongings of her recently deceased mother.

The freezer was in a storage room in the building’s garage area. When she opened it, she found the body of the new-born.

Preliminary data indicate that the baby is believed to ha e been born after a pregnancy of between 32 and 34 weeks and is thought to have breathed. However, it will be the autopsy carried out by the Galician Institute of Legal Medicine that will clarify the circumstances and causes of death.

Identity of the baby and circumstances of the death under investigation

Investigators have already taken statements from several people close to the former owner and have sent DNA samples to a laboratory in Madrid in an attempt to identify the baby's biological parents.

According to "La Región", investigators are also not ruling out that the death may have occurred elsewhere in the province and that the body was later moved to Allariz inside the freezer itself.

The investigation remains open and is being conducted under judicial secrecy, ordered by the court in Ourense in charge of the case. Officers are trying to determine when and how the baby died and to clarify how the body ended up hidden in the chest freezer.

World.title: Cyberattacks target Italian foreign minister and company behind Brenner Base Tunnel project
World.content:
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Saturday that he was being targeted by hackers over Italy's support for Ukraine.

 

In a post on social media, Tajani said "cybercriminals" had been sharing his personal data on the dark web over a number of days.

He said the hackers were "seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," while also targeting his family.

"Our stance on Ukraine is the political reason why I have been targeted: for these criminal organisations, defending the freedom of a sovereign state and taking a clear stand in favour of a nation’s democracy and independence is dangerous," he wrote.

In a statement released on Saturday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her support for Tajani.

“The sale of confidential information concerning public officials is a cause for great concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination,” Meloni said.

It comes as the company behind the under-construction Brenner Base Tunnel project - a 55 km rail link between Innsbruck in Austria and Fortezza in Italy - confirmed it had also been hit by a cyberattack in recent weeks.

BBT SE said the incident occurred on 17 October and that the company had quickly "activated its cyber security protocols, immediately isolating the affected systems and enlisting the support of external cyber security specialists to carry out the necessary forensic analysis."

The attack reportedly involved non-public data that was stolen through access to the company's internet-connected network.

The Tiroler Tageszeitung, which first reported the attack, said initial investigations pointed to a pro-Russian hacker group known as Everest.

World.title: US launches new targeted strikes on Iran as Trump claims progress in talks with Tehran
World.content:
US military carried out what it said were limited new airstrikes in southern Iran on Friday night, further raising fears across the Middle East and among Gulf states sparked by the possible resumption of an all-out war, but Qatar and the US insisted that the negotiations for a diplomatic settlement are continuing.

 

US President Donald Trump told the media on Friday evening that a “minor” military action targeted Iranian air defence systems on Qeshm Island.

“They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," Trump said.

Trump insisted that “we are not fighting” and made it clear that in parallel with the “minor strike,” the US has made “a lot of progress with Iran” with the ongoing negotiations spearheaded by chief mediator Qatar.

“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal,” Trump said.

Iranian state-run media reported that two missiles hit the Suza area of Qeshm Island without identifying the targets or the damage, while locals went on social media reporting the explosions.

Earlier on Friday, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) claimed that it shot down a US military drone over southern Iran, but the US did not confirm the claim.

Friday’s strike is the first since the Democratic Party scored a major victory in midterm elections, with officials and analysts tying the result to voters' disagreement with Trump’s decision to enter into a war with Iran.

The attack follows another series of what the US military called defensive strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the Strait of Hormuz and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

In an earlier speech in Florida on Friday, Trump appeared to defend his Iran war decision by stating that “if I allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, today there would be no Israel,” and that “Israel would have been wiped off the face of the Earth.”

Qatar presents new proposals to Iranian officials

Qatar rushed to deny conflicting reports circulating on Friday night about the purported collapse of the negotiations, insisting in a statement that “Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with the United States and Iran to support ongoing negotiations.”

Earlier on Friday, two Middle East government officials told AP that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the US about Tehran’s nuclear program.

But one of the officials stressed that the Iranians, at least at the moment, remain unwilling to engage in negotiations with the Trump administration over their atomic activities until the US agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement, according to the AP.

Differences with Iran over its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue, and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the more than eight-month-long war.

Tehran insists on several concessions from the US which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks are the ending of the US military blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli military operations in Lebanon.

Meanwhile, a flurry of diplomatic phone calls between leaders in the Gulf and beyond indicates intense efforts to prevent the resumption of an all-out war which would have devastating consequences for the region.

Trump called Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani on Friday night to discuss “the ongoing diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region (and) to pave the road for reaching a comprehensive agreement that resolves the crisis and ensures security and stability in the region,” according to Qatar’s national news agency.

“In this regard, His Highness emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region, and safeguarding freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies,” the statement said.

Also on Friday, US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth spoke with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, according to the Qatari government.

In parallel, Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani told an Oxford University event on Friday that “for the past couple of weeks, we have worked with colleagues in the US administration who have very genuine intentions to find a way to contain the situation and de-escalate it,” as this crisis “cannot be left unresolved”.

He insisted that the ongoing negotiations aim “to prevent the situation from spiralling out of control,” and that “thanks also to some wise voices in Tehran, we have prevented that from getting out of control”.

“We will never have a perfect peace deal, but we cannot just wait for this moment of a perfect deal and avoid having a good deal,” Qatar’s prime minister said. "Our engagement did not stop and will not stop.”

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he also held phone calls with no less than 12 foreign ministers over the last two days to explain Iran’s “fundamental positions".

In an Instagram post, Araghchi called for “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.

Iran’s military continued its threatening rhetoric on Saturday, with army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia warning that “we will never allow the enemy’s bases in the region to be rebuilt,” Iran’s Fars news agency reported.

Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department and Iran specialist Danny Citrinowicz said in a post on X that "Tehran is not intimidated by the prospect of another confrontation with the United States and Israel."

"If attacked, Iran is likely to seek to expand the war from the outset, targeting Gulf states it views as a vulnerable pressure point against Washington."

"Tehran is also improving its missile capabilities and preparing its regional partners, including Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Iraqi Shiite militias, for possible involvement," Citrinowicz said.

"The Iranian leadership believes it can withstand another military campaign, impose significant costs on the United States and its allies, and ultimately force Washington to accept the regime's survival," he added.

"The central danger is that Washington may envision another short military operation, while Tehran is preparing for a much broader and potentially prolonged regional war."

World.title: US offers $20 million reward and 'possible relocation' for information on 'Iran’s nuclear program'
World.content:
The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million as well as "possible relocation" for information on "Iran’s nuclear program," according to the US military.

 

The State Department's Rewards for Justice initiative is offering the reward to people who can provide knowledge of its "facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above," US Central Command said.

The Rewards for Justice programme was established in 1984 to offer money for information that could help protect national security.

In a statement on the reward, the State Department said: "The regime’s lack of compliance with the IAEA on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges."

President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that US forces have "obliterated" Iran’s nuclear facilities.

"We're also ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said on Friday during a speech at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. "They will never have it. Not even close. They're not close."

"If they did have it, if we didn't go in with those beautiful B2 bombers a little more than a year ago, if I allowed them to have it today, there would be no Israel," he added.

Tehran's nuclear ambitions have been central to negotiations over ending the Iran war, which began in late February following US and Israeli strikes on the country.

Trump's comments came as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian confirmed that his government was continuing efforts to resolve the conflict through dialogue.

World.title: South Africa's ANC facing worst-ever performance in local elections
World.content:
Near-final results show South Africa's once dominant ANC will see its lowest-ever vote percentage. The party is taking the blame for shoddy municipal services, including water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) is heading for an historically poor election performance, with the near-final tally from Wednesday's municipal polls showing it coming in with just over 30% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said Saturday in sharing the results after 98% of votes were counted.

South African voters in 2026 are angry about water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are other pressing issues.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed the poor performance as of Saturday evening. However, during the week, he admitted in his weekly presidential letter that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC's steady decline with voters

Although the ANC will still be the single largest party by overall vote percentage, it had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

DA opposition holds large cities

South Africa is now looking at complex coalition negotiations for municipal level governing alliances.

Runner up in the polls looks to be the pro-business, center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), coming in at 24% of the votes.

The DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

World.title: More than 40,000 gather as Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass in Uruguay
World.content:
Massive crowds have turned out for the pontiff as he celebrates the first Mass of his South America tour. A nighttime prayer vigil in Montevideo is expected to draw more than 60,000 young people.

The Vatican and local authorities in western Uruguay say an estimated 40,000 people turned out on Saturday morning to participate in the first Mass of Pope Leo XIV's 12-day, three-nation tour of South America.

The Vatican said 30,000 people from Uruguay as well as neighboring Argentina and Brazil had registered for the event, adding that another 10,000 had braved the rain to attend the religious service, which took place in Paysandu — a city on the Uruguay River, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) west of the capital Montevideo.

Leo, who underwent surgery for lung cancer on October 13, was greeted by throngs of cheering fans as he made his way from the local airport to Paysandu's sprawling Paris London Park.

"He's the representative of Christ but he's human," said Soledad Sanchez, who told France's AFP news agency that she had traveled far to be in Paysandu.

"We weren't sure if he could make it but he pushed through for us," said Sanchez as tears welled up in her eyes, "He made it here to give us a message of peace because he knows our world needs it right now."

What to know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why are young people reacting so strongly to Pope Leo XIV?

The 71-year-old US-born pontiff, who holds US, Peruvian and Vatican citizenship, is seeking to raise interest in the Catholic Church in Uruguay, South America's most secular country, as a remedy for helping the nation and its citizens cope with the troubles of the modern world.

Saturday morning's Mass was dedicated to the Blessed Jacinto Vera, who was appointed Uruguay's first bishop by Pope Leo XIII in 1878.

On Friday, the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics spoke of Bishop Vera, noting that he had walked the countryside and helped the poor, adding that those whom he encountered "found something of Christ's goodness" in him.

Leo will underscore the need for that kind of outreach on Saturday afternoon when he visits a Montevideo neighborhood beset by drug violence and in which the Church has invested in public housing and rehabilitation projects for addicts.

At Pope Leo's final event in the country — a prayer vigil in Montevideo's Centenary Stadium that is expected to draw some 60,000 young faithful — the pontiff will call on young people to reject religious indifference and turn to Christ's teachings.

Leo's emphasis on charity and brotherly love has struck a deep chord with young people in Uruguay and elsewhere.

One 18-year-old attendee at Saturday morning's Mass told AFP: "I wouldn't call myself religious, but I like this pope. He has a really good message for humanity. Even for non-believers, there is something to take from his ideas."

On Sunday, Pope Leo will depart for Argentina, where he will meet with President Javier Milei, a libertarian-populist and close ally to US President Donald Trump, who previously lashed out at the leader of the world's largest Christian faith over his calls to end wars and cruel immigration policies.

World.title: At least 6 killed in shooting in Polish city of Krakow, police say
World.content:
At least six people were killed and fifteen injured after a shooter opened fire from a car in Krakow's main market square.

At least six people, four women and tow men, were killed and fifteen injured in a shooting near the main market square in the southern Polish city of Krakow on Saturday.

The perpetrator, a 24-year-old Polish citizen who acted alone, was wounded during an exchange of fire with police, authorities said.

He has been taken to a hospital, police said.

Shooter aimed at random people, police say

According to Krakow police, the gunman aimed at random people as he drove by the city's main square. Among the wounded are police officers.

"At around 3 pm [1400 GMT], a man who had driven into the market square in a car began shooting at random people from inside the vehicle," police said on X.

"The perpetrator was shot by police ‌officers and is currently being ‌transported ​to a hospital," police said.

According to Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, the perpetrator wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest and used a long gun in the attack.

Numerous other weapons and ammunition were found in the perpetrator's car.

Initially, authorities urged people in the immediate vicinity to evacuate to a safe place.

Police personnel at the site of shooting Image: Jakub Włodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/REUTERS

Police secure an area near the city's main market square Image: Jakub Włodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/REUTERS

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk calls it a 'tragic' incident

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted on X that police are investigating the attack and called it a "tragic" incident to have occurred.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki wrote on X that his thoughts were with the victims and wounded, as well as their families.

In the wake of the shooting, European politicians showed solidarity with Poland.

"I am deeply saddened by the events in Krakow. My thoughts are with the victims and their families," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote on X, adding that "Germany stands alongside Poland as a friend and partner during these difficult times."

Krakow is located about 250 kilometers (155 miles) from Warsaw, the capital of Poland.

With a population of over 800,000, Krakow is Poland's second-largest city, as well as a popular tourist destination. Key attractions include the main square, Wawel Castle, and the cathedral on Wawel Hill.

World.title: Journalism and AI: Who owns the news?
World.content:
Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?

Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events.

A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences.

Explaining what is happening in the world, why it matters, and what it means has traditionally been the work of journalism. Media organizations send reporters into the field, commission investigations and conduct research, producing stories that help audiences understand global events. But as more people turn to AI tools for information, the relationship between those producing journalism and those distributing it is changing.

"In the past, search engines like Google indexed our websites and directed users to their articles, generating traffic in return," Julia Becker, publisher of Funke Media Group, told a panel at the Global Media Forum (GMF) in Berlin. "But now that exchange has broken down."

"AI companies draw on our quality reporting to generate answers, yet the reporting itself often remains largely invisible by the end of this process," said DW Director General Barbara Massing in a keynote address at the forum.

Their remarks reflect a worry that is growing across the media industry. Publicly available news is copied and summarized by AI chatbots, while news organizations are becoming less and less able to rely on the money and visibility that used to come from distributing that work.

Publishers, legal experts, and tech companies debated who should pay for journalism used in AI systems at the Global Media Forum in Berlin Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

Journalism and AI: A growing imbalance?

There has been growing concern about how copyrighted material is collected, used, and reproduced by artificial intelligence, and whether the companies that build those systems should pay the people and organizations that created the material.

Media houses are now pressing "Big Tech" companies to ask permission before using their work and to pay for it.

In October, German broadcasters ARD and RTL, along with the country's Federal Association of Digital Publishers and Newspaper Publishers (BDZV) and the Association of Private Media (VAUNET), called for stronger copyright protections for media companies.

In the US, lawsuits are adding pressure. The New York Times has sued internet company Brave Softwar for allegedly using its content without permission and getting around its paywall.

Meanwhile, legal institutions in the EU, including the European Court of Justice (ECJ) are examining whether AI-generated answers can themselves infringe copyright.

In February, a coalition of media organizations, including the Guardian, the BBC, and the Financial Times, called for rules that would give publishers more control over how AI systems copy and reproduce their content.

The problem goes beyond whether AI companies may use journalism. It also concerns how publishers and journalists can get paid when their work becomes part of the answers AI systems generate.

"AI systems shouldn't just use quality journalism. They should also pay for it," Massing said.

Is the internet dying? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How could AI companies pay for the content they use?

Professor Martin Senftleben, who directs the Institute for Information Law at the University of Amsterdam, separates two ways AI companies use journalistic material: Training their models and generating responses to individual user questions.

Payment for training is a more complicated legal question, he said. The more urgent issue is what happens when an AI system uses journalism to answer a question in real time.

He argued that European copyright law may already offer a way to address part of the problem. Under existing EU law, publishers and journalists may be able to claim payment collectively, without waiting for a new legal framework.

"What are we waiting for? Germany is a large member state. This should be introduced in Germany," he told the forum.

One option, Senftleben suggested, is a legally required payment system in which every AI response that draws on journalism triggers a payment. A collecting organization would gather the money and distribute it among publishers and journalists, in the same way that music royalties are collected and distributed.

Once such a system exists, publishers and authors could use its rates as a starting point when negotiating individual licensing deals with AI companies.

Existing deals and concerns about too much regulation

Lutz Mache, senior manager of government affairs and public policy at Google, told the GMF panel that Google is willing to negotiate agreements with German media companies and to discuss new AI products with them.

Google has also started testing other ways to pay publishers for their contributions to AI-generated answers. Its "AI Contribution" pilot, which is being tested with selected publishers, aims to reward content that plays a significant role in answers produced by products such as Gemini and AI Overviews. But the program is still an early experiment, not a general payment system open to all publishers.

Google says its ancillary copyright agreements cover more than 800 German publications with payments already being made Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI have recently said they support clearer, standardized signals that let website owners state whether their content may be used to train AI models.

However, not everyone thinks more regulation is the answer.

Jörg Heidrich, a lawyer who specializes in technology law and serves as AI commissioner at the German media company Heise, warned against adding new rules without considering their effects on the wider tech sector.

Europe has already fallen behind in the global AI race, he argued. More regulation, he warned, could make it harder for European companies to compete with major providers based elsewhere.

Heidrich also pointed to smaller players, including startups, independent developers, and research institutions. They depend on access to data to build and train AI systems. He argued that the debate over copyright and payment risks overlooking these groups, and that new restrictions could hurt their work.

World.title: Son of Iran's shah receives 'Freedom Prize' in Frankfurt
World.content:
18,000 people gathered in Frankfurt to show support for Reza Pahlavi, the son of the Iranian monarch ousted in 1979. Factions in the opposition have accused him of not distancing himself from his father's rule.

Iranian opposition leader Reza Pahlavi on Saturday received a "Freedom Prize" in Frankfurt in the central German state of Hesse.

Some 18,000 people rallied to show support for Reza Pahlavi, according to a police statement.

The event was held at St Paul's Church. The building hosted the Germany's first-ever elected parliament in 1848-1849, known as the Frankfurt Assembly.

Pahlavi is the son of the last shah of Iran, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi, an autocrat who fled into exile after being deposed in a 1979 revolution.

The 1979 revolution was followed by the transformation of Iran into an Islamic republic and the consolidation of power around the Shiite Muslim clergy.

Pahlavi was handed the prize by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is tied to the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP).

Thousands of supporters, mostly of Iranian origin, rallied in Frankfurt in Pahlavi's support Image: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

What did Reza Pahlavi say about the prize?

Pahlavi said that Iran "is a country not waiting to be taught democracy, this is a country being prevented from practicing it."

"A people ready to die for the right to vote is willing to exercise the right to vote," he said.

Rights groups say thousands were killed in a government crackdown on protests in January.

"You could not have chosen a people who better understand the meaning of the word 'freedom,'" he said.

He also stressed that he was receiving the prize only as a "trustee" until a democratically-elected government comes to power in Iran.

"I hold it only temporarily," he said. "One day I will place it in the hands of its rightful owners, not on foreign soil but in the capital, Tehran."

The speech was accompanied by chants of "Long live the shah, long live Iran!" from the crowd.

Pahlavi has in the past offered to lead a transitional government in the event of a democratic transition in the West Asian country and has said he does not aim to use this proposed position to reinstate the Iranian monarchy under his father's dynasty, instead planning to leave the decision to a later referendum.

Some in the audience of Pahlavi's speech yelled out 'long live the shah, long live Iran!' Image: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

Iranians criticize Freedom Prize for Pahlavi prince

While Pahlavi has emerged as a figurehead for factions within the anti-government protest movement, others have criticized him for his vocal support for Israel and have accused him of failing to distance himself from his father's autocratic rule.

Around 200 prisoners held in Iran signed a letter protesting Pahlavi's receipt of the prize, Sahar Sanaie, spokeswoman for the Society for German-Iranians in Hesse, was cited by the AFP news agency as saying.

The letter described him as the symbol of a "bygone dictatorship."

The Frankfurt branches of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the environmentalist Greens boycotted the event and said he could not be considered a legitimate representative of the Iranian people.

Meanwhile, the socialist Left Party argued that the church could not by used as a venue for the event due to Frankfurt city statutes that prevent the use of places of worship for political gatherings.

World.title: After victory in the midterms, what next for US Democrats?
World.content:
Donald Trump's Republican party has lost its majority in both chambers of the US Congress. But the president still has a lot of power — and the Democrats have yet to agree on how best to use theirs.

A "blue wave" has rolled across the United States. Some are even calling it a "blue tsunami." The Democrats scored a decisive victory in the midterm elections on November 3, wresting the majority from President Donald Trump's Republicans in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. They also won gubernatorial elections in former Republican strongholds such as Texas.

Pictures from Tuesday evening show Democrat politicians and supporters across the country celebrating, hugging, even weeping with joy. However, as the White House reminded Americans in a post on X the day after the elections: "Trump is still your president."

Trump has the power to veto any proposed legislation Congress puts before him, and his veto can only be overruled by a two-thirds majority. Also, in the past he has, on occasion, simply ignored the Congress's decision.

How much power do the Democrats have?

Patrick Malone, professor at the public administration and policy department at American University in Washington DC, told DW that a presidential veto is not necessarily the end of the matter — even though the Democrats don't have a two-thirds majority in either Congressional chamber.

"There are Republicans, especially on the House side, who are not going to want to tie themselves that closely to Trump anymore," says Malone. "The Republicans that survived had a very strong message sent to them. It would be illogical and foolish for them to point to a neighboring district [that turned blue] and say, 'Well, that can't happen here.'"

For that reason, Malone predicts that Republicans and Democrats may come together to overrule a Trump veto. "It could happen very easily."

The day after his party's dismal showing in the elections, Donald Trump focussed on the construction of his White House ballroom Image: Mandel Ngan/AFP

Will Trump be impeached again?

A question at the front of many people's minds is: Might the Democrats make another attempt at impeachment? One possible basis for this would be that Trump started the war with Iran without congressional approval. The US Constitution says only Congress has the power to declare war. But as commander-in-chief, the president also has a degree of military authority. How far this extends without Congressional approval is legally disputed.

From January 2027, Democrats will have the simple majority required to bring charges against him in the House of Representatives. They will not, however, be able to muster the two-thirds majority in the Senate that would be needed for a conviction and Trump's removal from office. Some Democrats say it is nonetheless imperative that the impeachment process be initiated, as a way of keeping the president in check.

Others remain skeptical. "If we make Donald Trump the center of our focus, we will lose this moment in history," the Democratic senator Cory Booker said. "We need to deal with the American people's problems."

This does not mean that Democrats won't try to launch investigations into Trump, or into members of his family or government. Quite the reverse. Malone believes the Democrats in Congress take their control function very seriously and will definitely initiate investigations. These, he says, serve a purpose beyond the documented outcome: "Another thing about Congressional investigations: They have a much stronger impact on public opinion than on legislation. They catch people's attention."

What a Democrat-led Congress could mean for EU, trans-Atlantic unity To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will Hegseth be sacked as secretary of defense?

While Trump will most likely get to keep his job, Pete Hegseth might be about to lose his. Observers assume the Democrats will demand a different secretary of defense. "There's a lot of speculation about what's going to happen to Pete Hegseth," says Brandon Conradis, a former DW journalist who is now an editor at Bloomberg Government in Washington DC. Whether Trump will actually fire Hegseth is a decision for the president. All the Democrats can do is exert political pressure.

From January onward, the Democrats will have a majority in Congress, which is where decisions are made on how government funds are spent. Conradis says one possibility for the Democrats to get their way would be to link the financing of Trump's pet projects to specific conditions. "One thing Democrats might do is say, 'Look, if you want more funding for these conflicts, Pete Hegseth needs to go.'"

As secretary of defense, Hegseth is being held at least partially responsible for the US's relative lack of success in the war with Iran. This could also be a reason for Trump to fire him.

Democrats not a unified bloc

After their success in the midterms, the Democrats have been enjoying a brief moment of unity. But Malone says it won't last. "The Democratic Party was unified for maybe 24, 36 hours. Now they're not really going to unify for a bit."

Unlike Germany, the US does not have governing coalitions at the federal level. There are, however, various political groupings within the Democratic Party itself. On the left wing of the political spectrum there are the progressive Democrats, including, among others, the prominent young representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. "[Progressives] have very aggressive policy ideas, whether it be environment or social programs," comments Malone.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez campaigning for the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who was elected senator for Michigan Image: Andrew Roth/ZUMA/IMAGO

In the middle are the mainstream liberal Democrats, who see themselves as politically pragmatic and good at compromising. But there are also moderates. "This is an important group on the Democratic side," Malone says. "There were a lot of Democrats [in the midterms] who won elections in former red districts or really, really conservative blue districts. They won't be able to go back to their districts and say, 'Look, AOC wants this.'"

It will be no easy task for Democrats in Congress to agree on one clear direction. But many believe that it's vital that they do. "They're going to have to figure out a positive governing agenda that they can all agree on," says Malone. Just opposing Trump won't be enough for the Democrats to sustain their current success, the pundit argues.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for cyberattack on minister
World.content:
Antonio Tajani has said hackers published personal data stolen from him as Giorgia Meloni blamed pro-Russia criminals for the incident. The news follows a string of bomb threats that have grounded flights across the EU.

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Saturday announced that personal data had been stolen from him and published on the Darknet.

In a statement on the social media platform X, Tajani said he had been targeted because of the Italian government's "position on Ukraine," and claimed criminals were "prepared to pay for other details on me and my loved ones," adding, "For days, cybercriminals have been spreading my personal data on the dark web and seeking other information, in fact exposing me and my family to new threats and intimidation."

Italy, like other EU and NATO member states, has provided humanitarian and military assistance to Ukraine as it continues to defend itself against a nearly five-year Russian invasion.

The foreign minister did not specify what kind of information had been shared but suggested the criminal activity targeting him remained ongoing.

"I will not allow myself to be intimidated in any way," he said, adding, "I will continue working to defend my ministry, and Italy, and I will further strengthen the ties and cooperation to protect ourselves together."

What did Italian Prime Minister Meloni say about the hack?

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was unambiguous in her assertion that "pro-Russian hackers" were behind the security breach, calling it "a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination."

Accusations of Russian involvement in the Tajani hack come as Europe reels from a dizzying number of suspected "hybrid attacks" thought to be orchestrated by the Kremlin.

These have included drone incursions and sabotage in NATO territories, as well as attacks on food supplies, and most recently, threats against media outlets as well as a string of bomb threats that have forced the cancellation and rerouting of airline flights in the bloc.

World.title: Yemen: 22 killed in strike near Sanaa, Houthis say
World.content:
The Iran-backed Houthi rebel group accused Saudi Arabia of hitting several homes in the village of al-Shariya near the Yemeni capital. There was no initial comment from Riyadh.

Airstrikes on the village of al-Shariya near the Yemeni capital Sanaa killed at least 22 people on Saturday, the Health Ministry for Yemen's Houthi rebels.

At least 30 people were wounded, according to the ministry.

Ministry spokesperson Anees Alasbahi told the Associated Press that Saudi Arabia had carried out the strikes.

He said in a post on X that that the strikes had hit several homes.

The Houthi-linked Al-Masirah broadcaster showed purported footage of the attack showing piles of debris and wounded people in a hospital.

There was no initial comment from Saudi Arabia on the reported strikes.

More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is the state of the war in Yemen?

The Iran-backed Houthis have controlled Sanaa and large swathes of western and northern Yemen since the outbreak of the southern Arabian country's civil war in 2014, while Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's Aden-based internationally recognized government.

A yearslong truce in the war fell apart over summer, with the Houthis pushing forward in an offensive and taking more territory along the Red Sea coast in September, including the port city of Mokha and strategic islands in the crucial Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The rebel group has also hit targets in Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities and military infrastructure, and has also targeted Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

The United Nations says over 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since the intensification of fighting.

Also on Saturday, pro-government media reported that Yemeni government forces had pushed back a Houthi attack on the al-Aqroud front in the contested Taiz province in southwestern Yemen.

Saudi-led coalition forces also reported that they had intercepted a Houthi missile launched towards Saudi Arabia's Riyadh province.

On Friday, an airstrike on a market in southern Yemen killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials.

The Houthis and Yemeni government forces traded accusations of being behind the strike.

World.title: Sánchez llama a una votación masiva el 29-N: “La mejor receta contra la involución se llama movilización”
World.content:
Los socialistas son conscientes de que el desánimo en sus bases puede ser el peor enemigo de cara a las elecciones generales del 29-N, con la mayoría de encuestas apuntando a una mayoría suficiente del Partido Popular y Vox para gobernar. Por eso el presidente-candidato Pedro Sánchez ha enarbolado este sábado, en Tarragona, la bandera de la movilización. “La mejor receta contra la involución se llama movilización. Si votamos en masa, mandamos a casa a Feijóo y Abascal. A votar y a ganar cuatro años más”, ha asegurado ante unas 2.000 personas. “¡Hasta el Papa ha votado!”, ha añadido Sánchez, en referencia al hecho inédito de que León XIV hiciera pública su decisión de participar en las elecciones de medio mandato de EE UU y donde hay pocas razones para pensar que apoyara a los republicanos de Donald Trump.

Ya en las pasadas elecciones generales del 23-J, una parte del electorado progresista -hasta dos millones de personas- decidió quedarse en casa o votó por partidos que no obtuvieron representación y el PSOE está lanzado a no dejar escapar ningún voto. Sánchez, que ha estado acompañado de la vicepresidenta europea Teresa Ribera y del president de la Generalitat catalana, Salvador Illa, ha apelado a la movilización con un discurso en clave de soberanía nacional y recordando que su apuesta es poner a la ciudadanía en el centro. “No vamos a permitir que España sea el patio trasero de la internacional ultraderechista”, ha advertido, recordando que la eficiencia de los servicios públicos no se verá supeditada a grandes intereses económicos internacionales.

“¡Hasta el Papa de Roma ha votado en EE UU!“, ha exclamado el presidente del Gobierno entre aplausos, en un intento de remarcar la singularidad de la coyuntura democrática. “No se que vota pero sí que defiende”, ha añadido para después recordar su defensa de los inmigrantes y los más necesitado. El mensaje tiene como marco Tarragona, la capital de una de las provincias en las que el Partido Popular ha optado por no presentarse al Senado, gracias a un acuerdo con Vox. De ahí que la idea de supeditación se usara con dos sentidos. “Este 29-N diremos que España se gobierna desde España, no desde Washington, desde Israel o desde Moscú”, ha asegurado, insistiendo en el mensaje del viernes en la noche en Valencia, con que se rompió la interrupción de la precampaña por el accidente ferroviario.

“Lo siento mucho por Santiago Abascal y por Alberto Núñez Feijóo, que se querían montar a la ola ultraderechista, pero esta se está desmoronando”, ha seguido Sánchez antes de hacer un repaso también por los resultados electorales en Brasil o en Israel. Tanto él como Illa, que le ha precedido en la palabra, han puesto en esos hitos sus esperanzas para un cambio en la tendencia de las encuestas. El primer secretario del PSC ha defendido que “los votos le pueden ganar al algoritmo” y de ahí sus llamamientos a la movilización. “Nada está escrito, el futuro lo escribimos nosotros”. El president ha recordado que, en las últimas tres citas electorales internacionales donde la ultraderecha y la izquierda han topado, los resultados también parecían escritos de antemano, y que un vuelco fue posible.

Sánchez ha intentado tirar de épica para transmitir la necesidad de movilizarse -“Vamos a seguir siendo el faro, vamos a seguir inspirando al mundo”- y ha pedido una “mayoría amplia y progresista” no solo para ganarles la partida a Vox y al PP sino para poder seguir avanzando en derechos sociales. Por ejemplo, para seguir revalorizando las pensiones o blindar el derecho al aborto en la Constitución, algo que no pudo conseguir en este mandato. “Ahora que vuelven los cantos del PP y de Vox de revisar el aborto, yo me comprometo a que lo vamos a blindar”, ha dicho. Necesitaría para ello el apoyo de 3/5 partes de las Cortes.

El segundo eje ha sido la gestión de las crisis. Con el accidente ferroviario de Toledo aún reciente —69 muertos— y con el aniversario de la dana valenciana sobrevolando también el mitin de Tarragona, Sánchez ha reivindicado que su Ejecutivo “siempre ha dado la cara frente a los que han dado la espalda”. No ha necesitado ni referirse directamente al exlíder valenciano Carlos Mazón para que su nombre retumbara entre los asistentes.

La batalla por Tarragona

La elección de Tarragona para este este mitin de precampaña no ha sido gratuita. Es una de las tres provincias donde, en virtud del pacto con Vox para el Senado, el Partido Popular no presentará candidatura. Lo han recordado tanto Illa como el candidato por Barcelona, el ministro de Industria Jordi Hereu. “Tarragona es el kilómetro cero de la rendición del PP a Vox”, ha dicho el presidente de la Generalitat.

“El 29-N, el presidente del PP en Cataluña, Alejandro Fernández [que es de Tarragona] votará a Vox”, ha espetado el primer secretario del PSC. “Como si el Senado no fuera importante. Es nuestra Cámara territorial y la han convertido en un ariete contra el Gobierno”, ha dicho. Hereu, por su parte, le ha agradecido a Sánchez su apuesta por la convivencia en Cataluña tras los años convulsos del procés. “Es el que ha dicho al otro lado del Mediterráneo que el único camino es la paz. Por eso, Pedro, te apoyaremos”, ha remachado.

Ambos también han recordado que el candidato catalán de Vox Jordi de la Fuente tendrá que sentarse en el banquillo en julio del año próximo acusado de participar en el asalto al centro de menores de El Masnou en 2019. Y han contrapuesto ese perfil al de la doctora Ione Montalvo, cabeza de lista del PSC por Tarragona.

World.title: Feijóo, desde Valladolid: “El PSOE está a punto de canonizar al señor Puente, qué falta de respeto”
World.content:
El PP ha elegido Valladolid para retomar los actos de precampaña tras el parón por el accidente de trenes de Urda. Valladolid, ciudad de la que el exministro Óscar Puente fue alcalde durante ocho años. Por eso, Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha querido dejar claro desde el primer momento que la ubicación del mitin de este sábado estaba escogida desde hace tiempo y que, en todo caso, si se tratara de protestar por el accidente de Urda, se habrían plantado delante de La Moncloa, porque para el líder del Partido Popular el culpable máximo del siniestro ferroviario es el presidente Pedro Sánchez y la “corrupción” larvada en el seno del Ministerio de Transportes. Eso sí, Feijóo ha centrado buena parte de su discurso en el siniestro, que dejó 69 fallecidos, y ha censurado que los dirigentes del PSOE y el propio Sánchez defiendan como “dignidad” política el gesto hecho por Puente al dimitir.

“Están a punto de canonizar en la basílica de San Pedro al señor Puente. El PSOE ya le nombró beato, están a punto de santificarlo. ¡Pero qué falta de respeto!“, ha ironizado Feijóo. ”Esperaba de un partido con más de 100 años un poco de respeto por la verdad, por la ética, por la dignidad", ha añadido el líder del PP, asegurando que todo forma parte del “relato” y que de ahora en adelante, con la vuelta a la campaña, los socialistas van a tratar de “manipular a la gente” bajo el discurso de que no todos los políticos son iguales. “La dignidad es la mejor España que aparece en los peores momentos”, ha remachado Feijóo, ensalzando a los efectivos de la Guardia Civil, de la Policía Nacional, bomberos y sanitarios implicados en atender a las víctimas de la tragedia. También a los vecinos de Urda que se movilizaron tras el choque. “Lo del PSOE es otra cosa y no nos representan”.

Feijóo habló este sábado por primera vez tras conocerse las últimas pesquisas de la Unidad Central Operativa (UCO) de la Guardia Civil en el marco del caso Koldo. Investigaciones que el PP liga con los problemas en las infraestructuras ferroviarias. “[En] este Ministerio de Transportes primero fue la corrupción, después fue el machismo, después fue la incompetencia y después la soberbia”, ha lanzado Feijóo. Ahora nos dicen que hay que poner a un ministro provisional”, ha continuado en referencia a la designación de Carlos Cuerpo al frente de la cartera. Para los populares ya no hay más salida que “el cambio necesario”, según su lema de campaña, del Gobierno de Sánchez por el de Feijóo.

En caso de ser investido tras el 29-N, el líder del PP ha prometido que hará una auditoría a fondo de las cuentas de La Moncloa, entre las que destaca la del Ministerio de Transporte. “Si el dinero de la seguridad de los trenes ha acabado en el Partido Socialista o en el bolsillo de alguno de los suyos, no bastará con que se marchen”, ha deslizado Feijóo. “Tendrán que responder ante la justicia y, si han robado el dinero destinado a proteger la vida de los españoles, tendrán que salir del poder para entrar en la cárcel”, ha espetado.

El Gobierno de las orgías

Al margen del accidente de tren, el candidato del PP ha enumerado también como problemas claves de España la crisis de Ceuta, la falta de poder adquisitivo de los jóvenes o la “inseguridad” de las calles. “Toca garantizar una España mejor para las mujeres. Sois las que más sufrís la inseguridad y el descontrol. Las mujeres que levantan este país merecen que el Gobierno de las orgías se vaya”, ha aseverado Feijóo, con el foco puesto en la lucha contra la inmigración, bandera en la que pugna con Vox. De ahí que el PP arranque la campaña el próximo jueves por la noche con la pegada de carteles en Badalona —feudo del alcalde y número uno al Congreso por Barcelona, Xavier García Albiol, y enseña de la lucha del partido contra la inmigración ilegal y la okupación—.

Los populares, con un gran poder territorial tanto autonómico como local, buscan apuntalar la caravana de Feijóo con actos paralelos de sus barones autonómicos. Pero también con la movilización de las Diputaciones, que tienen orden de recorrerse las provincias sin descanso hasta la cita en las urnas. “Que nadie piense, a pesar de todo, que está hecho”, ha asegurado el líder del PP en Valladolid. “Que nadie piense que van a venir solos los votos. El 29 hay que ir a votar, hay que ir a votar todos, hay que ir los que en algún momento votaron al Partido Socialista y hoy se avergüenzan de ello, hay que ir a votar aquellos que nos votaron a nosotros y ahora creen que votando a otros nosotros vamos a gobernar”, ha finalizado llamando a la concentración del voto en torno al Partido Popular.

World.title: Irene Montero llama a secundar la huelga en su presentación con Rufián en Madrid: “Hay que paralizar el país”
World.content:
El atuendo de él, tan comentado en el primer acto conjunto hace dos semanas en Barcelona, permite a Gabriel Rufián comenzar su discurso con una broma: “Hoy había que ir de amarillo. Así de conectados estamos, porque esto no lo habíamos hablado. Amarillo de ERC, ya la hemos fichado totalmente”, dice mirando a Irene Montero, que lleva un jersey de idéntico color al suyo. Los cabezas de lista de Podemos y ERC a las generales del 29-N han presentado este sábado a mediodía su propuesta política en el corazón de Madrid con alusiones a la actualidad, como la huelga general por la vivienda o la corrupción. “El 11 de noviembre hay que llenar las calles y hay que paralizar el país para que bajen los alquileres, los alimentos y la energía”, ha arengado la candidata a cuatro días de la convocatoria.

Sobre un escenario circular en el Espacio Delicias de la capital montado para el espectáculo circense La Isla de Nunca Jamás –un emplazamiento que ha debido improvisarse en los últimos días después de que el acto quedase cancelado la semana pasada por la catástrofe de Urda–, ambos han cargado contra el Gobierno y la coalición de izquierdas (“el Frente somos nosotros”, ha desafiado Rufián pese a desearle “suerte” a todos los progresistas). “Estamos en un sitio peculiar, donde nos dejan. Pero la cosa no va de tenerlo todo, sino de hacerlo todo con lo que tienes”, ha justificado la eurodiputada, arrancando los aplausos del público.

El acto, presentado por la actriz Kiti Mánver, que ha llamado a “levantarse y subir mucho el volumen siguiendo el ejemplo de los jóvenes de Francia y de quienes hicieron en España de Maricarmen un símbolo”, ha supuesto el regreso oficial a la precampaña del partido y es el primero de Montero y Rufián en Madrid, que ha dejado a cientos de personas fuera por las limitaciones de aforo.

La exministra de Igualdad, que tiene por lema en estos comicios “Paz, casa y trabajo”, ha hablado de nuevo de vivienda, llamando a secundar el paro del próximo miércoles, cuestionando a los empresarios que elevan los precios de los alquileres y también a “los gobiernos cómplices que, pudiendo, no han hecho nada”, en referencia directa a la coalición entre PSOE y Sumar. “Esa es la gran brecha de la sociedad, no entre derecha e izquierda, sino entre arriba y abajo, entre el 1% y el 99%. Nos hacen mirar para el lado equivocado y no para arriba”, ha reiterado en uno de los argumentos desplegados en estas elecciones.
