This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

Now, it seems, spending is mandatory.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.

As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?

Stirred up

The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.

Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.

The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.

Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.

On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.

The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

“The latest wording is that they (head office) encourage us to ask people to leave,” says Zhang Yi, a part-time Starbucks barista. “They want us front-line staff to persuade non-paying customers to give up their seats in whatever way we consider peaceful.”

However, because the practice isn’t tied to their performance review, employees might be reluctant to enforce the new rules, Zhang adds. “If I’m on shift, I won’t do it. I’ll just work the way I always have.”

In the grind

Starbucks built its “third place” branding concept based on the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg’s 1989 book, “The Great Good Place,” in which he describes the human need for communal, welcoming social environments separate from home (the “first place”) and work (the “second place”).

This positioning requires providing space for relaxed socializing. But when revenues don’t keep pace with increases in rent and operating costs, it becomes a potential pain point.

When Brian Niccol was appointed CEO of Starbucks in September 2024, same-store sales — a metric that measures revenue growth from established locations — were on the slide in the U.S. market.

To reverse the trend, he launched “Back to Starbucks,” a plan aimed at “rediscovering the power of third places” by improving the in-store experience, such as reintroducing old-school ceramic mugs and handwritten names on cups, as well as more comfortable seating. He then scrapped the 2018 open-door policy.

Investor data suggests the changes have already had an effect in North America, where same-store sales were up by 8.1% year on year in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (Sept. 29, 2025, to Sept. 27, 2026) and same-store transactions grew by 4.5% over the same period.

In China, recent growth in same-store sales has been powered more by product innovation, deliveries, and price adjustments, according to Cathy R. Smith, Starbucks’ chief financial officer.

As online take-out orders increase and in-store spending declines, running a brick-and-mortar “third place” becomes more expensive. In this case, seat-hogging shifts from being a tolerable service issue to an operational problem.

Pressing issue

In April this year, Starbucks completed a $4 billion joint-venture transaction with Boyu Capital, a China-focused alternative asset management and private equity firm based in Hong Kong. The deal gives Boyu a 60% share in Starbucks’ China retail business and transitions all 8,000 coffeehouses into licensed operations.

The U.S. coffee giant says it expects the transaction proceeds, along with the value of its retained 40% stake and licensing agreement, to account for more than $13 billion over the next decade. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Starbucks’ international segment operating margin increased to 19.1%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.

However, while the deal benefits global headquarters, Starbucks China still faces pressure to expand. At a partner forum in April, CEO Molly Liu confirmed the company is already two-thirds of the way to its goal of opening stores in more than 1,500 counties over the next three years.

With this in mind, the purchase-required seating policy looks more like an efficiency drive, as the company attempts to cut costs.

This also comes amid a major restructuring of Starbucks China’s workforce. As all staff are now part of the joint venture, they can no longer hold Starbucks shares, which trade on New York’s Nasdaq exchange. This means the end of the Bean Stock program in China, which since 1991 has awarded full- and part-time employees shares after a certain tenure.

Liu said at April’s partner forum that benefits would continue through fiscal 2026, with a new long-term incentive plan to be introduced in the fourth quarter. As of Nov. 4, there had been no further announcements.

As social insurance contributions are mandatory only for permanent staff in China, barista Zhang believes the company prefers to hire part-time workers. Jiemian News reported in January that Starbucks China’s official recruitment channels were promoting vacancies in 269 areas, with full-time positions making up just over 20%.

Behind its new seating policy is a contradiction Starbucks China cannot easily escape: the “third place” concept justifies the brand’s premium, yet recent growth has come from deliveries and discounts, bringing sales without a customer ever sitting down.

The joint venture and its target to grow to “as many as 20,000 locations over time” sharpen that contradiction. Smaller markets and leaner per-store costs make it hard to build to the original standard.

Therefore, tightening seating rules, restructuring its workforce, and expansion look less like separate decisions than part of one cost logic.

(Due to privacy concerns, Li Kele and Zhang Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Zhan Fangge.

A version of this article originally appeared in Baobian News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A sign asks customers to make a purchase before taking a seat at a Starbucks. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.content:
A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.

The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.

“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

The mini-program previously allowed users to submit reports without photo evidence. However, after users raised concerns about the potential for people to maliciously target hotels without evidence, the program was updated in late September to allow users to upload photographic evidence. Photos can be either uploaded or taken directly via the mini-program — in the latter case, the app automatically adds a watermark showing the time and location.

“I’m simply the initiator,” he said. “The goal is to get everyone involved in managing the mini-program’s data and reviews.”

Hotels can also appeal bedbug reports — indicated on the map by blue semicircular icons above such locations — as well as upload disinfection records, business licenses, and photos of pest-control operations.

The creator said he even recruited volunteers at one point to inspect the hygiene of hotels that filed appeals. However, the function was soon taken down because of concerns about volunteers’ safety, among other issues.

He said that managing the mini-program alone has “brought pressure and criticism,” adding that he hopes the government will “provide professional guidance to improve (the app’s) credibility.”

In an interview with domestic media, Lin Feiran, a lawyer at Beijing King & Capital Law Firm, suggested the company bring in professionals to identify insects reported at different locations.

State media outlet CNR News wrote in a Monday commentary that “a map pieced together by internet users being used to fill the gap in hygiene information shows that formal (reporting) channels are lacking,” encouraging hotel booking platforms to display bedbug records publicly.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.content:
A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.

I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.

It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

The challenge of protecting intellectual property is not unique to Chinese cuisine. It affects chefs around the world. Business schools often hold up KFC’s fried chicken recipe as a classic example of a trade secret, but the company’s real competitive advantage lies in its supply chains, restaurant network, and brand value. The law does not prohibit you from reverse-engineering KFC’s fried chicken and making it yourself, or even selling it to your neighbors, provided you don’t market it as “KFC Original Recipe Chicken.” For smaller restaurants, therefore, protecting a recipe may matter less than building the brand and reputation that give it lasting commercial value.

The celebrated 18th-century Chinese food writer Yuan Mei associated dishes with particular names as a way of preserving their origins. For example, in his influential cookbook “Suiyuan Shidan” (“Recipes from the Garden of Contentment”), he included dishes called “Prefect Wang’s eight-treasure tofu” and “Governor Yang’s tofu.” In this way, no matter how often later generations copied these dishes, their names remained tied to their origins.

However, this naming convention has its limitations. Prefect Wang, Governor Yang, and the better-known Kung Pao (of Kung Pao chicken fame) all refer to the chefs’ employers rather than the people who actually did the cooking. Only in his “Biography of Chef Wang Xiaoyu” did Yuan Mei praise a chef, elevating an obscure kitchen worker to a culinary figure remembered by later generations.

Similarly, General Tso’s chicken is familiar to almost everyone in the United States, yet few know the name Peng Chang-kuei, the chef credited with creating the dish and introducing it to America. Diners know the name of General Tso, but not the person behind the dish.

One way to recognize innovative chefs would be to give them explicit credit for their creations. For example, instead of simply labeling a dish “Chef’s Recommendation,” menus could identify the chef or team of chefs who developed it, along with the restaurant and year it first appeared. This would acknowledge the contributions of both the creators and the restaurants that invested in their work.

Chefs could also license their original recipes to restaurants and large chains. Another possibility would be to establish an industry-wide registry of original dishes, where chefs and restaurants could record development dates, launch locations, photographs, and successive versions of their recipes. That way, even if other restaurants later copied a dish and achieved greater commercial success, its creator’s contribution would not simply be forgotten.

Of course, implementing such measures would not be easy. The greatest resistance might not even come from imitators, but from within the restaurants where new dishes are developed.

For restaurant owners, naming a dish after its creator also poses risks. Chefs tend to move between jobs, and when one leaves, dishes bearing their name could become an awkward legacy, potentially even requiring a restaurant to overhaul its menu. At the same time, chefs have traditionally enjoyed relatively low social status. Within restaurants, they often have little say in day-to-day operations and limited bargaining power to protect their own interests, making it difficult to secure adequate recognition for their contributions.

These two problems are closely related. When chefs receive little recognition for their work and feel little ownership over the dishes they create or the restaurants where they work, they may be more inclined to leave. This, in turn, gives restaurants even less incentive to credit individual chefs. It may help explain why, in the rare cases in which a dish bears its creator’s name — such as Fei Da Chu’s chili stir-fried pork, sold in cities across China — the chef behind it is also the restaurant’s owner.

Protecting and rewarding the creators of original dishes, whether through naming rights or other institutional and technological mechanisms, could help raise chefs’ social status, strengthen their bargaining power, and create a more equitable relationship between chefs and restaurant owners. Restaurants, in turn, could attract diners who appreciate the work of individual chefs and are willing to pay for originality. The result could be a positive cycle of culinary innovation, recognition, and consumption.

A dish may be replicated almost perfectly, but the experience, creativity, and reputation behind it cannot. The chef who conceived the idea, the sous chefs who tested the recipe, the team members who continually refined it, and the restaurant that provided the resources and space for experimentation all contributed to the story behind the dish. Recognizing their contributions is about more than giving credit where it is due. It is also about respecting the generations of chefs who have shaped Chinese cuisine and ensuring that their knowledge, skills, and traditions continue to be valued.

(Header image: The illustration in the center depicts Yuan Mei, a Qing Dynasty poet, scholar, and artist, in a 19th-century painting by Chinese artist Ye Yanlan. Images from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.content:
China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.

PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.

Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.

The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.

China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

Development of the new formula began in 2024 and received regulatory approval in September 2026. The research team has also worked with companies to develop everyday foods for PKU patients, including noodles, steamed buns, cookies, and mochi.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: From the Shanghai Morning Post)

World.title: UP outguns Ateneo in altercation-marred thriller to clinch Final Four anew
World.content:
HEATED. Ateneo coach Louie Alas charges to the UP bench as team officials try to pacify the veteran mentor.

For the eighth straight UAAP season, the UP Fighting Maroons stay firmly in title contention after surviving a testy encounter with Katipunan rival Ateneo

MANILA, Philippines – The UP Fighting Maroons earned their seventh straight win of the UAAP Season 89 men’s baskeball tournament in style, downing rivals Ateneo Blue Eagles in a heated 82-74 duel at the Araneta Coliseum on Saturday, November 7.

Potential MVP candidate Veejay Pre led four Maroons in double-digit scoring with 16 points, 7 rebounds, and 3 blocks, while guards Elliot Dimaculangan and Rainer Maga added 13 markers apiece as UP clinched the first Final Four spot with a league-best 9-2 record.

However, it was the 5 points that forward Jacob Bayla added that sparked the most intrigue in the nip-and-tuck battle, as his last-second dunk to set the final score enraged Ateneo head coach Louie Alas, enough for him to confront the UP bench at the buzzer.

Though cooler heads prevailed, Maroons mentor Goldwin Monteverde insisted that no malice was intended, and that the play was simply to strengthen their place in a tight standings race, if ever they need to involve late tiebreakers.

Alas, meanwhile, kept his position that the play was disrespectful in nature.

“I quickly accepted that what happened happened, but they have to at least know that it was wrong,” the veteran tactician said in Filipino after the game. “Part of it, I was wrong, but [Bayla] was also wrong.”

Sideline events aside, the win gave the Maroons — who are marching to the Final Four for the eighth straight year — the inside track on the coveted twice-to-beat advantage as it stayed comfortably ahead of NU (7-2), FEU (6-4), and La Salle (6-4).

Ateneo, meanwhile, dropped its second straight game on the way to a 4-6 slate, still in fifth place ahead of a frantic season home stretch.

Super rookie Kieffer Alas once again paced the losing cause with 14 points on 4-of-12 shooting, 5 rebounds, and 2 steals, while running mate Jared Bahay added 13 markers on a 5-of-14 clip, 6 assists, and 3 boards.

The Scores

UP 82 – Pre 16, Maga 13, Dimaculangan 13, Ududo 10, Payosing 7, Bayla 5, Remogat 5, Yñiguez 5, Briones 3, Stevens 2, Palanca 2, Alter 1.

Ateneo 74 – Alas 14, Bahay 13, Espinosa 9, Tuano 9, Rogers 8, Roberts 7, Kapihe 6, Baruwa 4, Bongo 4, Espina 0, Leal 0.

Quarters: 13-20, 36-39, 64-57, 82-74.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala survives Greek opponent, rain-hit Hong Kong semis for title berth
World.content:
Filipina tennis superstar and world No. 17 Alex Eala keeps up her torrid surge through the 2026 Hong Kong Open, this time surviving Greek veteran Maria Sakkari in the semis to arrange a final match against Claire Liu

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala closes in on her first WTA 250 title as she survived Greek veteran Maria Sakkari, 7-5, 3-6, 6-4, in the 2026 Hong Kong Open semifinals on Saturday, November 7.

World No. 102 American Claire Liu now stands in the way of the world No. 17 Filipina superstar in the final, after her own 7-5, 6-4 semifinal sweep of Russian challenger Alexandra Shubladze.

Reeling from a 3-6 setback in the second set, Eala aimed to exorcise ghosts of meltdowns past with a blazing 3-0 start in the final frame, and kept a huge 4-1 advantage with the final within grasp.

The 31-year-old Sakkari, however, refused to go down without a fight as she staged her own clutch three-game rally to stage a 4-4 tie, before Eala stopped the bleeding in the ninth game, giving up only a single point to go up 5-4.

Perhaps running out of gas late, Sakkari failed to keep up with Eala’s final onslaught, only saving one match point in the end as the Filipina ace wrapped up another hard-earned three-set victory.

“I think the ability and conscious choice to stay there and be positive was a really big point of my match today and my mentality,” Eala said after the match.

Despite multiple brief rain delays that disrupted the match, Eala managed to maintain her rhythm when it mattered.

“I think I was just blank,” Eala said. “It was a lot of patience but a lot of focus gave me time to really focus in on the next point. I am really happy I managed to come out of that as a better player.”

Ahead of the final, Eala also aims to avenge an earlier upset loss, as Liu — then ranked world No. 305 — stunned the top-50 Filipina out of the 2025 Guangzhou Open first round in their only head-to-head meeting so far.

Regardless of result, the Hong Kong Open will be Eala’s final official event of the year as she soon heads home for a wind-down homecoming celebration at the sprawling Philippine Arena on December 8. – Rappler.com

World.title: No Pax Silica deal at ASEAN Summit, says US envoy
World.content:
HOST. The welcome sign at the entrance of the Philippine International Convention Center complex and World Trade Center in Pasay City, on November 4, 2026.

Pax Silica decisions ‘will be made in full consultation’ with the Philippines, says US Ambassador Lee Lipton ahead of the ASEAN Summit in Manila

MANILA, Philippines – A United States envoy dismissed reports on Saturday, November 7, that a framework agreement for the US-backed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone would be signed during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila this month.

“No such announcement on the Pax Silica Economic Security Zone was ever planned. Decisions will be made in full consultation with the government of the Philippines at the appropriate time,” US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said in a statement.

“As stated previously and as part of this process, we expect rigorous discussions on impacts to all stakeholders.”

Lipton’s clarification came after the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) earlier floated that the signing of the initiative — which aims to transform the Philippines into a hub for artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, and advanced industries — could be among the major developments during the summit from November 16 to 18.

US President Donald Trump will be among the global leaders expected to attend the regional event.

Envisioned as a massive 1,620-hectare industrial hub in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, the Pax Silica development is estimated by the BCDA to attract up to US$70 billion in investments and create as many as 190,000 direct jobs.

The project, however, faces mounting criticisms in the Philippines, with many noting that the hub could harm the country’s environment, displace indigenous communities, and strain the Luzon energy grid because of its massive power and water needs, among others.

“We look forward to working alongside the government of the Philippines about this exciting initiative to secure supply chains and attract quality investment in support of economic growth and jobs at home for the people,” Lipton said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Taduran dangles last Filipino world boxing crown against Romero
World.content:
FACE-OFF. Filipino champion Pedro Taduran and Brandon Romero of Spain during the weigh-in ahead of their IBF minimumweight bout.

‘I won't let this title be taken away because I am the only world champion of the Philippines now,’ says Pedro Taduran, the pride of Libon, Albay who looks to defend his IBF minimumweight crown

MANILA, Philippines – Pedro Taduran is the last champion standing in Philippine boxing.

He promised that it would stay that way after his fourth defense of the IBF (International Boxing Federation) minimumweight crown against Spaniard Brandon Romero on Saturday, November 7 (Sunday, November 8, Philippine time) at the Kiva Auditorium in Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA.

“I won’t let this title be taken away because I am the only world champion of the Philippines now. I’ll fight for it to the best of my abilities,” Taduran said in Filipino during the pre-fight press conference on Friday, November 6.

Bookmakers believe the pride of Libon, Albay, would succeed in his noble mission.

The 30-year-old Taduran, owner of a 20-win (14 knockouts), 4-loss, 1-draw record, is the heavy favorite. With an 87 percent chance of winning and staining Moreno’s clean 16-0 slate with 5 knockouts.

Moreno admits he holds Taduran in high esteem, but thinks his movement and ability to adjust during fights will be key to his dream to win a world crown in the United States.

Taduran spent the early part of his preparations at the Elorde Sports Center in Sucat, Paranaque, before finishing his training at the Knuckleheads Boxing Gym of MP Promotions president Sean Gibbons in Las Vegas, Nevada.

Former world junior bantamweight king Jerwin Ancajas and his longtime trainer/manager Joven Jimenez supervised Taduran’s training in the United States.

“He has made weight and is ready to fight,” Jimenez told Rappler hours before the official weigh-in.

True enough, Taduran checked in at 104,8 pounds, while Romero tipped the scales at an exact 105.

Taduran became the lone Filipino world champion after Melvin Jerusalem yielded the WBC (World Boxing Council) minimumweight belt to Siyakholwa Kuse on May 16 in South Africa. – Rappler.com

World.title: Harvesting 30 years of music: Gloc-9 brings ‘Mga Ani’ to vinyl
World.content:
Gloc-9 drops 11 of his most impactful songs in his first vinyl release, sharing some advice for young artists on mastering their craft

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino hip-hop pillar Gloc-9 marks nearly three decades in the music industry with Mga Ani ni Gloc-9, his first vinyl release. The limited-edition collection features 11 of his most iconic storytelling tracks from different record labels.

From his greatest hits to hard-hitting commentaries, the record serves as a compilation of the social realities and personal struggles that define his musical legacy.

“Kaya ‘Ani ni Gloc-9’ ang ipinangalan namin dahil feeling ko, sa almost 30 years ko in the industry, I just hope na halos lahat ng mga songs na ginawa ko, somehow buhatin ako kung gaano ko pa katagal puwedeng gawin ito,” he said.

(That’s why we named it ‘Ani ni Gloc-9’ [Gloc-9’s Harvest], I feel that, after nearly 30 years in the industry, I just hope that the songs I’ve created will, in some way, carry me forward for as long as I’m able to keep doing this.)

Some of the songs in the vinyl collection are“Sirena” featuring Ebe Dancel, “Magda” featuring Rico Blanco, and “Upuan” featuring Jeazell Grutas.

Other included tracks: “Simpleng Tao”and “Bagsakan,” which he recorded with Parokya ni Edgar and the late master rapper Francis M. Also part of the list are songs like “Love Story,” “Walang Natira” featuring Sheng Belmonte, “Lando” featuring Francis M, “Takipsilim” featuring Regine Velasquez-Alcasid, “Walang Pumapalakpak” featuring Gary Valenciano, and“Kumpisal”featuring Skusta Clee.

Reaping his harvest

The title of the collection, Mga Ani ni Gloc-9, also pertains to what Gloc-9 has reaped in all his years in OPM.

“Ganoon naman talaga, lalo na sa industriya na ito,” he said during the launch. “Mas madami kang itinanim, mas madami kang aanihin. Hindi naman lahat ng ani mo, ay [may makukuha] ka. Kailangan mo siyang ulitin nang ulitin.”

(That’s just how it is, especially in this industry. The more you plant, the more you harvest. But you don’t necessarily get to keep everything you harvest. You have to keep doing it over and over again.)

For Gloc-9, something that can be said to be his ani or harvest, are the moments when he’s at events while singing, and he also hears people singing his songs, to the point that he doesn’t even need to sing in the first place.

“Honest, iyon yung mga moments na gusto kong maiyak,” he shared. “Siguro enough na yung nilagay kong pagtatanim sa tagal ng panahon. Baka sakali puwede na kong umani.”

(Honestly, those are the moments when I want to cry. Perhaps the seeds I’ve sown over all this time are enough. Maybe it’s time for me to reap the harvest.)

In his many years in the business, Gloc-9 has said he hopes to collaborate with Popstar Royalty Sarah Geronimo in the future.

Gloc-9 shared that the songs he chose for this milestone — the vinyl collection came out under Sony Music Philippines, Star Music, and Universal Records — are not necessarily his greatest hits.

“Hindi yung hits siguro, pero kung ano yung may pinaka may nakalabit na mga songs, kaya namin nilagay diyan,” he said.

(Maybe not necessarily the hits, but we included the songs with the greatest impact, which is why we put those in the vinyl collection.)

He also said among the songs in the collection, the award-winning “Upuan” has taken on a completely different meaning for him over time.

Written 17 years ago when Gloc-9 was 33, the track reflects a time when he admits he was still naive and hopeful.

“Naririnig ko na kapag kinakanta ko siya sa harap ng ibang tao, alam ko kung ano ang intentions ko,” he said. “Pero may times na naririnig ko siya sa iba’t-ibang lugar na alam ko din na hindi na iyon ang intensyon ko sa kanta. Napalitan na.”

(When I sing that song in front of others, I know my intentions. But there are times when I hear it in various places, and I know that’s no longer the intention I had for the song. It has changed.)

A message for the youth

Gloc-9 has always been known for commenting about current issues through his music. Again, he cites “Upuan” as the song from his vinyl collection that should resonate the most with the youth today.

“Siguro dahil sa mga nangyayari ngayon,” he explained to Rappler. “Siguro magtuturo iyon ng awareness sa kanila. Maging matapang sila. Naniniwala kasi ako na hindi dahil ako yung gumawa ng song, ako iyong kumanta nung song, ako lang ang kakanta noon. Ito ay ginawa namin, para kantahin iyon. Maging boses din nila.”

(Maybe it’s because of the things happening nowadays. The song should teach awareness to the youth. I hope it makes them brave. I believe that just because I wrote the song and sang it, it doesn’t mean I’m the only one who should sing it. We created this so that others could sing it, too. It could become their voice as well.)

Gloc-9 also shared his advice to anyone who might want to follow in his footsteps.

“Napaka-simple lang, noh,” said Gloc-9. “I think ang dapat magawa ng kabataan ngayon ay whatever it is na gusto nila i-pursue sa buhay nila, is to identify kung ano yung gifts nila. Kung ano yung specific na gift nila. I think iyon ang pinaka-importante. Kapag nakita mo siya, na-identify mo siya, the earlier the better. Tapos after that, you build. You build, you build, you build.”

(It’s really simple. I think what young people today should do, regardless of what they want to pursue in life, is to identify their gifts. They need to figure out what their specific gift is. I believe that is the most important thing. Once you discover or identify it, and the earlier, the better, then you build. You just keep building.)

“Kung saan ka masaya na ginagawa mo ‘yun, regardless of anything,” he added. “Pera, oras, opportunity, kung anong katayuan mo sa buhay. Kung lahat nang iyon, ‘di mo papansinin, tapos masaya ka sa ginagawa mo, iyon ang i-build mo, tuloy-tuloy. Eventually, may mangyayari. Imposibleng wala.”

(Your calling should be what makes you happy. You do it anyway regardless of money, time, opportunity, or whatever your circumstances in life. If you’re happy with what you do, build on that. Eventually something will happen — it’s impossible that nothing will happen.)

He gave more advice for those who also want to get into the music industry.

“Kahit ‘di ikaw yung uso, kung ang craft mo iyong ginawa mo with purity and good intentions, hindi mo kailangan maging uso,” he shared. “Laging merong makikinig sa iyo.”

(Even if your music is not the trend or the current rage, if you do your craft with purity and good intentions, you don’t need to be trendy. There will always be someone who will listen to you.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Bigger bank, broader base: TG Limcaoco’s BPI years
World.content:
LAST DANCE? BPI president and CEO TG Limcaoco speaks at the bank's 175th gala on October 26, 2026.

From overseeing a bank merger to scrapping transfer fees and bringing banking into neighborhood stores, it's been a busy five years for Limcaoco

After five years at the helm of the 175-year-old Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco is ready to say goodbye to the country’s oldest bank.

Limcaoco will step down as president and chief executive officer in April 2027, making way for consumer banking chief Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go, BPI’s first female CEO. He will remain on the board and take on other senior roles within the Ayala Group.

Five years is a short chapter for a bank that has survived colonial governments, wars, and economic crises. But Limcaoco was hardly new to BPI or the Ayalas when he took the helm in 2021. He had been president of BPI Capital and BPI Family Savings Bank, then spent six years as Ayala Corporation’s chief financial officer.

The bank he inherited from Cezar “Bong” Consing was already one of the country’s largest. The one he will leave behind is considerably bigger.

BPI’s annual net income rose from P23.88 billion in 2021 to P66.62 billion in 2025, while assets grew from P2.42 trillion at end-2021 to P3.9 trillion by September 2026. Its customer base more than doubled to over 19 million, helped in part by the 2024 merger with Robinsons Bank.

But enough of the numbers, and back to the man of the hour. Limcaoco isn’t your typical banker who shies away from the media. He’s frank, sometimes even blunt, and always ready to break down a tough banking topic with an example or two.

Ask him about bank secrecy, and he’ll point out that few countries have laws as restrictive as the Philippines’. Ask about reserve requirements, and he’ll explain why he prefers interest rates as a monetary policy tool.

When Rappler asked last July why BPI made transfers free, he explained that under new central bank rules, it could charge only around P1.50. Why bother customers over that amount?

“You’re just needling the customer,” he said.

BPI became one of the first major commercial banks to permanently waive InstaPay and PESONet fees, with others following with cuts of their own. There was a business case, too. Free transfers could keep customers using BPI and perhaps bring in more business.

Much the same thinking has gone into the bank’s expansion into agency banking under Limcaoco. Customers can now open accounts, deposit, and withdraw money at participating supermarkets and convenience stores — often for free — while BPI avoids some of the costs of branches and ATMs.

In a March interview with McKinsey, Limcaoco summed it up: “Our philosophy is, if you cannot come to the bank, we will bring the bank to you.”

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Deputy Governor Bernadette Romulo-Puyat, who has taken a particular interest in the program, had some rather warm words for Limcaoco.

“Ang galing ni TG (TG’s great),” she told Rappler in a recent chat about financial inclusion. “My experience with him, he was really looking for ways to help give everybody a bank account. He’s made it so simple.”

Unfinished business

At BPI’s 175th anniversary gala in October, chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala credited Limcaoco with bringing “real dynamism” to the bank, while welcoming to its next chapter under Go.

Limcaoco, meanwhile, spent much of his own speech looking beyond his time at the bank. He wondered aloud what banking might look like 25 years from now, when BPI celebrates its 200th anniversary.

“I don’t think any of us can predict exactly what banking will look like by then,” he said.

Yet he was clear on one unfinished job: “Millions of Filipinos still have limited access to formal financial services.”

GALA. BPI president and CEO TG Limcaoco (right) looks on as BPI chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala congratulates writer Roel Landingin. BPI

But Limcaoco isn’t always dressed up to the nines. A rather different side of him was on display two months earlier, on August 1, BPI’s actual birthday, when the bank launched a Disney-themed savings account for children.

After a morning of golf, Limcaoco, a grandfather himself, was at Glorietta — an Ayala mall, of course — talking to children about setting aside part of their allowance. As he often does, he brought the idea down to their level. Compound interest might mean little to a child, but saving for a bicycle or a dog was easy enough to understand.

“Maybe a kid puts P100 a month,” he told Rappler afterward. “The magic of interest, even though it’s small, really is meaningful.”

Meanwhile Go, then still a few months away from being officially announced as his successor, took the chance to tease her boss, joking during her remarks about whether the children should call him “Lolo TG.”

For that morning, at least, the man running one of the country’s biggest banks was simply Lolo TG, talking to kids about what they could do for their future. – Rappler.com

WALL ART. Customers gather next to sculptures of lower halves of people appearing to sit on a ledge in a swimming pool, at a theme cafe in Beijing, China, on October 31, 2026.

A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

MANILA, Philippines — Democrats took control of Congress in the US midterm elections on November 3, making extraordinary gains deep in Republican territory with voters delivering a sharp rebuke to President Donald Trump and his agenda.

A wave of anger over Trump’s policies, particularly the US-Iran war’s role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44. Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives.

Donald Trump’s party has been defeated in states where it hadn’t lost for a generation — or longer: Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. These have been red states for quite some time, but this shows the Republicans really suffered in their own heartland.

Meanwhile, Malacanang announced on November 5 that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has chosen Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as the country’s 28th Supreme Court chief justice.

Zalameda, the third most senior among the chief justice nominees, replaces Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo who retired during the weekend. Zalameda will serve as chief justice for seven years or until August 2033, when he reaches the mandatory retirement age of 70.

World.title: FACT CHECK: SC didn’t rule Marcos’ budget signing unconstitutional
World.content:
The Court faulted Congress for raising the President's proposed budget, and with the decision not yet final, no formal probe has been opened

Claim: The Supreme Court (SC) ruled that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s signing of the national budget was unconstitutional.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A graphic shared by the Facebook page Makata Ng Bayan on November 1 shows an edited photo of Marcos, former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo, and Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla.

The text on the graphic reads: “Sinabi na ng Supreme Court na Unconstitutional ang Pagpirma ni Marcos sa Budget! Tungkulin ng Ombudsman, DOJ at COA mag Imbestiga, Pero bakit di nila ginawa? Mga Duwag ba sila o Mukhang Pera?”

(The Supreme Court has already said Marcos’s signing of the budget was unconstitutional! It’s the duty of the Ombudsman, Department of Justice (DOJ), and Commission on Audit (COA) to investigate, but why didn’t they? Are they cowards or money-hungry?)

At the time of writing, the post had 4,900 reactions, 1,200 comments, and 2,400 shares.

The facts: The SC did declare national budgets unconstitutional, but because of what Congress added to them, not because of the President’s signature.

In a ruling released on October 20, written by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the Court voted 13-2 to strike down the 2024 and 2025 national budgets, along with two rules in this year’s budget on how standby funds can be released.

The Court said Congress is not allowed to make the budget bigger than what the President proposed. In 2024, lawmakers added P449.5 billion in standby funds to the budget, and P17.99 billion more for the 2025 DPWH Special Road Fund. (READ: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations)

Not yet final: Court spokesperson Camille Ting said the ruling is not yet final, and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) could file a motion for reconsideration within 15 days from notice.

The OSG has since filed a motion for clarification and partial reconsideration, signed by Solicitor General Darlene Berberabe. The motion asks the Court to spell out which projects already funded under the budgets can continue, and to declare that the 2025 Special Road Fund increase was constitutional.

It also asked the Court not to count standby funds under the same spending limit as the rest of the budget, and to treat its new rules on releasing those funds as guidance rather than binding requirements.

No ongoing investigations: As of writing, the Ombudsman, DOJ, and COA have not opened a formal probe. The Ombudsman is also waiting for the SC’s final decision.

In 2025, it temporarily put on hold a graft complaint against House leaders over the 2025 budget until the Court resolved the constitutional question with finality.

The Court said officials behind the budget increases could still face criminal, civil, or administrative cases, unless the proper court or body finds they acted in good faith. On October 26, Remulla announced a “budget watch” and said he would form a team to study the decision and determine who may be held liable.

Vice President Sara Duterte said Marcos and Congress should answer for approving the budgets, while Malacañang said it disagreed with parts of the ruling. Senator Panfilo Lacson and Representative Leila de Lima welcomed the decision as a win for accountability. – Jake Gomez/Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: China Wields Carrot and Stick at Beijing Meet, Regime Seeks Elections in Shan, and More
World.content:
We’ll always hold your hand, Beijing promises Myanmar regime

“China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday.

The reassurance came as part of a carrot-and-stick package amid alarm in Beijing over recent meetings between U.S. and Myanmar officials that seemed to augur the start of re-engagement.

The U.S. has released an Integrated Country Strategy for its mission in Myanmar, which identifies goals for expanding Washington’s diplomatic, economic and humanitarian influence in the country. Besides singling out scam networks, it also sets goals for boosting American exports to the impoverished war-torn country and gain access to Myanmar’s “bountiful” rare earth resources—besides aiming to “counter China’s influence.”

Myanmar is China’s most important external source of rare earth minerals and a major global source of heavy rare earth elements, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which are essential for electric cars, wind turbines, advanced electronics and military technologies. But mines are concentrated in areas beyond the reach of the regime in Kachin and Shan states.

Online scam operations have become a major point of convergence and competition in the two superpowers’ approach toward Myanmar. During the meeting with Aung Kyaw Hoe, Wang urged his regime to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to the vast scam compounds that flourished there.

China grows impatient over stalled investment projects

But in the same meeting Wang applied plenty of stick, urging Myanmar’s regime to get a move on in realizing long-stalled projects that form part of the planned China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) that would provide Beijing with overland access to the Indian Ocean. Wang told Aung Kyaw Hoe the two sides must “coordinate development and security” so they can “steadily advance” key CMEC projects.

Wang’s message echoed remarks made by his President Xi Jinping during regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Beijing in June, when Xi also called for swift implementation of CMEC projects.

The corridor’s flagship schemes include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and special economic zone in Rakhine State and a planned railway linking Kyaukphyu with Yunnan via Mandalay and Muse. On China side, the railroad is already entering its final phase but on the Myanmar side fighting continues across many parts of the route.

Aung Kyaw Hoe promised the regime is doing all it can but, true to form, also used the occasion to beg for even more Chinese investment.

Border trade gates reopen as armed groups consolidate control

China has significantly eased restrictions on trade through several Myanmar border crossings controlled by Beijing-linked ethnic armed organizations, allowing fuel, medicines, construction materials and other previously banned goods to enter northern Shan and Kachin.

The move suggests China is adjusting its border policy to accommodate new realities on the ground, where it appears the military regime in Naypyitaw has permanently lost control. With Operation 1027, key border trade gates and routes in northern Shan fell into the hands of the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and its erstwhile partner in the Brotherhood Alliance, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

Beijing initially closed the crossings to pressure them into making peace with the generals, but trade has long resumed and is now growing exponentially.

According to Chinese Customs at the Mengding crossing with MNDAA-controlled Chinshwehaw, the total value of trade there and at nearby Mangka eached 4.92 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 49.3 percent on-year.

Customs figures also show increased trade through Namhkam crossing controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, as well as through the Kyin San Kyawt gate controlled jointly by the Brotherhood Alliance in Muse Township, which once accounted for some 70 percent of cross-border trade. The regime still controls a couple of crossings in Muse, where it bans the import of fuel from China.

In a move to prevent those groups from financing their armies through cargo taxation, the cash-strapped regime is now reduced to blocking routes south of Lashio, imposing a crackdown on what it calls “smuggled” goods—which in reality means roadside extortion.

Late last month, Min Aung Hlaing urged his ministers to intensify their crackdown on illegal trade and make sure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through “legal” channels, i.e. those his regime controls. Myanmar’s consul general in Kunming met with the customs department director this week to discuss facilitating flows of “officially traded goods” between the neighbors and improving cooperation on customs procedures.

Naypyitaw seeks to roll out elections into Shan borderlands

Defence Minister Yar Pyae who also chairs the junta’s peace negotiation committee, this week visited areas held by China-linked ethnic armed groups with a view to rolling out the regime’s sham elections across their part of the country as well.

Yar Pyae went to Panghsang, the headquarters of United Wa State Army (UWSA), and Mongla, the fiefdom of the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA) near the Chinese border. The visit comes after Chinese Special Envoy to Myanmar Deng Xijun urged granting “high-level” autonomy to ethnic minorities.

Together with the MNDAA, they are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, with Chinese widely spoken and the yuan used as the major currency in their territories.

All three trace their origins to the 1989 mutiny that fractured the Communist Party of Burma. Most people in NDAA territory are ethnic Chinese with roots in Yunnan, but the Wa are a Mon‑Khmer-speaking people more closely related to the Palaung.

Both the UWSA and NDAA have long upheld ceasefires they signed with the military in 1989 in return for de-factor autonomy in their areas, sustained by cross‑border trade and Chinese investment.

In Mongla, Yar Pyae discussed holding the vote, which was omitted there when the regime orchestrated polls in the parts of Myanmar it controls in the winter of 2025-26 that led to military dictator Min Aung Hlaing declaring himself president. Naypyitaw is aiming for next April, regime media said. But none of the townships under the control of the UWSA or NDAA were included on the junta’s recently announced list of constituencies slated for catch-up and by-elections.

Historically, no national elections have been conducted either in Mongla or Panghsang, although voting has taken place in some townships of the constitutionally defined Wa Self-Administered Division where government administration was present. Formally, the UWSA is stuck at a stage of demanding official statehood, and the NDAA is demanding official autonomous status.

World.title: Arakan Army Faces Second Front at Bangladesh Border
World.content:
Amid intensified fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) closes in on the Arakan (Rakhine State) capital of Sittwe, a second front is heating up along the border with Bangladesh, where regime-aligned Rohingya armed groups are escalating conflict.

These attacks are not isolated border incidents. They reflect a history of cooperation between Myanmar’s military and Muslim armed organizations during the 2024 battles for Buthidaung and Maungdaw. For Bangladesh, they raise difficult questions about its security interests and the prospects of repatriating the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees now within its borders. For the AA, they raise the question whether it can maintain stability across its home state.

A major concern is that armed networks established during the military regime’s territorial retreat are continuing to exert pressure on the AA while the main body of its forces confronts the regime elsewhere.

From cooperation to proxy warfare

During the 2024 Arakan offensive, the military suffered major territorial losses. Facing the AA’s advance, it cast around for additional manpower and local allies, and alighted on armed organizations that, ironically, were associated with a population it had systematically persecuted. One of them was the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The International Crisis Group has documented the regime’s ammunition supplies to ARSA, along with recruitment arrangements that transferred Rohingya refugees to military facilities for training.

ARSA and another armed group, the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), received training, weapons and tactical support during the fighting while maintaining contacts with regime personnel after the AA captured Maungdaw in December 2024, according to the Transnational Institute.

Here was the military that was responsible for the 2017 atrocities that drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh, brazenly cooperating with Rohingya armed organizations against the AA.

For the junta, however, the strategic advantages outweighed any qualms it might have had. Armed groups operating along the state’s northern frontier could challenge AA positions even after its own conventional military bases had fallen, and thereby divert precious resources from the AA’s other battlefronts.

As a bonus for a regime that has long sustained itself by divide-and-rule tactics, it risked deepening mistrust between the state’s Arakanese and Muslim communities.

Maungdaw remains a strategic front

Thus when the AA eventually captured Maungdaw, it transformed the military balance along the Bangladesh border but could not fully eliminate the armed groups operating through remote terrain and cross-border networks.

In September last year, ARSA fighters attacked an AA border security position near Inn Chaung village in northern Maungdaw. AA forces subsequently retook the position, while the attackers reportedly fled to Bangladesh.

Further clashes followed, and by late October this year, residents reported that ARSA was renewing recruitment, armed movements and attacks against AA outposts in northern and southern Maungdaw.

“ARSA activities have resurged in both northern and southern Maungdaw Township,” one resident told my news organization, Development Media Group.

With the AA confronting regime forces around Sittwe, repeated ARSA attacks could now force it to divert much-needed troops, intelligence resources and supplies to the border.

This would benefit Myanmar’s military even without direct command of these operations.

There is an important caveat. ARSA, RSO and a third militia active at the border, the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) have distinct leadership structures and interests. Their historical cooperation with the military regime does not mean that every recent attack was centrally coordinated.

Bangladesh’s border dilemma

A further complication lies in Bangladeshi involvement in these skirmishes. The AA accuses certain officers of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) of providing the Rohingya armed groups with logistical assistance, ammunition and intelligence, and allowing them to operate near border security positions.

The International Crisis Group, too, has documented the complicated relationships between these groups and elements of Bangladesh’s security establishment.

The allegations require credible investigation, but any such shenanigans must also be distinguished from official Bangladeshi government policy. Publicly, the BGB has denied supporting ARSA or the RSO.

Bangladesh faces legitimate challenges involving border security, with more than 1 million Rohingya refugees and the prospect of their eventual repatriation creating a massive headache for Dhaka.

But it will eventually have to confront the reality that the territory from which the refugees fled is now controlled by the AA, and that fundamentally changes the political realities.

Some Bangladeshi security personnel may still regard these avowedly Muslim armed organizations as potential leverage over the AA. But helping them with their cross-border attacks would now in fact undermine border stability and make peaceful repatriation more difficult.

In other words, Bangladesh’s security interests would be better served by stopping ARSA and co. from exploiting refugee communities, and instead maintaining effective communication with the AA authorities controlling the opposite side of the border.

Beyond armed groups and military control

The motivations behind Rohingya armed mobilization long predate any cooperation with Myanmar’s military.

Decades of discrimination, statelessness, displacement and uncertainty have created grievances that armed organizations can exploit. Refugees facing declining humanitarian assistance and limited opportunities are particularly vulnerable to recruitment and intimidation. But that cannot justify attacks on civilians, abductions or forced recruitment.

Nor should ARSA, RSO and ARA be treated as representative of Muslim communities as a whole. The Arakanese, Muslim and other communities in Maungdaw face threats from armed violence, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity. Abuses by all armed participants, including the AA, require impartial investigation and accountability.

The AA’s territorial gains have brought responsibilities extending beyond military security. Effective governance means it must protect civilians regardless of ethnicity or religion, address grievances and prevent communal tensions from escalating.

The Maungdaw conflict demonstrates that territorial control does not necessarily end a war.

Myanmar’s military has lost most of its positions in Arakan, yet its airpower, remaining military strongholds and historical relationships with armed groups continue to complicate the AA’s security calculations.

Preventing further escalation requires credible investigation of alleged weapons supplies and cross-border assistance, effective border management, protection of refugees from coercive recruitment, and sustained engagement between Bangladesh and the AA.

It also requires meaningful dialogue with Muslim civilian representatives and equal protection for all communities.

Unless the networks and grievances sustaining violence are addressed, no lasting peace can come to Arakan.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.
