World.title: Erdogan to visit Baku after hijab dispute: what concessions has Ankara made, and what does Baku want?
World.content:
Turkey–Azerbaijan relations

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told journalists on 5 November that he planned to visit Azerbaijan on 8 November, Victory Day, provided no extraordinary circumstances arose. He also said he had spoken by phone with President Ilham Aliyev and sent Turkey’s intelligence chief and foreign minister to Baku.

“The unbreakable ties between our countries rest on a shared history, culture and destiny – and, God willing, a shared future.”

However, Erdoğan’s planned visit comes amid a two-month cooling of relations between the two countries. On 30 October, President Aliyev skipped the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States in Ankara, even though the meeting marked the transfer of the organisation’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan to Turkey.

We reported in October on Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan’s visit to Baku.

What steps has Ankara taken to resolve the disagreements, what does Baku want, and what does the current situation reveal about relations between the two countries?

How did the dispute erupt?

In September, new school uniform requirements came into force in Azerbaijan. Although the rules do not explicitly mention the hijab, schools began turning away pupils who wore one. Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan criticised bans on wearing the hijab in schools without naming any specific countries. In Baku, his remarks were seen as an indirect criticism of Azerbaijan.

The subsequent events unfolded as follows:

2 October. At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”.

At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”. 12 October. The Interior Ministry reported that police had detained 37 people during protests against the new school uniform requirements. On the same day, Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral wrote on X: “It is unacceptable to deny girls who wear the hijab the right to education in Azerbaijan! The hijab is not an obstacle, but a requirement of faith!”

The Interior Ministry reported that police had detained 37 people during protests against the new school uniform requirements. On the same day, Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral wrote on X: “It is unacceptable to deny girls who wear the hijab the right to education in Azerbaijan! The hijab is not an obstacle, but a requirement of faith!” 13 October. The New Azerbaijan Party described Saral’s remarks as “populist and irresponsible” and called on Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) to “abandon this harmful policy”.

The New Azerbaijan Party described Saral’s remarks as “populist and irresponsible” and called on Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) to “abandon this harmful policy”. 19 October. The Azerbaijan Press Council reported what it called a “biased campaign” in the Turkish media. In the council’s view, reports had taken the school uniform decision out of context and portrayed it as a “ban on wearing the hijab”.

The Azerbaijan Press Council reported what it called a “biased campaign” in the Turkish media. In the council’s view, reports had taken the school uniform decision out of context and portrayed it as a “ban on wearing the hijab”. 21 October. Azerbaijan banned 31 Turkish citizens from entering the country. The list included New Welfare Party leader Fatih Erbakan, MP Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu and several journalists. The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit.

Azerbaijan banned 31 Turkish citizens from entering the country. The list included New Welfare Party leader Fatih Erbakan, MP Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu and several journalists. The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit. 25 October. Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser.

Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser. 30 October. Aliyev did not attend the Ankara summit. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov represented the country at the meeting.

What concessions has Ankara made?

The most significant step was Erdoğan’s dismissal of Oktay Saral as his chief adviser. According to Middle East Eye, which cites its own sources, Baku made three demands of Ankara:

Dismiss Erdoğan’s adviser, prosecute commentators who insulted Aliyev, and block the social media accounts named on a list. The publication reports that Ankara has already blocked some of those accounts.

Saral himself, however, has not retracted his remarks. He said he left his post at the president’s request but stressed that he had said nothing that warranted an apology: “Azerbaijan is my homeland too.”

According to Middle East Eye, Turkish officials have described the disagreements as a “misunderstanding”. Speaking at the summit, Erdoğan made no direct reference to Azerbaijan but said:

“There is no room for division, hostility or discord in the family photograph of the Turkic world.”

On 3 November, while travelling to South Korea, Erdoğan also sent Aliyev Victory Day greetings as his plane passed through Azerbaijani airspace. He delivered the message over the radio through the aircraft’s pilot.

What does Baku want?

Baku has not officially explained why Aliyev skipped the summit. According to APA, the president was due to attend the closing ceremony of the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku that day.

Baku has also taken issue with other statements from Ankara. Middle East Eye reports that, at an event organised by a foundation in October, Erdoğan said Turkish children no longer had to go abroad to study because of restrictions linked to their clothing or political views. Azerbaijan also interpreted these remarks as another rebuke.

An Azerbaijani source cited by Middle East Eye summed up Baku’s position as follows: Turkey must recognise the principle of “one nation, two states”. In other words, Baku does not want Ankara to interfere in Azerbaijan’s domestic affairs.

Elman Fattah, head of the Khazar Centre for Research and Analysis, shares a similar view. In an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, he said: “This means rejecting Turkey’s right to veto.” Fattah believes Aliyev is “deliberately shifting the hidden tensions between the two countries into the religious sphere”.

Political analyst Asif Narimanli, meanwhile, argues that

“The tensions between Baku and Ankara have deeper roots.”

Speaking to TodayPress, he noted that Aliyev’s absence…на саммите дает основания для такого вывода.

What lies behind the disagreements?

One of the deeper sources of tension concerns Israel. In Turkey, Azerbaijan’s close ties with Israel have caused considerable discontent, particularly since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip. Middle East Eye reports that Erdoğan declined to attend the October summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) to avoid meeting Israeli President Isaac Herzog. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also boycotted Herzog’s address. Baku saw this as an unfriendly gesture towards Aliyev.

Another source of disagreement concerns Armenia. According to an analysis by OC Media, Ankara wants to normalise relations with Yerevan, while Baku insists that this process must remain linked to a peace settlement between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

At the same time, the two countries share significant interests. According to OC Media, on 30 September they signed defence contracts worth around $500 million in total. In early 2026, they also reached a 15-year agreement on gas supplies from the Absheron field to Turkey. Azerbaijan accounted for around 22% of all the gas Turkey imported in 2024. According to figures from Turkey’s Ministry of Trade, bilateral trade reached $4.3 billion in 2025.

What could the visit change?

Political analyst Elkhan Shahinoglu described Erdoğan’s decision to visit Baku as “the right one”. He said:

“If tensions arise between two allies for any reason, they should not delay resolving them.”

Shahinoglu recalled that Erdoğan also visited Baku and addressed the Milli Majlis in 2009, when Turkey was moving closer to Armenia. Relations between the two countries returned to normal afterwards.

There is another sign that tensions may be easing. According to the newspaper Karar, when Turkey considered nominating former Foreign Minister Feridun Sinirlioğlu for the post of UN secretary-general, Azerbaijan backed a candidate from the United Arab Emirates instead. However, in late October, Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry spokesman Aykhan Hajizada welcomed Turkey’s nomination of Sinirlioğlu.

The next test for relations will be the UN climate conference COP31, which will take place in Antalya this month. Middle East Eye reports that Ankara hopes Aliyev will attend the conference. Baku has yet to confirm his visit.

World.title: Abkhazia to raise electricity tariffs for businesses by 40% to pay for Russian power imports
World.content:
Electricity tariffs for commercial customers in Abkhazia will rise by 40%. However, the increase will apply only during the autumn-winter period, when the region imports electricity to cover its energy shortfall.

The Inguri hydroelectric power plant is Abkhazia’s only source of electricity. However, its output falls from around November until March or April as water levels in the Inguri River drop. Electricity consumption in the region, meanwhile, rises.

In 2025, a shortfall of 500 million kWh was covered by electricity imports from Russia. Russia provided some of this electricity to Abkhazia free of charge as humanitarian aid, but the authorities had to buy the rest at market prices.

This comes at a high cost for Abkhazia: Russian electricity is significantly more expensive than the domestic tariffs charged to consumers. The current rate is 2 roubles [$0.02] per kWh for households and 3 roubles [$0.03] for legal entities. Under the agreement with Russia, however, Abkhazia will have to pay 5.5 roubles [$0.06] per kWh for imported electricity.

This is why the authorities decided to raise tariffs for businesses.

“When we pay 5.5 roubles per kWh for imported electricity but sell it to households for 2 roubles, this is also an example of the state’s social responsibility towards its citizens.

“But for commercial enterprises and institutions – where businesses make money – the tariff should match the purchase price during periods when we import electricity,” Abkhaz President Badra Gunba said. He instructed the government to approve this as the republic’s new tariff policy.

World.title: The evacuation from Oleshky: How Russia turned a humanitarian mission into a propaganda story
World.content:
The evacuation from Oleshky

The evacuation from Oleshky (Oleshky, formerly known as Oleshky/Aloshky) in Ukraine’s Kherson region, during which around 800 civilians were evacuated and aid was delivered to those who remained, was a rare example of Ukraine and Russia working together under international mediation. For Russian state media and Z-bloggers, it also became an opportunity to launch a new information campaign.

The Ukrainian side stressed the need to save lives and continue humanitarian missions. Russian media, meanwhile, portrayed the evacuation as an act of concern by Moscow for the residents of occupied territories, sought to discredit Ukraine and tried to intimidate those considering returning to territory under Kyiv’s control.

Four narratives stood out in the media coverage: Russia cast as a humanitarian intermediary; residents’ alleged unwillingness to return to Ukraine; attempts to frighten men with the prospect of forced mobilisation; and efforts to shift responsibility for threats to civilians onto Ukraine.

Some of these claims contradicted both the circumstances of the operation and statements by official representatives of the parties involved.

A report by Novosti Donbassa By Yulia Tararui.

A catastrophe whose causes the propaganda ignores

Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since February 2022. After Ukrainian forces liberated the right-bank part of the Kherson region in the autumn of that year, the city found itself on the front line.

The situation deteriorated dramatically in June 2023, when the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant was destroyed. Flooding, damaged infrastructure, disruptions to electricity and water supplies, and restrictions on movement made life extremely difficult for residents.

By 2026, the situation had become critical. Fighting, landmines and drone attacks had left the city in urgent need of food, medicine and other essentials, while opportunities to leave safely were almost nonexistent.

Russian publications described the hardships faced by residents in detail, but avoided the central fact: Oleshky had been under the control of Russian occupation authorities throughout this period.

Russian media circulated the account of a local woman who tried to leave in an ambulance but could not get even as far as the outskirts of the city because the road was mined.

Other reports described elderly residents cycling to Radensk during a ceasefire to buy food and medicine – a journey of around 20 kilometres each way.

These stories conveyed the scale of the catastrophe. But they also helped construct a narrative convenient for Moscow: the suffering was blamed on the proximity of the fighting, while the occupation administration’s responsibility for meeting residents’ basic needs was left out of the picture.

A joint operation turned into a story of Moscow’s concern

Agreements on a temporary ceasefire and the evacuation were reached with international mediation, including the active involvement of US First Lady Melania Trump.

According to figures she cited, around 750 people left the city. Reports mentioned 25 buses.

Residents were free to choose their destination: territory under Ukrainian control or Russia.

Those who chose Ukraine were evacuated via Belarus. The Russian side arranged an airlift from Anapa to Gomel using military transport aircraft.

Evacuees who chose Russia were taken to a temporary accommodation centre in Simferopol.

Food, water, medicine, fuel for generators and hospital equipment were brought into the city. A total of 105 pets were evacuated from Oleshky.

According to Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, the ceasefire lasted five days, 19 hours and 59 minutes. The operation also made it possible to arrange the repatriation of the bodies of fallen soldiers and civilians from morgues in Oleshky and other settlements.

The Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners said that both sides had fulfilled their obligations and thanked each other.

Russian media coverage, however, focused on Moscow’s role: the military aircraft, the transfer of evacuees to Simferopol, medical assistance and the work of Russian officials. In this way, the joint operation helped promote the image of a state that not only controls occupied territory but also looks after its residents.

The fact that an international operation was needed to evacuate people from a city that had been under Russian control for more than four years was barely examined in these reports.

The story of evacuees being mobilised: What a Z-Blogger claimed

One revealing episode involved Russian Z-blogger Sergei Kolyasnikov, better known as Zergulio. He circulated a claim that men who chose to travel to Ukraine were detained by staff from territorial recruitment and social support centres (TCCs and SPs, Ukraine’s equivalent of military enlistment offices) immediately after the evacuation and sent to the front.

The story drew on a familiar image of Ukraine, where men of conscription age are supposedly bound to become victims of forced mobilisation. But it had a problem with the timeline.

When the claim began circulating, evacuees heading towards Ukraine had, according to published reports, been flown to Gomel, the regional capital of Belarus. The allegation that they were detained by TCC staff after arriving in Ukraine did not match the known evacuation route.

The reports provided no publicly available evidence of mass detentions of evacuated men.

Lubinets stressed separately that no screening had taken place during the evacuation, including for people with problems concerning their documents. He said: “There was no screening whatsoever. Moreover, we had people who said they had problems with their documents – for example, they had lost them. There were no problems.”

He added: “There was not only no screening, there were no checks of phones or documents either.”

These remarks concerned the evacuation procedure and did not describe all subsequent actions by state authorities after people returned to Ukraine. But they offered no support for the blogger’s claim.

▇ Disinformation exploits people’s genuine fears of war and mobilisation, attaching them to a specific event.

Such a message could also have been aimed at residents of occupied territories, particularly men of conscription age and their relatives.

For people who have lived in information isolation for years, a story about evacuees being sent to the front could become a reason not to leave, even in the absence of evidence.

Why people chose to leave: An attempt to undermine their decisions

The Russian military blog Kotsnews claims that most men of conscription age refused to travel towards Ukraine. According to the blog, those who left were mainly elderly people, women and children, and they did so for personal reasons rather than out of political conviction.

The author of the post writes: “Not out of any great love for ‘independent Ukraine’, but to sort out their personal affairs. People in Oleshky have long felt no gratitude towards Ukraine.”

This explanation serves several purposes at once. It diminishes the significance of people’s decisions by portraying them as pragmatic choices – for example, a chance to reunite with relatives or move to Europe.

It creates the impression that residents of the occupied city no longer see their future as being tied to Ukraine. It also reinforces the narrative of inevitable mobilisation.

The result is a self-reinforcing argument: men do not want to go to Ukraine because they fear the TCCs, while those who do make the journey are supposedly immediately confronted with mobilisation. Russian commentators provide no reliable statistics on the evacuees’ reasons for leaving.

Lubinets said the parties had agreed not to disclose how many people chose Ukraine and how many chose Russia. According to him, honouring that agreement was necessary to ensure that humanitarian operations could continue.

Meanwhile, various figures circulated in the Russian information space. Russian Z-war correspondent Romanov initially reported that 17 buses had travelled to Ukraine and four to Russia, but later deleted the figures from his post.

Newsmax journalist Alex Salvi reported 11 buses heading to Ukraine and four to Russia.

Without official figures, these reports do not make it possible to establish how the evacuees were divided between the two destinations. But the very attempt to interpret their choices as an indication of political allegiance became part of the information war surrounding the operation.

Accusations of violating the ceasefire

At the same time, Russian officials accused Ukrainian forces of breaching the agreement. Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large, claimed that a Ukrainian drone had attacked a civilian vehicle leaving Oleshky.

According to Miroshnik, the vehicle was carrying civilians travelling to Radensk to buy food. Two people were injured. He alleged that attacks on civilians had resumed before the agreed ceasefire had expired.

These accusations contradicted statements that the terms of the agreement had been observed. After the operation, Lubinets said that both sides had fulfilled their commitments.

Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, gave a similar assessment. International media also reported that there had been no confirmed violations of the local ceasefire.

Miroshnik’s statement therefore remains an accusation made by the Russian side, not an established fact.

Such reports serve an obvious purpose. They portray Moscow as willing to take part in humanitarian initiatives while reinforcing the image of Ukraine as the side posing a threat to civilians.

Even during an operation that officials from both countries described in positive terms, the Russian information space continued to recycle familiar accusations.

The ceasefire ended, but the problem remains

Russia refused to extend the ceasefire. According to AFP, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry had proposed prolonging the agreement, but the Russian side rejected the offer.

The ceasefire ended on 1 November. The ombudsmen said they were considering organising further humanitarian missions.

The need for evacuation has not gone away. Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who has been helping residents of Oleshky since 2022, told the Agency that not everyone who wanted to leave had been evacuated.

According to her, some residents of the city’s suburbs were turned back at checkpoints, while no transport arrived for some people with limited mobility. The most vulnerable are elderly people, people with disabilities and those unable to reach an evacuation point on their own.

Lubinets said 22 ambulances had to be deployed. Some people were too unwell to withstand the planned journey.

In one case, medical staff initially approved a person for transport but, after examining them on site, decided they would not survive the journey. An alternative arrangement had to be made. Several families are now continuing their journey to Ukraine by road.

The ombudsman also said that the Ukrainian side had managed to deliver medical equipment and medicines to the hospital in Oleshky. But he acknowledged that it was still impossible to assess the quality of medical care there.

Russian reports focused on the number of vehicles involved, the aid delivered by Russia and the organisation of transport. The fate of those left behind amid the crisis received far less attention.

Why this poses a threat to future evacuations

Disinformation can put people’s safety at risk. If a resident of an occupied city believes that returning to Ukraine will mean being detained and sent to the front, they may refuse to evacuate even when a safe route is available.

Claims that large numbers of people are unwilling to return can make those who remain feel that choosing Ukraine is dangerous, unpopular or pointless. The reality is more complicated.

People choose where to go based on their health, whether they have relatives there, their documents, housing and access to assistance.

For an elderly person, for example, reuniting with children or grandchildren may be the priority. A person with a disability may need medical care. For a family with children, safety and the ability to continue their education may matter most.

None of these decisions, in itself, reveals a person’s political beliefs. Turning evacuation figures into a vote for either Ukraine or Russia is therefore a form of manipulation.

▇ Choosing an evacuation destination is not the same as voting for Ukraine or Russia.

The information war could also complicate future humanitarian missions, the need for which both sides acknowledge.

World.title: Pakistani PM congratulates President Ilham Aliyev on occasion of Victory Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 7. Prime Minister of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif sent a congratulatory letter to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Excellency,

On behalf of the people and Government of Pakistan, as well as on my own behalf, I wish to extend our heartiest felicitations on the anniversary of Azerbaijan's Victory in the 44-Day Patriotic War.

This historic day stands as a fitting testament to the courage, unity, and indomitable resolve of Azerbaijan in safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity. Today, Azerbaijan stands strong and confident, reaping the fruits of its momentous victory into reconstruction, development, and the promise of lasting prosperity for its people. Your Excellency's visionary and sagacious leadership has been the guiding light of this remarkable national journey.

Pakistan takes great pride in the exceptional strength of our bilateral relationship, characterized by our mutual trust, shared values, and deep-rooted fraternal ties. We remain unwavering in our commitment to translate our special relationship with Azerbaijan, into a robust, multifaceted, and a dynamic strategic partnership, in the days ahead.

It is in the same spirit, that we look forward to Your Excellency's long-awaited visit to Pakistan, at mutually convenient dates. It is my firm belief that Your Excellency's presence in Islamabad, would provide an excellent opportunity to exchange views on bilateral, regional, and global issues, as well as formally launch a number of mutually beneficial initiatives, to further strengthen our strategic and economic partnership.

Availing myself of this opportunity, I convey my prayers and best wishes for Your Excellency's continued good health, happiness, and success, as well as for peace, progress, and prosperity of the brotherly people of Azerbaijan.

Please accept, Excellency, the assurances of my highest consideration," the letter reads.

World.title: When it comes to data centres, politics is getting very local
World.content:
As anyone with a relative who has slipped into the anti-data centre algorithm can attest, there are some truly bonkers myths out there.

Spend five minutes scrolling and you too could become convinced electromagnetic fields are killing all the bees, while the low-frequency noise emanating from the giant computing stacks is giving tinnitus to entire towns.

But not all the effects of data centres are imagined, as many residents across the US have learned.

From huge volumes of unaccounted water consumption to soaring electricity bills, there are ample cases to illustrate some fears are very real.

Musk's midterm donations backfire Elon Musk's home state of Texas accounted for 25 per cent of the US's planned data centre capacity, but that idea may now be dead in the water.

It's why data centres became a politically potent cost-of-living and local community issue in the US midterms, helping reshape gubernatorial campaigns in Texas, Georgia and Ohio.

The strongest evidence of direct voter rejection occurred at an even more local level, where dozens of ballot measures restricting data centres were approved in communities across California, Illinois, Maine, New York and other states.

While US politicians ignored the risks of the AI boom at their own peril, the same cannot be said for Australia, where most MPs have a well-worn script about capitalising on the upside while mitigating the bad.

But that political consensus could prove fragile once the enormous sums of money being promised are weighed against the much more immediate concerns of voters.

Getting ahead of the backlash

After a few false starts, the federal government has at least recognised the danger early enough to try to avoid the worst of the US experience.

There is broad agreement in Canberra that tech companies seeking to build in Australia must bring their own energy supply, efficiently and transparently manage water usage and consult with the community.

The challenge is in how to realise those broad principles in practice.

In just a few weeks, a parliamentary committee examining all these issues will hand down its final report.

Jo Briskey and Jonno Duniam co-chair the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

That work, along with a rapid review into the OpenAI Medicare data breach, will feed into national AI standards flagged by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in July.

As Labor's self-imposed, end-of-year deadline to unveil the detailed proposal looms, the US results offer a timely reminder that the economic promise of artificial intelligence will count for little if voters see no benefit.

In some respects, the data centre backlash in the US has only strengthened Australia's bargaining position with tech giants scrambling to find safe harbour for their billions of dollars in investment.

That does not mean voters here are yet convinced that whatever Australia actually gets out of hosting the infrastructure will be worth the cost.

Limits of political consensus

This explains why the Commonwealth and states are placing a premium on community consultation, particularly with regards to where data centres are located.

Though no-one is suggesting these giant structures will be taking up prime housing or agricultural land, suggestions there will be none in the "suburbs" likely depends on definition.

People power costs NEXTDC A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has wiped $3 billion from a listed company in a day and made the AI boom a little shakier.

Those vehemently opposed to data centres would say any proposal within cooee of a residential street was unacceptable.

But to rule out construction in the many industrial areas interspersed through Australia's towns and cities, including near houses, would be impractical.

It's the sort of semantics that mean, even with settled national standards, the risk of local backlash will remain high going forward.

As for concerns about electricity and water, the broad political agreement on protecting consumers conceals some fairly fundamental disagreements about how to do it.

National cabinet has papered over divisions on energy, with Queensland Premier David Crisafulli confident coal-powered data centres can meet requirements to protect electricity consumers, while federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen insists only renewables will stack up.

"We must balance the benefits of data centre investments and AI infrastructure against impacts to water security, and the community's expectation that new industry does no harm," Murray Watt says. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

Those following AI closely argue that water consumption can be significantly mitigated through advances in cooling technologies, but the sheer scale of the projects is staggering.

Sydney Water has warned the industry could consume up to a quarter of the city's drinking water by 2035.

Queensland initially stood alone in rejecting minimum water standards proposed by federal Water Minister Murray Watt, including requirements to minimise consumption, report usage and pay for infrastructure.

But the Crisafulli government subsequently signed up to the national standards, perhaps realising how exposed the state would be if things went wrong.

All politics is local

All signs suggest the national AI standards have a bipartisan path through the parliament, but signing up is much easier in the abstract.

Where there are real-life proposals, consensus can quickly fray.

Take the agreement signed by AI company Anthropic to use part of a $32 billion data centre proposed near Dalby, about 250 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

Liberal federal member for Groom, Garth Hamilton, last month broke ranks with his party to voice his concerns that locals were not being heard, revealing the proposed data centre was frequently raised "unprompted" by voters in his community.

The proposed Western Downs Digital Park in regional Queensland would consist of four data centres, the first of which has been leased by Anthropic for use as early as 2027. (Supplied: Urbis)

In July, Labor minister Sam Rae and neighbouring federal MP Alice Jordan-Baird released a statement critical of a plan by Syncline Energy to develop a 350-hectare, 2.4GW data centre in Plumpton in Melbourne's outer north-west.

The pair noted community concerns about the potential impact on energy, water, traffic and ongoing noise, stating they would not support developments that failed to meet the government's expectations around those issues.

The problem there is the project is progressing ahead of standards that do not yet exist and are due to be legislated only next year.

This scenario is precisely why some members of the crossbench and the Greens are supportive of a moratorium on new projects until the prospective AI laws are in place.

For now, Labor is resisting that approach, effectively asking communities to trust that the promised safeguards will arrive in time.

Loading

The price of playing AI host

Even if Australia gets everything right on data centre construction, there is still the question of how the country can extract ongoing value as a computer host.

Independent ACT senator David Pocock wants an immediate 5 per cent levy on all data centres to guarantee Australia a slice of the economic value.

Will AI crush the things that make life meaningful? In a rush to force AI on us, policymakers are embracing a technology that is exceptionally good at destroying the things that bring meaning to our lives.

Labor has long argued Australia needs to participate in the higher-value parts of the AI industry, with Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton raising the prospect of securing computing power to support homegrown innovation.

He has drawn comparisons with Australia's gas boom, where governments made the mistake of allowing an enormous export industry to develop without locking in sufficient benefits for domestic consumers.

It's a reminder and a warning that attracting investment is not the same as securing a return on it.

As it stands, Australia is still well placed to benefit from the rush to cash in on the AI boom that has sparked fierce backlash in the US.

But it is not immune from the political forces that turned a technological gold rush into an electoral liability.

World.title: Has the curtain come down on the age of Trump?
World.content:
The Trump political juggernaut has hit a wall. But while Democrats are celebrating, the battle for America's political future is only just beginning.

In the year America celebrated its 250th birthday, voters delivered a once-in-a-century election result signalling a break from a president who has dominated US politics for the past 10 years.

Donald Trump, to mark both the US semi-quincentennial and his own 80th birthday in June, put on a cage fight on the South Lawn of the White House. At these midterm elections, he was repeatedly body-slammed by voters. This was a very personal repudiation of a pharaoh-like figure who had tried, implausibly, to convince Americans they were enjoying a "golden age".

It represented the rebuke of a leader with authoritarian leanings who has sought to turn the White House into something akin to a palace, and Washington into a monument to himself.

Needless to say, exit polls showed voters were angry about the spike in fuel, food and, in rural states, fertiliser prices caused by a trade war that Trump framed as a "Liberation Day". The conflict with Iran had turned every gas station in America into a billboard for the Democrats. But alleged government corruption was also prominent in voters' minds, even higher in some exit polls than cost-of-living concerns.

Ahead of the election, a poll by Fox News showed alleged government corruption was actually the number one issue.

The billionaire president and his family have been getting ostentatiously richer while many Americans are suffering personal recessions.

Donald Trump and his family have increased their wealth during his presidency. ( )

Hard-pressed voters eyed decadence in the gold-bedecked walls of the Oval Office when their own quality of life was deteriorating. When Trump flew into the heartland to campaign, he did so aboard a $400 million Boeing 747-8 luxury airliner gifted by the Qatari royal family.

This wasn't simply an "it's the economy, stupid" election. It was also about the self-enrichment of Trump, his family members and acolytes such as Elon Musk, the world's first trillionaire. American voters were rejecting the excesses of an increasingly imperial presidency. Ending his campaign in front of the renovated Reflecting Pool in Washington seemed to many voters the perfect expression of his narcissism and tone-deafness.

Fantasy politics for the Democrats

More so than winning this election through the attractiveness of their policies, Democrats became the beneficiaries of the anti-Trump backlash. And theirs was a landslide win. The stuff of fantasy politics.

In regaining control of the US Senate, they took deep red Republican bastions: Texas, Kansas, even South Carolina.

The Democrats' "bluenami" included Gina Hinojosa's win in Texas. ( )

In the House of Representatives, Democrats will enjoy at least a 50-seat advantage. It is the kind of lopsided congressional majority not seen since Barack Obama's victory in 2008 which took a couple of successive waves to achieve. The cumulative vote in all the House seats, which gives the national picture, showed the Democrats had close to a 13-point lead over the Republicans.

To put that in historical perspective, in the famed "Republican revolution" of 1994 the GOP beat the Democrats by 6.8 points.

For the first time in 16 years, the Democrats will control a majority of governorships. These include noteworthy racial firsts. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor of an American state. Texas will now have a Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa. Disquiet and fear amongst Hispanic voters over ICE raids helped her triumph.

Not only the landscape but the face of US politics changed. For the first time in the country's history, the House of Representatives will have a Black speaker, New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries.

Small wonder, the term "bluenami" is being used. But it is also a red meltdown.

Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor of an American state. ( )

This is the first time in the Trump era his Republican Party has been severely punished. This result recalls the post-Watergate midterms in 1974 when Republicans were punished for the transgressions of Richard Nixon. Nixon had been forced to resign the presidency less than three months before Election Day.

That 1974 election brought about a generational shift. The Class of '74 included the so-called "Watergate babies". Remarkably, 87 members of the new Congress were aged under 40.

This election hasn't produced quite such an infusion of young blood. Still, at a time when Capitol Hill has often looked like a gerontocracy, the average age of lawmakers will be significantly lower. James Talarico, the Presbyterian seminarian with choir boy looks who won in Texas, is 37. Incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff, who comfortably regained his seat in the Republican target state of Georgia, is 39. Abdul El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim US Senator, is 42. Annie Andrews, who took South Carolina, is 46. Melat Kiros, who was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America in Colorado's first district, became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. She is just 29 years old.

A political realignment is on hold

What this election does not necessarily signify is a long-lasting political shift, or permanent realignment.

While the Republican Revolution of 1994 seemed to herald a period of conservative domination, just two years later Democrat Bill Clinton won his second term as president.

The 1974 midterm elections foretold that Republicans were set for a prolonged spell in the political wilderness. Yet Ronald Reagan won the presidency in 1980, and Republicans dominated the presidency for the next 12 years.

Democrats, understandably, are joyous about the outcome of the 2026 midterms. Yet their celebrations should come with circumspection.

A poll conducted in the run-up to this election suggested 52 per cent of voters had an unfavourable view of the Democratic Party; only 29 per cent had a favourable view. For months beforehand, the Real Clear Politicspolling average showed the American public looked on the Democrats only marginally more favourably than the Republicans.

Nevertheless, this is a mighty political achievement, which raises an important question: has the curtain come down on the age of Donald Trump?

A Trump dynasty snuffed out

As always, it is dangerous to write off or underestimate Donald Trump.

Just seven weeks after the storming of the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 as Congress met to certify the 2020 presidential election results, I watched as Trump was greeted like a conquering hero at a conservative conference in Orlando, Florida. The event had the feel of a cargo cult.

Likewise, after Trump-backed Republican candidates failed to make expected breakthroughs in the 2022 congressional midterms, pundits composed obituaries for the MAGA movement which proved wildly premature.

Yet this week's results are certainly a game-changer.

Any ambitions Trump might harbour of illegally defying the 22nd Amendment, which limits presidents to two terms in office, have surely been snuffed out. The notion of Trump 3.0 is even more outlandish now. A Trump dynasty also seems more unlikely. The thought of President Donald Trump Jr taking the oath of office in 2029 or 2033 requires a giant leap of imagination.

The notion of Trump 3.0 is even more outlandish now. ( )

Instead, Trump has been badly weakened. His fear factor, within a Republican Party that over the past decade has come to resemble a Trump Party, has been diminished. Signs of his waning power have come already from his Vice President JD Vance who, in a 600-word screed on social media, broke spectacularly with the president.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

But the president had not said so last night, and the ambitious vice president, who is eyeing a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, is already trying to distance himself from a damaged brand.

US Vice President JD Vance is eyeing a presidential bid in 2028 as he distances himself from Trump's damaged brand. ( )

In anointing his political heir, Trump might not be the all-powerful kingmaker after all. Maybe Republican presidential aspirants will not even crave his endorsement. When Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz published his own 1700-word election post-mortem on X — he described the midterms as "an ass kicking" — it did not include a single word of praise for a president who is used to sycophantic encomiums from his party.

Trump, however, still commands fierce loyalty from millions in his MAGA base. His approval rating among self-described "MAGA Republicans" is 96 per cent. Again, it is worth remembering what happened in the aftermath of January 6. Republicans could have banished Trump into the political wilderness. Instead, his grip on the party tightened. He successfully managed to purge the party of Trump critics, such as former Congresswoman Liz Cheney, and easily saw off the challenge from rivals such as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis in the 2024 Republican primaries.

The MAGA agenda survives

This election was not only a rejection of Trump but a repudiation of his hyper-aggressive style of politics.

In Michigan, he slandered Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as a "jihadist" and "terrorist", repeatedly called him "Mohammed". But in this bellwether of bellwethers, El-Sayed won comfortably.

The defeat of Trump acolyte, Vivek Ramaswamy, was also emblematic. Ramaswamy aired one of the most vile political attacks in US campaign history, which featured the mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Aston, castigating her daughter as a liar for accusing her ex-husband, who had been criminally charged of rape and then fled from police, of sexually molesting her as a child. Senior Republicans, including the state's outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, called for Ramaswamy to take down the ad. Trump described it as "very powerful".

Voters overwhelmingly rejected that kind of hateful politics.

James Talarico, who Trump labelled "Talafreako", made this yearning for a gentler kind of politics the centrepiece of his victory speech in Texas.

"We are tired of being told to hate each other," said Talarico. "It has been 10 years of this kind of politics, politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning, politics as professional wrestling."

Much of the MAGA agenda, however, will survive. Strong borders. Economic nationalism. A rejection of globalisation and frictionless free trade. The insistence that US allies must cough up more money for their own defence.

The MAGA agenda will survive the Republicans' midterms defeat. ( )

Democrats will be more wary of pushing what might be called "woke" issues. Even New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez remarked in August that "Woke 1.0 was crazy".

Democrats have already made concessions to Trumpism.

This election they focused on economic issues rather than identity politics. Crucially, however, in the 11 years since Trump came down that golden escalator he has not managed to create a pre-eminent new political order.

For much of the past century, as the historian Gary Gerstle noted in his 2022 landmark study, The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order, US politics was dominated by two political orders.

First, the New Deal created in the 1930s by Franklin Delano Roosevelt, marked by broad consensus between Democrats and Republicans on the role of the state in regulating capitalism and providing a basic welfare safety net for the economically disadvantaged.

Next, from the 1970s to the 2010s, came the neoliberal order, based on a reduced role of government and greater emphasis on the market, which was championed by Reagan and acquiesced in by Clinton, who presented himself as a market-friendly "New Democrat".

Since the Great Recession of 2008, however, no party has managed to impose its ideas on the other, or accrued enough power for long enough in Washington to do so. Instead, we have entered what Gerstle describes as an "interregnum characterised by disorder and instability".

This election offers further proof that we remain in this liminal phase, with neither side establishing lasting dominance.

Trump believed there had been a conservative vibe shift in 2024 after he regained the presidency by winning all seven battleground states. Republicans also controlled both houses of Congress. Two years later, Trump and his party have been hammered.

Where to for the left?

In a chronically polarised nation, we are witnessing a period of unusual political volatility.

At the presidential level, three consecutive two-term presidencies (Democrat Bill Clinton, Republican George W Bush and Democrat Barack Obama) have been followed three consecutive one-term presidencies (Republican Trump, Democrat Joe Biden, Republican Trump).

Not since the late 19th century, when Grover Cleveland lost the presidency only to win it back four years later, have we seen the presidency switch quadrennially between the parties. Likewise, no party has managed to command Capitol Hill for an extended period. Already this century the House has changed hands five times.

In the entire second half the 21st century, during which Democrats dominated the House of Representatives, that scenario has only occurred three times. In the final 25 years of the 20th century, the Senate changed majority control just three times. In the first 25 years of the 21st century, it has flipped eight times.

Now we will see divisions not only between the parties but within them. Progressive Democrats will point to the success of El-Sayed in Michigan, and the energising effect of Zohran Mamdani's 2025 mayoral victory in New York, as proof that a left-wing version of economic populism can succeed at the national level.

The success of US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is viewed as proof a left-wing version of economic populism can succeed at the national level. ( )

Among the Democratic victors on Tuesday were a record number of candidates backed by, or affiliated with, the Democratic Socialists of America. Centrists will cite the breakthrough in Texas of Talarico, a moderate Christian Democrat, and the mega-church pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas as evidence that the party should occupy the middle ground.

All the party's winning presidential candidates since World War II — Harry Truman, John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson, Jimmy Carter, Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — have been pragmatic centrists.

The orthodoxy that only a moderate can win the White House will now be challenged, and contested, ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Where to now for the right?

On the right of politics, what remains of the more traditionalist wing of the Republican Party might argue the party has to move away from its Trump branding and become more recognisably Reaganesque. Reagan was a free-trade internationalist who backed traditional conservative governance, compared with Trump's populist nationalism that embraces economic protectionism and rejects global alliances and institutional norms.

MAGA diehards will remain faithful to Trump, though some will argue he has not been MAGA enough, especially by launching an unpopular war with Iran. Think-tanks, such as the Heritage Foundation which produced the controversial policy blueprint Project 2025, have lurched a long way to the right. So, too, have media channels such as Fox News and NewsMax, whose "angertainment" business models are based on stoking culture war outrage.

So, it is by no means inevitable that the party will move back towards what is sometimes called the sensible centre.

The future shape of the Republican Party is yet to be decided. ( )

How could the Republicans remain viable if MAGA voters withdrew their support? Some are now likening the Trump Republican Party to the Trump casino empire. That did not end well.

If, moreover, Texas becomes the new California — the Golden State voted Republican in every presidential election between 1968 and 1988 but Democrat ever since — then it could face a prolonged shut-out from the White House. Try gaining an Electoral College majority without at least one of the country's two most populous states.

Looking to the future, the youth vote does not augur well for the Republicans. Nationally, in House elections, exit polling suggest 66 per cent of voters aged 18-29 voted for a Democrat candidate.

Always, though, we must be wary of over-extrapolating in the aftermath of what look like transformative elections. I have seen too many victorious parties over-reach and then face push-back from voters. Remember the heady talk after Barack Obama's election in 2008 that suggested he would usher in a phase of post-partisanship, and even post-racialism.

As a correspondent in the US at the time, I witnessed how the country's first African-American president was followed into the White House by the untitled leader of the Birther Movement, who placed himself at the head of the anti-Obama white backlash. As Obama himself described the shift after Trump's victory in 2016: "History doesn't move in a straight line. It zigs and zags."

Democrats have authority to scrutinise

For the past decade, anti-incumbency has so often been the driver of American politics. That, and the negative partisanship that comes with it. Voters often cast their ballots against a party rather than for a party. In these midterms we saw it again. In a 50/50 nation, where for much of this century the results of elections have been far narrower than on Tuesday night, politics has been marked by deadlock not dominance.

What we do know for sure is that the Democrats have just won the authority to scrutinise and investigate. When the new Congress meets on January 3, expect Democratic lawmakers to use those subpoena powers to the full.

Robert Garcia, the top ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, which tends to spearhead congressional investigations, has said already that allegations of Trump family corruption will be his main priority, with the president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, coming under closer scrutiny. On election night, he posted two words on social media: "LAWYER UP!"

Robert Garcia is the top ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee. ( )

Garcia also released a statement pledging to take on "the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS [Department of Homeland Security] and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files". Hakeem Jeffries has accused the "Trump Cartel" of "massive corruption" and warned: "We are going to hold the crooks accountable."

With a majority in the House, the Democrats could for a third time impeach Donald Trump (previously, only two presidents — Andrew Johnson and Bill Clinton — have faced the charge of committing high crimes and misdemeanours). But winning a conviction in the Senate trial that would ensue requires 67 votes, the kind of super-majority the Democrats are not close to achieving. Besides, attempts to punish Trump have often worked in his favour, by allowing him to claim a political form of martyrdom.

The Democrats could also try to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth for waging military hostilities without congressional authorisation, which is a violation of the 1973 War Powers Resolution. Moves are already afoot in what is now a lame duck Congress, spearheaded by the anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie, to trigger an impeachment vote against Hegseth as soon as this week.

Accountability and action

The newly-elected 120th Congress, whose members will take their seats in the new year, could become known as the Accountability Congress. But House Democrats will also want to make it an Action Congress, by passing bills, on healthcare especially, that meet the concerns of struggling American voters — even though they could be blocked by Republican filibusters in the Senate, which require 60 votes to break, or vetoed by the president.

Ethics reform is an area the Democrats could highlight, such as beefing up financial conflict-of-interest rules in the executive branch and placing limits on presidential pardons. The post-Watergate Congress placed a heavy emphasis on ethics reform, with the creation of the Office of Government Ethics and independent Inspectors General within federal departments.

Among the challenges for the Democrats will be to restore the power of Capitol Hill, which has been the home for the past two years of an incredible shrinking Congress.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has sought to expand the power of the presidency and to govern almost by decree through signing so many executive orders with the flourish of his Sharpie felt tip pen. Already, he has signed 292 executive orders during his second term, well over 100 more than Joe Biden issued during his entire four-year term.

The conservative-dominated Supreme Court, while sometimes checking his power, has helped him create a more maximal presidency. In Trump v Slaughter, the court ruled in June that the president can fire the heads of independent regulatory agencies at his behest, without being required to show "cause".

In its landmark Trump v United States ruling in 2024, brought in connection with the criminal charges he faced over his attempt to overturn the presidential election, it decided presidents possess substantial immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office. Among the three branches of government, Congress has felt like the third wheel.

The founding fathers, however, had a very different power ranking in mind. The legislature was supposed to be the most powerful branch of government, which is why Congress was vested with the power of the purse. The presidency was meant to be second. The Supreme Court a distant third.

Democrats on Capitol Hill will attempt to restore parity with the executive branch, especially over trade policy, and to overtake the Supreme Court. Supreme Court Justice John Roberts has been a more influential figure than the departing Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will attempt to restore the sway of a role traditionally regarded as the second most powerful government position in the country.

Trump is no lame duck

After the Republicans' shellacking at the polls, it will be tempting to describe Trump as a "lame duck" president, the usual descriptor for an incumbent whose party loses control of Congress and cannot seek re-election. With Trump, that would be an act of folly. Normal nomenclature does not apply to such an abnormal president.

Trump will not be a lame duck until the final second of the final minute of his presidency. In his last supposed lame-duck phase, from his defeat at the 2020 election to inauguration day in 2021, he propagated the "Big Lie" about Joe Biden stealing the election, amassed his supporters in Washington and did little to restrain them when they first started storming the US Capitol.

Despite the midterm results, don't call Trump a lame duck. ( )

Trump still has enormous executive powers at his disposal. He remains the commander-in-chief of the world's most powerful military. He still has control of the FBI and Justice Department, and could use both in an attempt to take vengeance on political opponents. Overcoming a presidential veto requires a two-thirds super-majority in both houses of Congress, which alone the Democrats cannot muster. Trump has issued 12 vetoes over the course of his two terms; congress has only overridden one of them.

By appointing as his new White House chief of staff arch loyalist Stephen Miller, the hardline architect of the ICE immigration crackdown, Trump is signally there will be no retreat from MAGA. Heading the West Wing is a figure who Trump will regard as a wartime consigliere, an aggressively combative figure in upcoming battles with Congress.

Often, if presidents are thwarted on the home front by an obstructionist Congress, they look to make their mark in the foreign realm. Trump could press for a peace deal in the Ukraine war, on terms that would likely be highly favourable towards Vladimir Putin. He could renew the kind of summitry with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, which became such a feature of his first term diplomacy.

He might agree to carve up the world into spheres of influence as part of a grand bargain with Putin and President Xi Jinping of China, which would require concerns in Taiwan. Trump has made no secret of his desire for regime change in Cuba.

As the dust settles after such an extraordinary electoral event, it is worth noting what did not happen in the 2026 congressional midterms.

For sure, Donald Trump tried to disrupt the polls beforehand, by attempting to limit postal voting and demanding, unsuccessfully, that states surrender their voter registration lists to the Justice Department in Washington.

Yet worries that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, or even federal troops, would be deployed at, or in the close vicinity of, polling stations on Election Day did not eventuate. Nor has Trump tried to interfere with the count. The Republican defeat, of course, was too big to rig. In a closer election, disputed contests could easily have become flashpoints. But it is worth pointing out that, although he has distanced himself from the results, he had not disputed them.

In the year America marked its 250th birthday, the country faced a democratic test, and passed.

Nobody was assassinated during the campaign. Election Day passed without violence. On January 3, when the new Congress is seated we will not see a repeat of the American insurrection that unfolded on January 6, 2021.

That alone, in a country as divided and fractious as America, is cause for celebration.
