World.title: He stars in the most expensive show ever made, but Ismael Cruz Cordova’s journey to Middle-earth was not easy
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every morning while filming The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, actor Ismael Cruz Cordova would sit patiently while two make-up artists worked to craft his pointed elven ears. The prosthetics that transform him into dashing warrior elf Arondir are cast to the contours of his cheekbones and match his skin tone so well that Cordova himself cannot see the seam. But when they are done, there is no longer a reflection of one man in the mirror. Rather, Cordova sees three people looking back: the elven warrior who has become something of a poster boy for the Amazon Prime Video series, the actor, who cut his teeth on The Good Wife, Ray Donovan and The Undoing, and the barefoot kid from the Puerto Rican mountains who washed cars to save money for a used DVD player. Ismael Cruz Cordova plays Arondir, the Silvan elf in The Rings of Power. “I absolutely love my ears,” says Cordova. “As an elf, there’s something about these ears that everybody wants. Because elves are so close to humans in form, that little hint of difference, it’s elegant and it’s this magical, mystical thing. I remember the first time that I saw myself with them on, at that moment, when it was complete, I just cried the biggest tears. “It’s this ritualistic aspect of becoming. I’m a very physical actor, and as I transform into this character, by this point, there’s this sense memory. My voice begins to drop, my accent starts coming in. So for me, it’s this incredible rite of passage.” Related Article Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in November The man in the mirror, he says, is a “composite of three things ... these three beings that are inextricably tied. Ismael now, and Arondir on top of that ... but it begins with the little boy that sees the movies for the first time. I grew up in the mountains, a very poor community, very rural, not a lot of opportunities. That little boy has to wash cars, lawns, mow lawns, do any type of errand to find a little bit of money to buy a DVD player and then a DVD.”



The first two DVDs he owned? Moulin Rouge! and The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, both released in 2001. “This world opened up to me,” he says. “Moulin Rouge! was one of those movies that I was like, whoa, [it] blew my mind. But it was also the behind-the-scenes component [that came with the DVD]. I got to see what this was about from an abstraction to the reality, and it changed my life.” Ismael Cruz Córdova as Arondir in battle in season three of The Rings of Power. And The Fellowship of the Ring? “Truly from the get-go, I wanted to be an elf because the elves are so close to who I was,” Cordova says. “They loved nature, [they are a] contemplative people, like my reverence for sunsets. I was always this precocious kid concerned with beauty and with natural beauty and what nature did. I’m still that way.” In one sense, those ears – as expensive as they undoubtedly are – are a small line item in a big budget. The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is one of the most expensive TV series ever made. The five-season commitment will exceed $US1 billion ($1.44 billion) in costs. And we’re just three seasons in. Related Article ★★★★

Review I thought we didn’t need any more stories about Muhammad Ali. I was wrong The series, developed by show runners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay, is set during the Second Age of Middle-earth, thousands of years before the events of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. It follows an ensemble of characters – the younger iteration of the elven queen, Galadriel, the future ruler of Rivendell, Elrond, and a wood elf warrior, Arondir – as they confront the rise of evil in Middle-earth. The project began after Amazon secured the television rights from the Tolkien estate in 2017, and it sits in an ever-widening mosaic of Middle-earth-set storytelling. In 2024, under a different deal between movie rights holder Embracer and Warner Bros., Kenji Kamiyama directed an anime prequel, The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim, about the history of the fortress Helm’s Deep.



And a new film, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum – set between The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings in the established cinematic universe of the Peter Jackson films – will feature Andy Serkis as Gollum and Smeagol, Ian McKellen as Gandalf, Jamie Dornan as Strider, Leo Woodall as Halvard, a Dunedain ranger, and Elijah Wood as Frodo Baggins. Daniel Weyman as young Gandalf in The Rings of Power. All of that, on top of the new third season of The Rings of Power, and two more seasons to follow. By and large, the television series is faithful to the original works of J.R.R. Tolkien, on which it is based. That said, the television adaptation has ruffled canonical feathers of the diehard Tolkien fans because of some of the liberties it takes. Most of its characters are drawn from familiar legend: Isildur, the mortal man whom we meet as a boy and who will eventually cut “the ring” from the hand of franchise baddie Sauron, and Celebrimbor, the master ringsmith of the elves, who begins creating the magical rings that are central to the story. Related Article Streaming ‘Rip your jaw off’: The lengths Stephen Graham went to for his killer new role But Cordova’s Arondir is another story. He’s a piece of new canon, though his backstory is steeped deeply in Tolkien lore. The Silvan elves, of whom Arondir is one, are the elves who inhabited places such as Mirkwood and Lothlorien, and known for their connection to nature (that’s why they are called “wood” elves).



Arondir’s role in the story, too – the “watchwarden” of the Southlands – is based on the idea, in Tolkien’s postwar history, that after the defeat of the first Dark Lord, Morgoth, the elves kept a close watch on that part of Middle-earth. “I’m at the whim and trust of the creators of the show,” Cordova says. “I’ve known that from the beginning. I’ve known that he’s going to go where he goes, and it’s allowed me also to be present. I’ve given my absolute entire soul to each moment that I have, not thinking that I’m going to play an arc of five seasons or anything like that.” Charlie Vickers as Sauron on the set of The Rings of Power during filming of season three. While all art is not necessarily inherently political, it is true The Lord of the Rings as an over-arching “legendarium” deals with some potential political themes. The inevitable corruption of absolute power, Saruman’s transformation of Isengard from a green valley into a crater of military manufacturing, the destruction of Fangorn Forest, and Grima Wormtongue’s poisoning of King Theoden’s mind with misinformation. “About Tolkien’s [world], I think it’s open knowledge that it was created as a result of his experience during war and wartimes and industrialisation and seeing the landscape change, and seeing nature turned, human against human, and people not being able to see the beauty and the simplicity of things that are right in front of them,” says Cordova. Related Article Australian TV Why it will be crime time (all the time) on Australian screens next year “All art is political. I do not have a capacity to understand otherwise because existence is political. I am always open and flexible for my views to be challenged. I speak with certainty, the things that I say, but I’m also certain that they might be wrong.”

World.title: He may have got his start on reality TV, but Michael Theo’s acting career is now thriving
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV He may have got his start on reality TV, but Michael Theo’s acting career is now thriving Bridget McManus November 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The acting career Michael Theo manifested before our eyes on Love on the Spectrum has – to reference the favourite pastime of the charming breakout star of that dating show – taken off like a runaway train. Having been talent-scouted by Death in Paradise actor Ben Miller, who co-created the lead role for Theo in the ABC comedy-drama, Austin, Theo has wrapped the third season of the British-Australian series, appeared earlier this year in ABC Family’s mystery series, Caper Crew, completed voice work on the Shaun Tan adaptation, Tales from Outer Suburbia, and has been filming the forthcoming ABC series, Rural Crime Unit, in Adelaide. Michael Theo as Austin and Natalie Abbott as Haley in season three of Austin. “It’s a great experience. I’m loving it,” says Theo. “The character I’m playing in Rural Crime Unit, I don’t think he is on the spectrum. I think he might be neurotypical.” While Theo is relishing playing against type, Austin Hogan, the railway-obsessed forklift driver who discovers the UK branch of his family when he meets his biological father, Julian Hartswood (Miller), will always hold a special place in his heart.



Related Article Australian TV Why it will be crime time (all the time) on Australian screens next year “Working with Ben is a joy and a pleasure, but also the entire cast [which includes Sally Phillips, Gia Carides, Roy Billing, Stephen Curry, and new addition Justine Clarke]. I call them my screen family. I love them to the point that I’m actually terrified of losing them.” This season, he says, holds “a lot of blessings”. There’s a wedding, a funeral, and a new chapter for Austin to navigate with his girlfriend, fellow Whovian Hayley (Natalie Abbott). “The relationship between our characters on screen reflects that of us off-screen,” says Theo. “I consider Natalie one of my dearest friends. She’s someone I love working with. During season three, we have an intimacy co-ordinator. That suited me really well because if there were any kissing scenes, I wanted her to be absolutely comfortable.” Austin is a fictionalised version of Theo, whom the actor had a consulting role in creating.



“We both carry ourselves in a certain way. We speak formally,” says Theo. “But Austin takes a lot of things literally, more so than I do. And sometimes his ways are a little misguided, whereas I follow guidance from my family and friends. Also, we have very big hearts. We care about what’s important … Austin is also uncomfortable with physical touch, whereas I give hugs a lot. That’s part of my nature because I was raised in a Mediterranean household.” Aaron Cartwright as Todd, Michael Theo as Austin, and Stephen Curry as Cobb in Austin. Unlike Austin, Theo is not a fan of Doctor Who. He watches Thomas the Tank Engine on repeat. “I consider steam locomotives one of the most fascinating things ever created by mankind,” he says. “When I was a child, [animation] is what I was drawn to the most. Animation is healthier for the mind. I consider animation a sacred art form. And in supplying your voice to an animated character, that piece of work will outlive you even long after you’re gone. Maybe some people believe that animation is just for children, but I disagree with that.” Theo is currently single, having recently emerged from an 18-month relationship. He did not find love on reality TV, and wouldn’t recommend that process to everyone.



Related Article Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in November “My best advice is, just give it a go,” he says. “But people need to remember that romantic love is a treasure. And if anyone violates it, or disrespects it, or betrays it, there’s a chance you might not be able to get it back. You must always cherish your partner and treat her like gold. It’s not easy being in a relationship. It takes work. I know.” That sentiment is reflected through Austin’s emotional journey, which Theo hopes helps viewers to understand more about people living with autism. “People who are neurodiverse don’t want or need special treatment. We just want to be loved and accepted, like everybody else. Neurodiverse people are just as capable of navigating life as well as anyone else … It’s just a matter of finding your crowd.” Austin returns at 9pm on Wednesday, November 11, on the ABC and ABC iview.

World.title: Faith is neither blind nor restricted to religion
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion Faith is neither blind nor restricted to religion Barney Zwartz Contributor November 8, 2026 — 5:30am

November 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As always in the Trump era, doubts are being raised about the integrity of the US midterm elections, this time especially over alleged illegal voting. Few democracies have a more corrupt system for establishing electorates than the United States, where the political party in power in each state defines boundaries, and gerrymandering is rife. Donald Trump’s constant complaints about election fraud have helped contribute to the lowest level of trust by Americans in their electoral system for decades, surveys say. Trust in governments may be at a low, but faith in voting is a separate matter, with its own guardian in Australia. Andrew Meares What a contrast in Victoria, where we go to the polls in just under three weeks. Australians can and do have strong and justified faith in Australia’s system, run by an utterly independent electoral commission whose integrity seems beyond doubt. Our electoral commissions decide electorate boundaries purely on demographic grounds, not at the behest of or for the advantage of any particular party. My own electoral boundaries have changed a few times over the years, but no one ever suggested any malign influence.



For the November 28 election, the Victorian Electoral Commission is putting on at least 27,000 extra staff and running more than 300 education sessions in all 88 state electorates about the voting process. Sessions are being held in neighbourhood houses, in 18 prisons, in Indigenous communities, for people with disabilities, and for people whose first language is not English. I call my trust in the electoral commission “faith” because I cannot verify all the facts myself. It comes from 50 years of voting and observing, watching the conduct of the election and the processes leading up to it. And this is the point: true faith is seldom blind. It grows from experience, observation, evidence and sometimes even intuition. Similarly, the Christian faith is not blind. It is based on all sorts of evidence and arguments which weigh with people – or not – for reasons that are often beyond the purely rational. As the atheist Enlightenment philosopher David Hume observed, reason is always the slave of the passions. Related Article Faith

Religion In the small things, hope floats



For Christians, evidence includes the irreducible complexity of creation. The Psalmist wrote: “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands. Day after day, they pour forth speech; night after night, they reveal knowledge.” The Apostle Paul says God’s eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen in what has been made. There is the eyewitness testimony in the New Testament, and the way the whole Christian narrative coheres beautifully if given the initial premises – it is not irrational or illogical – and the innumerable human lives given meaning, consolation and hope through the faith. The Christian faith is not belief without evidence but a response to the evidence. Barney Zwartz is a Senior Fellow of the Centre for Public Christianity. The Herald charts the ups and downs of the creation of Sydney’s newest cultural institution. See all stories .

The stars have never aligned for the Powerhouse Parramatta. From the start it was controversial. The backlash began almost as soon as premier Mike Baird announced his plans in 2015 to create a new cultural landmark by selling off the Powerhouse Museum’s Ultimo site and moving the institution’s headquarters to Sydney’s geographical heartland. An attempt to nudge our city’s cultural centre of gravity westwards, while raising a handy $200 million to help pay for it, became a protracted dispute between the government, Ultimo locals and museum lovers, incensed at the Coalition’s zero-sum approach to raising Parramatta’s cultural capital and the deconstruction of a functioning facility. Much is riding on whether the city embraces it new major attraction. Steven Siewert Five years later, Baird’s successor Gladys Berejiklian cut her political losses (but increased the cost to the state’s coffers), deciding to keep the existing museum but also build a new cultural beacon on the banks of the Parramatta River, foregoing the multimillion-dollar payday expected from the sell-off of prime inner city real estate. Fears that the Parramatta site was a flood risk prompted a parliamentary inquiry (one of two into the development), while friends of the historic 1880s Willow Grove house campaigned, unsuccessfully, to save it from being dismantled to make way for the new glass-and-steel structure.





Treasury is yet to approve an operating budget for the museum. Its running costs were projected to be $145 million (as opposed to $69 million for the Australian Museum and $68 million for the Art Gallery of NSW). Treasury will be looking to trim that figure substantially. Doubts remain over whether projected earnings from gift shops and other commercial ventures will meet an optimistic $50 million contribution to expenditure. Staff fear job cuts are on the way. Related Article Visual story

Development Inside Sydney’s newest billion-dollar house The big test will be whether Sydneysiders embrace this bold experiment in museum reinvention, with an emphasis on arts and events rather than showcasing the Powerhouse collection. But true to the seemingly cursed history of the project, it has opened in the midst of a cost of living crisis, when all cultural institutions are reporting that discretionary spending on entertainment is down. Its business model depends on a lively and varied program to draw in the punters, but its straightened budget may not be up to delivering on this promise. Yesterday, the first visitors were wildly enthusiastic. Let’s hope that means its fortunes are turning, and it becomes a vibrant addition to Sydney’s cultural landscape.

World.title: Pitch battle: Cricket NSW stumps Bears’ plan for historic return match
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Pitch battle: Cricket NSW stumps Bears’ plan for historic return match Danny Weidler Sport columnist November 8, 2026 — 5:30am

November 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A romantic and historic return to North Sydney Oval by rugby league’s newest team, the Perth Bears, is being blocked by Cricket NSW, potentially denying their fans a perfect entry into the NRL next season. The Bears can’t play premiership matches at their spiritual home of North Sydney Oval because it’s not fit for the NRL. Bears fans Craig Gray and Josh Averell at North Sydney Oval. Steven Seiwert However, they are aiming to play their historic return match – a trial – at Bear Park in late February. It’s a no-brainer, considering how long the rusted-on Bears’ faithful have clung to hope that their team may one day return.



Negotiations between the Perth Bears, the NRL, Cricket NSW and the local council have been going on for weeks. And it’s not looking good for the Bears. The NRL had a meeting with Cricket NSW, who told them they would need to reschedule some Sydney grade cricket matches to accommodate the trial and the cost to take the pitch out and put it back in would be close to $200,000. It is not clear who would pay the bill, but it appears the Bears believe they will be on the hook. The Perth Bears are hoping to play an NRL trial match at their spiritual home ground, North Sydney Oval. Steven Siewert The machinery that does the relocating of the pitch is in Adelaide and needs a specialist team to operate it. It’s a time-consuming task: taking pitches out and putting them back is a five-week operation. The grass needs time to bed down after the pitch is removed and reinstalled. Considering the trial would be on the weekend of February 20-21 and club cricket’s schedule is limited after this, the Bears and NRL think it would be reasonable to just reschedule the remaining fixtures to avoid having to bring the crew from Adelaide to Sydney to put the pitch back in.



Cricket NSW is not interested in this proposal. It has shut down talks with the Bears. Cricket NSW was approached for comment. Bears great Don McKinnon is chaired from North Sydney Oval after his last game for the club in 1987. Stephen Lunam A glance at the cricket fixtures impacted by the NRL trial proves how silly this stand-off is. They won’t draw a crowd and could be moved to one of the many cricket grounds across Sydney. Cricket Australia also has no fixtures scheduled at the ground.



As I understand it, Cricket NSW has a contract over the venue with North Sydney Council, so this would be an act of goodwill to welcome the Bears back – a huge moment for the local community, but also rugby league in general. NRL executive chairman Peter V’landys has been pivotal in the Bears’ return and knows the importance of the Norths heritage, not to mention the huge ratings it would deliver for Foxtel/Kayo Sports. Schedule clash Cricket fixtures on the weekend of Feb 20-21 impacted by possible Bears NRL trial game. Jan 23 – Jan 30: UTS North Sydney v Bankstown; Feb 6 – Feb 7: North Sydney v Sydney; Feb 13 – Feb 20: North Sydney v UNSW Fixtures beyond Feb 20-21 impacted Cricket NSW has booked in three “internal academy trial” days at North Sydney Oval from March 9. Images of a packed North Sydney Oval would have even rival fans, maybe not from Manly, a little emotional. Bears roll out the red carpet for Burton



Bears recruit Toby Sexton will be trying to woo his former Bulldogs halves partner Matt Burton to join the NRL newcomers when Burton drops in to Perth on Sunday for a tour of the city and club. Burton, who is free to negotiate with rivals, will be floored on his trip by a $6m four-year deal to join the Bears. Toby Sexton is hoping his former Bulldogs teammate Matt Burton (on ground) will join him at the Perth Bears from 2027. Getty Images Through smart negotiating by his agent he is looking at a deal worth $1.1m a year without ratchet clauses. With the clauses, to cover pending salary cap increases, it is worth $1.3m a year. And when you add third-party allowances the Bears have and the deal is worth $1.5 million a year. Sexton and another Bears 2027 recruit, Canterbury back-rower Josh Curran, will both be selling the Perth dream to him when he lands at his potential new home.



The Bears will roll out the red carpet, with coach Mal Meninga playing salesman and tour guide. But it will be the former Dogs who may have a significant input. Sexton has been in Burton’s ear for some time. He is known to be keen to have his old halves partner by his side. The Dogs are comfortable with Burton finding out his worth and know that he loves the club he is at. Walker eyes PNG move The PNG Chiefs interest in Sam Walker doesn’t suit the Sydney Roosters. But what is of interest - the Chiefs have been aware for several months that Walker has had an interest in joining the Port Moresby-based club for some time. Walker’s girlfriend Bella recently holidayed in Europe with Kiana Flanet, the girlfriend of Chiefs recruit Connor Watson



The premiers are still determined to move in a different direction next season and don’t want to be a holding pen for Walker in 2027. Walker, who is contracted to the Roosters next season but is free to join another club after negotiations broke down last week, doesn’t have to leave and finding a new home isn’t straightforward. Sam Walker savoured the Roosters premiership win with Angus Crichton in the dressing rooms. Getty Images The best possible option is the Bulldogs, but that can’t happen without an early Matt Burton departure. And the Dogs told Walker’s agent they are not in the market for him.



Related Article NRL 2026 PNG Chiefs eye Sam Walker after missing out on Nathan Cleary The Queensland Reds rugby franchise has been engaging in discussions about Walker, but it would appear to be a long shot to get him to switch codes. That may in part explain the interesting sights at Rugby Australia’s agents accreditation day – revolving around Walker’s agent Clinton Schifcofske. He was in and out of the meeting with regularity. The other agents were taking note and wondering if something was cooking with Walker and RA. What we have been told is that the idea of Walker as the Wallabies World Cup No.10 has been floated. He was a gun in schoolboy rugby. We checked with his management and, so far, there has been no bite from RA.



I had a brief chat with Walker at Kangaroos training this week. He was last one off the training paddock and, in typical Walker fashion, he came and said hello. He didn’t spill any secrets, but he appeared very happy despite the obvious drama he has been dealing with. Ultimately, he will be fine financially, no matter where he ends up. The concern is he needs a club that can help his career prosper. Even great halfbacks need strong packs. Titans wild about Harry Gold Coast part owner Matthew Johns has distanced himself from the thought that he is the mastermind trying to lure Kangaroos and Storm hooker Harry Grant to the Titans.



Whoever is pulling the strings has a sharp mind - the attempt by the Titans to swap Cooper Bai for Melbourne’s Trent Loiero is a smart one on the playing level and beyond. Trent’s sister Brooke is Grant’s partner. Johns has a tight relationship with Grant and his family thanks to his son Cooper’s friendship with the Maroons star. It has been thought that Johns was driving the pursuit of Grant, who is free to negotiate with rivals for the 2028 season. Melbourne hooker Harry Grant is said to be in the sights of the Gold Coast Titans. Getty Images Johns also has an excellent relationship with the Storm.



Another perspective Cronulla Sharks With their leagues club finally unveiled, Sharks push for stadium deal The Storm would like Grant to have decided by now on his future, as chairman Matt Tripp is about to head overseas. Tripp was also hoping front-rower Stefano Utoikamanu would have decided on his future by now. Negotiations over the next couple of weeks will be more tricky with Tripp away. None of that is the Titans’ concern, but what is of importance to Johns is that his personal relationship with Grant is not compromised by business.



“Of course I would like to see Harry at the Titans,” Johns said. “But I sent him a text message outlining the fact that our friendship is more important than anything that may happen in a negotiation and that’s what is important to me. “Harry acknowledged that and will just have to see what happens. As for his friendship with Cooper and any help that may be, I honestly think that is more of a hindrance than something that can assist us, as is most things that Cooper involves himself in.” Cleary’s $12m sacrifice Panthers superstar Nathan Cleary stood to earn at least $20 million in tax-free dollars from the Papua New Guinea Chiefs over the same four-year period he is going to commit to at Penrith.



Loading While he was flattered by the huge and professional play, it was not an agonising decision to say no. He is not money-driven and, from what this column can gather, he said the Panthers’ $1.7m a year, plus third-party deals his manager would acquire for him, is right for him at the moment. Cleary has had it made clear to him that he sacrificed about $12m over four years by rejecting the Chiefs. On the mend, Nathan Cleary with his partner, Mary Fowler. Instagram



Cleary would have been earning the equivalent of $4.7 to $5 million a year at PNG, including the money he could have made from third parties. In effect, combined with third-parties deals that his agent George Mimis could source, it would be the equivalent of $20m. The Panthers’ money with his deals may be worth about $8 million over that time. Cleary is looking at doing a two-year extension with a two-year option in his favour. The Chiefs did make a formal approach and offer to Cleary – they knew it was a matter of importance to state their case the moment he was a free agent from November 1.



PNG made an incredible video pitch, which included the huge offer, to an injured Cleary, who cannot travel as he recovers from multiple surgeries to his legs. The presentation didn’t include the third-party offers, but given what Jarome Luai is making it was not hard to see what he could earn. It was by far the biggest play in history for a player and it had been incredibly well-thought-out and constructed by Chiefs football manager Michael Chammas. It was always a long shot. No surprises to see Farnworth move to Chooks If season 2027 is tricky for the premiership winning Roosters, with several players leaving, 2028 should be a boom year.



Captain James Tedesco will be playing his final season and there is every chance he will be able to impart his enormous knowledge to Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth, who is expected to join the Bondi Junction club. If he doesn’t, it would be a huge surprise. Herbie Farnworth has been heavily linked to the Sydney Roosters. Getty Images No club does the big signings better than the Roosters. They just about always grab the cream. The Roosters’ denial of this column’s story last week about interest in Nathan Cleary as a Sam Walker replacement was predictable. The fact is they reached out to those close to Cleary to ask to be part of the conversation around his future. Maybe they didn’t think it would reach the media.



No club boss wants to be interested in a player and then miss out. As it is, they were rejected by their premiership winning halfback Walker and they don’t need another recruitment miss. Munster sweeps the Cup You almost don’t need us to tell you which Kangaroo won the Melbourne Cup sweep. Of course, it was Cameron Munster who picked Cup winner Point Of Law. Loading



Who else would stand a chance with a scallywag like Munster involved. Morris going to America In a week when the Tigers confirmed our story that Ryan Carr would be the club’s new assistant coach, John Morris, the man who lost the job, has taken off to America to do a self-development course. Part of it will be a leadership and management course at Harvard University. John Morris has left the Tigers and is currently on an education/fact-finding mission in the US. NRL Photos



Morris reached out to the NRL’s American expansion boss John Vellis, who got the former Sharks coach into the NFL’s head office in New York for a number of meetings with key staff, including in rookie player development and concussion management. Editor's pick Wests Tigers NRL could strip licence from Wests Tigers’ owners after fresh board ructions He is also visiting the Boston Celtics, the New England Patriots and New York Giants franchises. “I want to better myself as a person and coach,” Morris said. “The NFL has been very accommodating. It’s important to continue learning and to challenge myself.” Morris said completing a master of coaching course towards the end of his playing career at the Sharks invigorated his desire for education.



“I was lucky to play under Tim Sheens (Tigers) and Brian Smith (Eels) and I admired how they were so innovative and always looking for different ways to do things to improve performance and gain an edge,” he said. “The trip will provide access to various high-performing cultures, that I’m sure I’ll learn a lot from and use in my future coaching. Also, my son Cruz, is going into year 11 next year and just signed with the Rabbitohs, so I felt it would be good example for him, seeing me value this education.” Morris has done no interviews since he left the Tigers. He was made the scapegoat for the Tigers 2026 collapse. He said the period since his exit from Concord has allowed him to spend quality time with his family, including a holiday in Bali. John Morris (left) and Tigers coach Benji Marshall had a difficult year together in the 2026 NRL season. Getty Images



“Which was a great opportunity to reset and gain some perspective,” he said. “However, as teams return to pre-season, I definitely have the itch to coach, so the timing of this trip is perfect.” And ultimately, there is an obvious goal in the NRL. “I want to be a head coach, however, when the time is right,” Morris said. “For now, my focus is on working hard on my personal development, to be ready for the next opportunity, whether it’s assistant or head coach. John Morris took the Sharks to back-to-back finals in his two full seasons at Cronulla. Getty



“I felt my time as head coach at Cronulla was an invaluable experience. “I was only 38 years old when I took over in 2019 and to play back-to-back finals as a rookie coach was something I am proud of. “It wasn’t all smooth sailing, as head coaching rarely is, however the adversity I experienced has definitely made me a better coach. I know what it takes to do the job and I’m confident when the right opportunity presents itself, I will be ready.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: I don’t know a bowler who hasn’t licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Opinion I don’t know a bowler who hasn’t licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist November 8, 2026 — 5:30am

November 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Firstly, a mea culpa. I was a bowler, I tried to swing the new ball, and when playing at the SCG or pre-drop-in pitch at the MCG, I definitely tried swinging the old ball. When the spinners had finished their turn, the ball needed some extra spit, sweat and polish for the quicks to be effective. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town in 2018. Getty Images The grassless, abrasive Bulli soil was ideal for natural scuffing, no external actors were required. My left-handed partner-in-shine-crime Michael Whitney was pretty good at getting the ball moving away from right-handers; my natural reversing action was away from left-handers.



Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Sandpaper scandal reviewer calls for fresh probe as Lehmann questions Khawaja’s motives Do not ask why. Theoretical physics cannot explain the mystery of “reverse” swing. The conversion from linear to curved space brings batting challenges. I do not know of a single bowler worth their salt who hasn’t licked, flicked, scratched, slobbered on or lifted the surface or seam of a cricket ball to get a little extra out of it. Originally termed “Irish” swing, the politically correct anti-cricket types objected to the phrase, so a neutral term emerged.



So here is a swing bowling guide for dummies. “Reverse” because when the ball is new it will move away from the shiniest side; when it’s old and the rub-a-dub-dub has been applied, then the ball will move towards the shiniest, smoothest side – that is, a reverse set-up. Former Test quicks Mike Whitney (left) and the author, Geoff Lawson, enjoyed swinging the ball. Steve Christo The long and short of the game says if the ball moves sideways, as opposed to gun-barrel straight, then skilful bowlers are more likely to get batsmen out, which is their collective raison d’etre and exciting for the fans. Certain actions on the ball are allowed; legal; encouraged, in fact. Shining a cricket ball is as natural as exhaling after a deep breath.



As kids we were proud of the red stain on our whites that mother’s laundry never quite erased. Batsmen have forever been coddled by the survival halo of “benefit of the doubt”, a spurious and undocumented notion that did not and does not exist in the laws of cricket. Pakistan swing bowler Sarfraz Nawaz took 7/1 against Australia at the MCG in 1979. Fairfax Media Bowlers need something, anything, and a touch of ball alteration is trivial. I first became aware of effective ball retouching in Pakistan in the early 1980s, although there was also perhaps Sarfraz Nawaz at the MCG in the middle of a 7-1 spell in 1979 – 3-305 became all out 310.



He had the old ball mysteriously swinging around corners. The pitches were bland and uninspiring for any bowler. The Pakistan pacers would get the haggard leather swinging after 20 or 30 overs, and it was revealed at the end of the series that bottle caps had been used to scar one side of the ball while vigorous shining of the obverse complemented the treatment. Former Test batsman Usman Khawaja says the entire team knew of the ball-tampering during the Newlands Test against South Africa in 2018. Dan Peled The Australian cricket team did not deem this behaviour as cheating. There was no outrage, no finger-wagging at opponents or demands on umpires to intervene. The ICC, the various cricket boards and the media couldn’t care less, and prime ministers kept their opinions to themselves.



Australian cricket teams that lose Tests get criticised. Sometimes the team gets changed. Pakistan were damned good at swinging it and we needed to catch up in the arms (and hands) race. Which brings us to 2018 in Newlands and the Australians trying desperately to keep up with South Africa. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith front an infamous press conference at Newlands. Getty Images Test matches are not the Melbourne Cup, carrying a handicap is not a part of the contest. Newlands 2018 was just another data point on the ball-fiddling timeline, rather than a catastrophic conclusion that led to David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft being banned for their roles in the sandpaper ball-tampering scandal. Bancroft was suspended for nine months, while Warner and Smith copped 12 months. Warner got a life ban from captaining Australia, while Smith couldn’t skipper for two years.



In an interview with this masthead about his upcoming memoir, Usman Khawaja said the entire team were aware of the plot in 2018. The list of cases of players caught tampering with the ball since 1990 extends to a number of national captains and world-class bowlers, including the man who captained South Africa during the abrasive 2018 Test. Cameron Bancroft stuffs a piece of sandpaper down his trousers in the infamous Test eight years ago. Nine Former South Africa captain Faf du Plessis has subsequently said he thought the punishment for Smith, Warner and Bancroft was out of proportion to the crime and he did not understand the reaction of the authorities or the public. He has a point. The ICC penalty for such abuses was previously five penalty runs and a changing of the ball.



The manner in which Australia were playing at the time was supported by the rest of the team. The hypocrisy that followed was startling but maybe not unexpected. Tim Paine appeals against Faf du Plessis in the 2018 Cape Town Test, where “sandpapergate” exploded. AP After 2018, the ICC severely increased the penalty for altering the condition of the ball. Smith was originally suspended for one match as the captain by the ICC and lost his match fee for “conduct contrary to the spirit of cricket”.



The ICC didn’t touch Warner, and the scapegoat Bancroft was slapped with a small fine by the international governing body. The new sanctions for ball-tampering are six Tests or 12 One Day Internationals on the sidelines. The punitive message delivered by knee-jerk reaction. The ball at Newlands did not swing, reverse or otherwise, and was not shown to be scratched, licked, flicked, pricked, chewed, zipped, spat on, roughed or bitten. Meanwhile, back in the batsman’s hut, the ICC penalties for cheating with a non-compliant cricket bat (that is, oversize in length, width or depth) are serious … you have to change your bat. That’s it. The ICC obviously thinks bowling shenanigans are the much greater of the evils; you can push the envelope on batting dimensions with no real downside.



Does this disparity go back to the days of the wealthy gentleman who batted and the working-class players who did most of the bowling? There has been no rational explanation as to why scratching a ball is punishable by transportation for life, yet using an illegal bat doesn’t warrant a slap on the wrist. The Australian team were vilified for being ineffectual cheats. The ball at Newlands did not swing, reverse or otherwise, and was not shown to be scratched, licked, flicked, pricked, chewed, zipped, spat on, roughed or bitten. The whole team has a duty to look after the ball – it is the bowling team’s principal resource. When the ball is new, you keep it off the ground to maintain the effective shine. If you want to rough it, then the fielders’ throws come in short, and bounce. Every player knows their job.



There’s even a skill to throwing the ball so it lands rough-side down. The team assigning scapegoats, rather than taking the collective rap, was un-Australian. The CA internal investigation was laughable but, then again, having a national crisis over the condition of a cricket ball deserves a few laughs. World.title: ‘I have completely broken down’: Wife’s grief after delivery driver’s death
World.content:
NationalVictoriaTribute ‘I have completely broken down’: Wife’s grief after delivery driver’s death Alexander Darling November 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Feng Jianming missed his daughter’s wedding last month, his wife understood. He was half a world away from his loved ones back in Beijing, but he never stopped thinking of them. Indeed, it was his wife Xu, his daughter Yawei and his son Changhui who occupied the delivery driver’s every waking moment, as he continued his relentless work in Melbourne to get money to send back to his family. Feng Jianming with his son Changhui when Changhui was a teenager. Few family photos exist due to Feng’s many years spent away from China supporting them. “He wanted to save the money and continue working,” Xu told The Age through a translator. “But he promised that when our son got married, he would definitely return. That was the plan. He would come home for our son’s wedding, and then we could finally be together as a family. We thought we only had to wait another year or two.” The chance for Feng to keep that promise was stolen from him on Friday night, when he was one of two riders allegedly stabbed by a man who had allegedly tried to take one of his food delivery orders. He was 47.



The other rider injured in the incident has since been discharged from hospital, according to Seven News. A 51-year-old Footscray man has been arrested by police, but no charges have been laid. The loss of her devoted husband – her breadwinner – is just the latest in a series of cruel twists of fate for Xu. Just two days after her daughter’s wedding, her father became seriously ill. He died on October 18. “I have completely broken down,” she said. “I cannot understand why so many terrible things have happened to our family: In such a short period of time, I have lost two of the people closest to me.” Xu last spoke to her husband just hours before he died, and she feels the words they exchanged are painful in their ordinariness. She called him because his Chinese identity card was about to expire, and she wanted to help him renew it. But she said there was no hurry.



“He said, ‘If there’s nothing else, I’ll get back to work. I’ll talk to you when I have time’. I replied, ‘Okay’.” Money had never come easy to Feng and Xu. Feng, who grew up in one of Shaanxi province’s traditional cave dwellings, known as a Yaodong, arrived in Australia in 2017. Xu said he never returned to China in the nine years he had spent here as he couldn’t justify spending on airfares – money he could send to his family. Feng Jianming, 47, is being remembered as a devoted father and hard worker. Xu knew that Feng’s frugal nature was a defining feature of his love. “He never spent much on himself. Sometimes, when he was working late, he would eat just a few biscuits and drink water instead of buying himself a proper meal. He wanted to save every dollar he could for us.” By the time he came to Melbourne, Feng had already spent several years in Moscow with the same goal of trying to raise money for his family back home. He went to Russia having been unable to support his family with the low wages from his work as a chef in Beijing.



“He hoped that moving to Australia would allow him to earn more,” Xu said. “No matter how hard we worked [in China], it always seemed that we didn’t have enough money to cover our family’s expenses.” Feng’s death has rocked Melbourne’s Chinese and business communities, prompting something of a reckoning. The Frederick Way laneway where he died is home to many Chinese students – many of them delivery drivers like him. Related Article Updated

Crime Emotions run high in Melbourne’s Chinese community after delivery rider’s CBD death A vigil in his honour on Saturday quickly turned into a protest voicing residents’ general feeling of unsafety in the CBD, with dozens letting Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece know their concerns at the candlelight vigil. But amid the anger, there has also been gratitude: Melbourne’s Chinatown Business Association has begun a fundraiser that has raised $65,000 in five hours, while others have remembered Feng for his tireless work and generous nature.



“Our community’s strength is measured not only by the celebrations we share, but by how we stand together during tragedy,” said MCBA president Christina Zhao on LinkedIn. “To Brother Feng’s family: you are not alone. Our community stands with you.” Xu has been unable to engage with the vigils and the tribute to Feng. As she begins the heartbreaking task of organising visas so she, Yawei, 26, and Changhui, 24, can come to Australia, they make his death feel more unbearable, she said. A second vigil held outside the State Library for delivery rider Feng Jianming on Saturday evening. Alexander Darling Nonetheless, she said she was grateful to those who had paid tribute, and has just one request of those wanting to help her. “I hope people remember him not just as a delivery rider or as a victim of a terrible tragedy, but as a husband, a father, a son and a man who worked incredibly hard for the people he loved.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I’ve just retired with $650k in super. Should I spend it faster?
World.content:
November 8, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’m 69 and have been retired for four years. I own my home and have about $650,000 in superannuation. I’m cautious with money and generally only withdraw the minimum required from my super. However, I’m starting to wonder whether I’m being too conservative. I’d love to travel more, but I’m worried about needing money for aged care or medical expenses later in life. How do I strike the right balance between enjoying my retirement savings now and ensuring I have enough for the future? Thanks for your question. This is a common problem for retirees because we don’t know how long we are going to live, and what our health situation might be like towards the end. No one likes to see their super shrink. Simon Letch Ideally, have your financial planner do some modelling for you. You can test different rates of spending and get a feel for what might be possible. We’d normally run some stress tests too, so you have a sense of resilience. If you are not already receiving a part age pension, you will likely become eligible in the years ahead. As you progressively use up your super savings, your age pension entitlement will grow. This provides a great inflation-adjusted income source that you know will keep paying for as long as you live.



The integration of the age pension with your other financial assets, principally superannuation, is a core aspect of Australia’s retirement system. As our age pension benefit rises, you need less from super, preserving its life. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert We want to gift our daughter $200k. Will that get us on the age pension? Noel Whittaker Money columnist To provide an increased level of certainty, you could complement your age pension with a life-time annuity. This would mean converting a portion of your super savings into an annuity. As an illustration, $250,000 converted to a lifetime annuity would pay you about $19,000 per year, with partial inflation adjustment. It would likely also give your age pension entitlement a bit of a boost. You would then have confidence that no matter how long you live, you will at least receive your age pension and annuity income regularly. Perhaps that would enable you to be more comfortable spending your other savings in the coming years, while you are fit and able to enjoy some travel adventures. Many years ago, when I bought my first home, I took out life insurance to protect against the mortgage. Over time, I’ve reduced the cover to keep premiums affordable. I’ve now paid more in premiums than the policy is worth, which feels like money wasted. I have no debts or dependants, and enough savings to cover funeral expenses. Should I cancel the policy and redirect the monthly premiums into savings? Or maintain the cover, having already paid so much into it?



The good news here is that you haven’t needed the insurance. The money you’ve paid in premiums hasn’t been wasted. You and your family had the insurance in place to protect you against a consequential adverse event. The hope with any insurance should be that you never need to claim, but we take out insurance where the impact of an insurable outcome would be financially significant. Insurance is not a savings vehicle. Having insurance in place provides peace of mind. Having now reached the stage in life where you have no debts or dependents, it may well be appropriate to cancel the policy. It would be worth just checking if there is any disability cover associated with the policy, as depending on your circumstances this could remain relevant to you. Paul Benson is a certified financial planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast.
