World.title: 2026: An election night of broken records, where special votes are key
World.content:
Although the final vote count and formation of a government remain unclear, the 2026 election has delivered numerous firsts and broken records.

With the Opportunity Party winning a projected 6 percent, it marks the first time a party has come from outside Parliament with no previous MPs as candidates and without winning an electorate.

Qiulae Wong is also the first Asian leader of a Parliamentary party.

AUCKLAND, NEW ZEALAND - NOVEMBER 07: Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong arrives at the Opportunity Party’s election night event on November 07, 2026 in Auckland, New Zealand. New Zealanders went to the ballot box with pre-polling showing a tight race as the economy faced persistent headwinds from increased fuel prices and government cost-cutting in a high inflation environment. (Photo by Phil Walter/Getty Images) Phil Walter

The Green and ACT Parties each secured record support, with the Greens nearing the record set for a tertiary party set by New Zealand First in 1996 with 13.3 percent, just shy of the 13.35 percent Winston Peters party secured then.

National also made history, but not in ways the party would be proud of.

As election night came to a close, it marked the first time a major party has secured an overhang, which also means it's the first time a major party has won no list seats under MMP.

That also means - with the exit of Nicola Willis from Parliament - it's the first time a finance minister or deputy leader has failed to return on the votes.

AUCKLAND, NEW ZEALAND - NOVEMBER 07: MP and Deputy Leader of the National Party Nicola Willis speaks to the media as she arrives at the National Party’s election night event at Viaduct Event Centre on November 07, 2026 in Auckland, New Zealand. New Zealanders went to the ballot box with pre-polling showing a tight race as the economy faced persistent headwinds from increased fuel prices and government cost-cutting in a high inflation environment. (Photo by Fiona Goodall/Getty Images) Fiona Goodall/Getty Images

It's a bitter consolation for the party that explicitly opposed the overhang strategy, yet that overhang also delivers the right bloc a two-seat majority, at least on these preliminary numbers.

Labour has not exactly covered itself in glory, either. Between the two, it's the first time the major parties have secured less than 60 percent of the vote. The previous low was 62 percent in 2002.

Put another way, it's also the first time the minor parties have collectively won more than 40 percent of the vote.

With a projected 11 overhang seats - six for National and five for Te Pāti Māori - it would also be the first time New Zealand has had a 131-seat Parliament, far surpassing the 123-seat record set in the previous term.

Samuel Rillston

It's also the first time the major parties have ended up on election night with party votes within one percentage point of one another, with just 0.2 percentage points separating them with 99.9 percent of the vote counted overnight.

However, that excludes the 700,000 special votes the electoral commission estimated would need counting as it confirms the results of the election over the coming 20 days.

That could change things markedly, with special votes traditionally favouring the left.

The final vote count in 2023, for instance, granted Te Pāti Māori an extra two electorates and the Greens one extra seat, while National lost two MPs.

RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

It meant National and ACT were no longer able to govern alone and would need New Zealand First's support.

World.title: Analysis: Five fresh new National Party MPs head to Parliament on Tuesday, but at what cost?
World.content:
While the party won the most seats - collecting 42 electorates on the night - there were more commiserations than celebrations because of what that success has cost the party.

With not one single list seat won after only pulling in 29 percent of the party vote, National is about to endure a procession of political funerals for some of its most senior colleagues.

Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith, and Gerry Brownlee are all gone.

It's a devastating outcome for a party that is still looking in a position to form the next government.

Proving that you don't need to be popular to be Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon is still in the hunt to keep his job.

With two confidence votes in his leadership and dire net approval ratings the entire term, Luxon's leadership lives on.

The question is for how long, once the caucus and wider party reach the anger stage of the grief process.

At this point Luxon has done enough - special votes allowing - to cobble a coalition together.

But he's looking set to be doing a deal with a combined Act and New Zealand First vote of 20 percent.

That's an incredible amount of power and influence for the two parties, which negotiated some significant coalition wins three years ago with just 14 percent between them.

It's not all bad news for National, but with so much loss it certainly took the shine off the wins for first-time MPs Mahesh Muralidhar, Blair Cameron, Matthew Paul, Lloyd Budd, and Jess Rowe.

Luxon and his team will have to work out how to redeploy ministerial portfolios once ousted MPs have their warrants expire in 28 days.

With special votes due back in 20 days, it's near impossible a new coalition and ministers will be sorted in time.

While some of the behind-the-scenes talks might get underway with Act and New Zealand First, it's not a given at this point the three parties would get across the line without Opportunity.

Act and New Zealand First had a good night on Saturday with both parties increasing their party vote by roughly three percent.

But it was Opportunity, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori who defied the odds.

As noted after the first wave of results rolled in on Saturday by New Zealand First's deputy Shane Jones, it's no easy feat breaking through the five percent threshold.

Opportunity has done what many said it couldn't and may still decide the next government depending on how the special votes fall.

The Greens have had an historic victory collecting the party's most successful result ever despite a parliamentary term defined by mayhem and loss.

And while Te Pāti Māori came as close as it could to self-imploding and wiping itself out of Parliament, its strategy to focus only on electorates saw it win five of the seven seats on the night.

Labour MPs will be scratching their head as to how those three parties, who all campaigned on a change of government in one form or another, capitalised and it didn't.

The party collected just two extra seats on its 2023 result, which is looked back on by the party as an election to forget.

There's a small window still for Labour to stitch together a government if they pick up enough seats on the centre-left through special votes.

On current numbers, however, the maths doesn't add up in Chris Hipkins' favour.

World.title: Election 2026: Has vote splitting saved a battered coalition?
World.content:
Analysis: Pretty early on election night, it became obvious that a handful of electorate races may well decide who has the best shot at forming a government.

In an MMP system where the party vote has always decided the make-up of Parliament, this is remarkable. It has thrust a handful of electorate races previously of passing national interest into a potentially decisive role for deciding the government.

The coalition probably lives or dies by whether or not National can cling on to - or claw back - a handful of tight seats.

On the election night numbers, it is very vulnerable in Mount Roskill, quite vulnerable in Hamilton East, and vaguely vulnerable in Whangārei. It has a good chance in Wairarapa and some dim hope in Hutt South.

This all adds up to a pretty reasonable chance at retaining the Beehive for a party that hemorrhaged about 9 percentage points of party vote support.

While it will shed five list MPs, it will likely end up losing only a net one or two, or even no electorate seats. Labour gains one, none or two electorate seats. ACT and Te Pāti Māori have lost one each, the Greens unchanged with three.

How did this happen? An unpopular Prime Minister, an election night result in the 20s and four of the party's most senior MPs - including its deputy leader - dumped out of Parliament. And yet, its electorate tally is practically unscathed.

Two of those four banished senior MPs alluded to part of the reason: a vote splitting campaign National did not endorse, and still does not like but that ultimately appears to have saved its bacon.

National voters were urged by some prominent people to split their ticket by giving their party vote to ACT or NZ First and candidate vote to National.

The aim was to grow National's overhang and boost its coalition partners' seats. It appears to have worked.

All across the country, in seats it's on track to win, National Party candidates outperformed the party vote by large margins - 17.2 points was the median gap.

These numbers don't lie: a large number of people ticked National for their candidate vote and a different party with their other vote. ACT and NZ First added roughly six percentage points to their tallies from 2023 between them, so you don't have to look far to see where most of National's support has gone.

This will really hurt National and its leader Christopher Luxon. If special votes don't take it out of his hands, Luxon will enter coalition talks with unquestionably the weakest hand a would-be prime minister has ever had. He and his party are severely diminished, whatever happens from here.

No wonder the outgoing Speaker and National Party grandee Gerry Brownlee was unhappy.

"It's like kids playing with matches," Brownlee said of the vote splitting campaigners.

There was "no doubt" that ACT had "benefited a little bit from that vote splitting campaign," he said.

Paul Goldsmith, beaten by ACT leader David Seymour in Epsom and now out of Parliament, was even more direct. "A lot of confusion was sowed" by the vote splitting campaign "which didn't help," he said.

There were no such quibbles for Te Pāti Māori who nailed their electorate-only campaign extremely successfully, adding another four seats to a huge 11 seat overhang.

Paul Goldsmith is among National's casualties. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Another kind of vote splitting

The suddenly outsized significance of the electorate seats puts into sharp relief a completely different - and unrelated - kind of vote splitting.

This happens in every election: a National or Labour Party candidate loses a winnable race where there are a good number of votes going to candidates from parties aligned with their own. It can be really annoying for those candidates and their supporters but it doesn't matter to the overall make-up of Parliament because the party vote has always decided that.

This time, the 'what-ifs' could have been - and may yet still be - much louder.

Mount Roskill is the worst example of this problem for Labour. National's Carlos Cheung had only a weak ACT candidate nibbling away a few votes from his column in this race. Labour's Michael Wood had a much more meaningful bite taken out of his vote by the Green candidate, and he probably lost a few to the Opportunity one as well. If even a quarter of the votes that went to the Green candidate had gone to Wood, he'd be much more comfortable this morning. As it stands, he could still lose.

Labour's Michael Wood

Nelson is interesting too. You can bet the 2952 people who voted for the Green candidate wanted a change of government. If they'd given those votes to Labour's Rachel Boyack instead, she would have gone ahead of National's Blair Cameron and we'd be looking at a hung Parliament.

National suffered this affliction too, albeit to a lesser extent. In Whangārei, there was no Green candidate so almost all of the left-leaning vote went to Labour's candidate Gary Payinda. There were, however, ACT and NZ First candidates who got a lot of support between them, leaving National's Lloyd Budd in a tight race with Payinda for the seat.

And Wairarapa is too close to call. If Ron Mark hadn't been on the ballot for NZ First, maybe it wouldn't have been.

The MMP features of an old school election

This unquestionably was, as National's defeated Chris Bishop said, a very weird election. The importance of the electorate races gave it the look of an old-school FPP race. But in other ways, it was very MMP.

The parties formerly known as 'minor' had their most successful election ever. Opportunity came from way back to surge over the 5 percent threshold and make it into Parliament. ACT, Green and NZ First all grew their vote.

NZ First and the Greens have both achieved more than 10 percent before, but it's the presence of four smaller parties over the 5 per cent threshold that stands out.

This was only possible because Labour and National both scored in the 20s, and there was very little vote siphoned off to parties that didn't make 5 percent.

How we compared electorates:

Electorate boundaries were redrawn in 2025, so some 2026 seats don't match a 2023 seat. We used 2023 Census population counts for small neighbourhood areas (Stats NZ statistical area 1) to work out where each 2026 seat's residents lived under the old boundaries.

If at least two-thirds of a seat's residents were in one 2023 electorate, we compare it with that electorate. This includes five renamed seats:

- East Cape (was East Coast)

- Mount Maunganui (was Bay of Plenty)

- Ōtāhuhu (was Panmure-Ōtāhuhu)

- Wellington Bays (was Rongotai)

- Wellington North (was Wellington Central)

Six seats didn't meet that test, so we treat them as new and don't compare them with 2023: Glendene, Henderson, Kapiti, Kenepuru, Rangitīkei and Waitākere. Rangitīkei kept its name, but 39 percent of its residents were previously in Ōtaki.

Four seats were close to our test's two-thirds. In Mt Albert, Mt Roskill, Botany and Wellington North, 70 to 72 percent of residents were in the same electorate in 2023. We still compare them, but some of the change there may come from the new boundaries.

World.title: 'Too close to call': Wait begins for special votes after cliffhanger Election night
World.content:
National appears on track to lead the next Government, but Labour hasn't conceded, and the final result remains too close to call without counting the special votes.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke around midnight to National party faithful gathered in Auckland, telling them it was "heartening" that his party was still the largest.

"We have a pathway to forming the next Government, but it is too close to call," Luxon said, acknowledging that "about 300,000 special votes" would have to be counted to determine the final result.

However it goes, Parliament appears set to have a new look with Opportunity arriving, and the exit of some senior National MPs, including Finance Minister Nicola Willis.

The result on the night, with 98.5% counted, gave National 29.3% of the party vote, down from 38.1% in 2023, but it did remain the biggest party by claiming 42 of the 64 electorate seats nationwide.

Winning so many electorates relative to their party vote result meant National had contributed to a 10-seat overhang in Parliament, along with Te Pāti Māori with 5 seats.

Samuel Rillston

Labour claimed 29.3% of the party vote for 35 seats, the Greens got 13.3% for 16 seats, and Opportunity crossed the 5% threshold with 6% for 7 seats.

"Tonight, New Zealand has spoken," Labour leader Chris Hipkins said as he carefully commented on how close the election race remained, and how the election night numbers could still move.

"It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said. Every vote matters, and every vote must now be counted," he said.

Coalition Government partners ACT and NZ First both recorded increases to their party vote from the 2023 election, returning 10.9% and 9.8% respectively for 13 and 12 seats.

While these numbers could still change slightly once the special votes were counted, there was no path back to Parliament for list-only Willis, nor senior National MPs Paul Goldsmith (Epsom) and Chris Bishop (Hutt South) who both lost their electorate races.

"Politics is a rough business, and we've given it our best shot, but ultimately it's the people who get to choose," Goldsmith said at the National election event in Auckland.

Willis was forward-looking, saying, "the National Party is an extremely strong team and institution". She called it a "process of renewal", and was "confident there will be a great team there".

She also reflected on how, "it's been a very difficult time to be in government, for governments around the world".

"You know, we've had petrol up at $3.60. We've had global tariffs. We've had extraordinary cost of living challenges for New Zealanders, and they have felt that deeply," Willis said.

Bishop, in conceding the Hutt South electorate race said the point of it all was the bigger picture, "it's not about me, it's not about Nicola and it's not about Paul".

"What actually matters is the type of government and the policies," Bishop said.

When Luxon spoke at the National party event in Auckland, and acknowledged his departing MPs, he omitted Bishop by name, despite naming lower-ranked candidates.

Speaker Gerry Brownlee would also exit Parliament, and he said he had "no regrets" about only standing on the list.

Fellow senior minister Mark Mitchell said National had "campaigned as hard as we could" on party vote, but said losing these colleagues was "a blow to our party".

"They've all been outstanding ministers, we don't want to lose any of our people," Mitchell told RNZ as he celebrated his own success winning the Whangaparāoa seat.

"I'm really happy with the result we're getting," Mitchell said, reflecting on how democratic elections had been challenging for sitting governments everywhere.

"If you look around the world, incumbent governments are finding it very hard," he said, explaining the shift to a "power order" had unsettled voters in other democracies.

National MP Paul Goldsmith Edward Gay

Willis, Goldsmith and Bishop between them held 19 ministerial portfolios, out of about 50 substantive ones, leaving a big hole to fill should National lead the next Government. Among them were major portfolios, including finance, justice, transport and housing.

The personnel changes and worse party vote result for National would likely impact coalition negotiations with the apparent right bloc voter shift to NZ First and ACT.

This meant a change to the balance of a coalition, and the two minor parties may lay claim to greater roles in Government with stronger positions based on total vote share.

Nicola Willis Fiona Goodall

The final result would not be known until the special votes were counted, with that total to be revealed in three weeks' time, on 27 November.

"What's clear is nothing's clear tonight," ACT leader David Seymour said at a party event in Auckland.

NZ First leader Winston Peters Mark Papalii

NZ First leader Winston Peters described the campaign as "difficult" in his brief election night speech acknowledging his party would be returned to Parliament.

Neither leader commented on the situation ahead, only taking a short opportunity to thank their supporters for campaigns that returned them a greater share of the vote.

While the Opportunity party was set to enter Parliament for the first time, with an election night count of 6%, they may not get to play the hyped role of kingmaker.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong was joyful at making it to Parliament, but spoke to party faithful before final count permutations could be calculated effectively.

"You have voted for unity over division," Wong said.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong Phil Walter/Getty Images

"To some of you watching, it might seem like we just arrived, but to many in this room this result has been a long time coming," she said, reflecting on the party's 10-year history.

Wong said the election had been "a really tight race" and reiterated the party would speak first to the party with the greatest number of votes.

That was a close run thing on election night with Labour on 29.3% and National on 29.3%.

Hipkins said he would "get straight to work" if Labour had the opportunity to form a government.

The election was still undecided, with special votes potentially able to sway the final outcome. The Electoral Commission had forecast about 700,000 special votes.

World.title: 'Fantasy' to expect US to go back to playing by the rules - expert
World.content:
New Zealand must rethink its foreign policy towards the United States, an international relations professor says, after the replacement for "the most important role in the White House" was announced.

Stephen Miller, a longtime aide to President Donald Trump, has replaced Susie Wiles as the new White House chief of staff.

"It's probably the most important role in the White House," said Robert Patman, a professor of international relations at the University of Otago.

Patman said the chief of staff would be the closest person to the president in organisational terms.

He said Miller's appointment showed Trump was "doubling down" after the Republican midterm losses this week, during which Democrats rode a wave of support to take control of both chambers of Congress.

"I think if people were hoping that Trump would take note of the midterm elections and begin to moderate some of his policies, they will be disappointed by this appointment."

Patman said the midterm elections showed a lack of popular support for Trump's tariffs and immigration policies, which Miller had defended and helped develop - including the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest targets.

"I think it does point to the need for New Zealand to rethink its foreign policy towards the second Trump administration. Because this administration, and in particular Miller, and Trump, neither of them believe in a rules-based international order, which has been the crucial vision of all New Zealand governments going back to 1945."

Patman said attempts to appease Trump in the hopes of better deals for New Zealand and of moderating the impacts of his policies had not worked.

"New Zealand has not been spared tariffs. Our exporters are now paying 12.5 percent on many products.

"And in addition, we certainly have not been spared the economic consequences of Trump's Middle East military adventurism. The economic consequences have been significant."

Robert Patman. Provided

Instead, Patman suggested cultivating ties with "alternative middle powers, such as Australia, Japan, Singapore, which is about the same size as New Zealand in terms of population, and many European powers".

He said New Zealand should seek cooperation with the US when interests overlapped.

"But where our interests diverge, such as Trump's attacks on the World Trade Organization, its attacks on the International Criminal Court, its aggressive use of tariffs and its threats, illegal threats against other countries, we have to stand very firm because after all, one of the lessons of the last two years is that keeping quiet does not actually protect you from the consequences of Trump's policies."

Patman said it was a "fantasy" to believe the US would return to its traditional role as "leader of the free world".

World.title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch may now have so much plastic, it’s changing ocean's colour
World.content:
Scientists have discovered that microplastics could be changing the colour of the ocean in areas of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch (GPGP) .

The GPGP is a swirl of plastic trash between Hawaii and California, more than twice the size of Texas.

Scientists at Norway's University of Bergen analysed three satellite datasets of seawater colour from parts of the GPGP between 2002 and 2022.

Findings were published in Communications Earth & Environment.

Shea Cheatham and her colleagues found there was a significant brightening of seawater - making it appear bluer and greener.

In 2016, seawater in the GPGP was found to contain 17 milligrams of larger microplastic particles per cubic metre.

To test whether the changes were due to natural causes, the scientists modelled how the colour of seawater changed in relation to the amount of microplastics present in it.

They found simulations with microplastics were four times more likley to experience brightening than those without microplastics.

This was the case with even small amounts of microplastics and was especially pronounced for cyan wavelengths.

World.title: Opportunity's success and what could come next
World.content:
Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong is today rallying her caucus and booking flights to Wellington, readying herself to become a first-time MP.

The party has made history as the first to enter Parliament from the outside under the MMP electoral system.

Where exactly it will sit is still unknown. At this stage, the right bloc of National, ACT and New Zealand First can govern without Opportunity.

But the special votes are still to be counted, which will take three weeks and could leave Opportunity with the balance of power.

As of 11pm Saturday, Qiulae Wong had not heard from either National leader Christopher Luxon or Labour leader Chris Hipkins. However, Luxon - who has repeatedly ruled out forming a government with Opportunity - did congratulate the party in his speech at National HQ.

Wong said if her phone had not rung once the weekend was over, she would make a call "over the next few days".

On election night she told reporters her party had made history.

"It is absolutely surreal to feel like we are actually in this position," she said.

"We are all - all of us that are going to be going in there as MPs - genuinely excited about making a positive difference for New Zealand."

Her first port of call on Sunday would be gathering the caucus to discuss what's next: 'new MP school' at Parliament which begins on Tuesday, and potentially some negotiations.

Wong told reporters she would stick to her promise of negotiating first with the party with the most seats, which at this stage is National.

"Just because we speak to the largest party first doesn't guarantee anything," she said.

"We need to see an alignment of values of where we're going to take the country and obviously meeting our bottom lines as well."

Wong said all options were on the table: a coalition, a confidence and supply agreement, or sitting on the cross benches.

For Opportunity to form a coalition, Wong said the party would need to feel "very confident" in the overall direction of the government.

"But the other minor parties play a significant role as well, and I imagine we will be talking to them too."

Wong said if she were Luxon - and if he relied on her to form a government - she would rather have that conversation than put herself in Opposition.

New ACT MP Paul Henry shares that perspective. On election night he said if Luxon did not get on the phone to Wong, ACT leader David Seymour would be urging him to make the call.

Wherever Opportunity sits, Wong said the result was the start of the next big challenge.

"We get one chance to make a good impression for New Zealanders on us being a viable and credible party in Parliament," Wong said.

"We want to be re-elected in 2029, so it's really important to us that we are in a position where we can demonstrate that.

World.title: Mahesh Muralidhar makes history as National takes back Tāmaki
World.content:
Mahesh Muralidhar is set to become the National Party's first Indian MP to win an electorate seat, taking back one of the party's traditionally safest constituencies in an election night upset for ACT.

The party's two previous Indian-origin MPs, Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi and Parmjeet Parmar, both entered Parliament through the party list.

Muralidhar led ACT's James Christmas by more than 5300 votes in Tāmaki after 97 percent of the votes had been counted on Saturday night.

He had secured 15,303 votes, compared with 9961 for Labour's Max Harris and 7659 for Christmas, who is expected to enter Parliament through ACT's party list.

The result marks a return of the electorate to National after former ACT deputy leader Brooke van Velden defeated National's Simon O'Connor in 2023, ending his four-term hold on the seat.

The closely contested election has Labour narrowly ahead of National in the party vote, with the two parties separated by less than one percentage point as counting nears completion.

Preliminary projections suggest National, ACT and New Zealand First could secure a narrow majority in Parliament, although special votes are yet to be counted, with that total to be revealed on 27 November.

Muralidhar said getting out into the community from the beginning of the campaign had been crucial to his success.

"The day after I was chosen as the candidate for Tāmaki, the next day I went out door-knocking, and that's the most important thing," he said.

He said he had knocked on about 16,000 doors during the campaign, crediting his visibility, party support and volunteers for helping secure the result.

"Tāmaki appreciates someone with a commercial background, and my campaign was launched by the prime minister," he said.

"I raised $15,000 for a community patrol in Glen Innes, and this is the result."

National's Mahesh Muralidhar speaks to volunteers at Colin Maid Rugby Club during election night. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Muralidhar is chief executive of Phase One Ventures, a venture capital firm investing in New Zealand start-ups. He also worked at online graphic design platform Canva between 2015 and 2017.

Tāmaki is one of the country's three wealthiest electorates, alongside Epsom and the newly created Wellington North.

Established in 1946, the electorate has voted Labour only twice.

Former Prime Minister Robert Muldoon secured the seat for National in 1960 and represented it until he left Parliament in 1991.

National's Clem Simich and Allan Peachey followed, before Simon O'Connor held the electorate from 2011 to 2023.

Even during Labour's landslide victory in 2020, when the party won the Tāmaki party vote with 39 percent against National's 37 percent, O'Connor secured more than 50 percent of the electorate vote.

That changed in 2023 when van Velden campaigned successfully to unseat O'Connor, winning by a majority of 4158 votes in what was considered a major upset for National.

Earlier on election night, Muralidhar told RNZ the mood at his campaign gathering was upbeat.

At Colin Maiden Rugby Club in Stonefields, he appeared confident as the results began coming in.

"The mood is really great, and I'm looking forward to seeing a centre-right government coming in and the National Party doing well," he said.

The result is Muralidhar's second attempt to enter Parliament.

In 2023, he contested Auckland Central but lost to Green Party MP Chlöe Swarbrick.

Muralidhar, who describes himself as a proud Kiwi-Indian, said he wanted to make sure the Indian community's concerns were heard.

"I'll be there for the community in regards to making sure that the community is understood and heard," he said.

He thanked Tāmaki voters for choosing him to represent them, saying he intended to live up to a promise his father had made during the campaign.

World.title: Ponga leads Kiwis to final after pre-match stare down lights up World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga has returned to the field 23 days after breaking his arm to lead New Zealand to its first Rugby League World Cup final since 2013.

Ponga, who suffered the broken arm in the tournament's opening match against Australia, had three try assists and a try-saving tackle to inspire the Kiwis to a 34-10 win.

But the highlight of the contest came before the opening whistle, when both sets of players engaged in one of the great moments in rugby league.

After New Zealand performed its Haka, in reply to the Sipi Tau from Tonga, the two sides stared each other down as time stood still.

A packed house at Hunter Stadium in Newcastle got louder as the stare-down lengthened, a precursor to the historic semifinal that was to come.

Kiwi centre Casey McLean, who scored a crucial second-half try for his country, told ABC Sport the pre-match stare-down was a special moment that had him ready to give everything for his teammates on Saturday.

"We have such mana boys in our team that are leaders," he said.

"We've just got to follow them, especially myself.

New Zealand defeat Fetu Samoa New Zealand cross-code superstar Stacey Waaka leads her country to another women's Rugby League World Cup final, scoring three tries in a dominant win over Fetu Samoa.

"I can learn so much off them, not just about being a player, but [also] my culture. They're front runners for Māori boys and Kiwi boys."

Ponga's impact on the match was immediate, setting up back-rower Briton Nikora for the opening try in the third minute.

New Zealand dominated the opening quarter, before Tonga winger Jojo Fifita made a line break from his own goal-line, setting up a break down the left wing by Tolutau Koula, who then threw it back to Fifita for the length-of-the-field try.

The belief in the Tongan camp grew, and they looked destined to score again when forward Demitric Vaimauga was clear and only had the much smaller Ponga to beat.

But Ponga produced a stunning try-saving tackle, one-on-one, to stop the much larger man.

"It just shows how much this Kiwi jersey means to him," McLean said.

"To be able to put on a performance like that, it just shows how much of an amazing person he is."

Just one minute later, Fifita was in for a second to give Tonga the lead off a perfectly executed scrum play.

But a mistake from fullback Lehi Hopoate allowed Kiwi Dane Gagai to score and give the Kiwis a 12-10 half-time lead.

Down by just two points, Tonga had every reason to believe they could advance to the World Cup final for the first time.

But a significant change in weather at half-time meant they played into a howling headwind for the second 40 minutes.

Hopoate was peppered with high kicks he could not reach as the wind made predicting the landing near impossible, while halfback Isaiya Katoa struggled to kick the ball much further than 30 metres at the end of sets.

It meant the Kiwis were able to camp themselves in the Tongan half of the field for the entire second half, wearing them down and scoring four tries to seal a 24-point win.

"No excuses, you've got to take your hats off to the Kiwis," Katoa said.

"The way they played footy tonight is the way you play in these conditions."

New Zealand will face either Australia or Samoa in next Sunday's final at Lang Park in Brisbane.

World.title: Demons rally and Kangaroos cruise into AFLW prelims
World.content:
Melbourne has stormed home with the last five goals of the game to beat Geelong by four points in their AFLW qualifying final.

After Demons star Paxy Paxman put them in front with a snapped goal, Chloe Scheer marked and had a shot at goal for Geelong with 20 seconds left.

But the Geelong forward missed and the Demons won 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52) on Saturday at Princes Park.

In the later game, North Melbourne booked its prelim ticket with a commanding 7.7 (49) to 1.7 (13) win over Carlton.

Melbourne kicked the only three goals of the last quarter after looking well out of the game in the third term.

Geelong onballer Georgia Prespakis was easily best afield in the first half, but Melbourne midfielder Liv Purcell helped spark the comeback and they had 34 possessions apiece.

It was the first time Geelong's Mick Stinear has gone up against his old club since the 2022 premiership coach left Melbourne at the end of last season.

Melbourne now has the week off, while Geelong's semi-final opponent will be the winner of Sunday's Sydney-Western Bulldogs elimination final.

The threat of lightning delayed the start of the game on Saturday by 10 minutes, but Melbourne's changeable spring weather meant much of the game was played in sunshine.

The Cats kicked clear in the second term, with four goals to one and led by 22 points at the main break. They twice led by 28 in the third quarter, before the Demons hit back.

With Purcell and 100-gamer Tyla Hanks leading the way, the Demons kicked four goals to three and cut the margin to 12 points at the last change.

Alyssa Bannan's accurate snap in the first 30 seconds of the final quarter brought the Demons to within a goal. Prespakis kicked a behind, then Bannan kicked her second.

Paxman put Melbourne in front for the first time since the first quarter with her goal at 17 minutes.

Injury concern in big Roos win

Two-time North Melbourne premiership player Alice O'Loughlin is a significant casualty out of the Kangaroos' comprehensive AFLW qualifying final win.

O'Loughlin was emotional on the bench after she hurt her knee in the last quarter of Saturday's 36-point win over Carlton at Ikon Park.

She was in agony and needed two trainers to help her off the field after Gab Pound caught her in a tackle.

It was the one negative for the two-time defending premiers, who withstood a game challenge from the Blues in the first quarter.

The usual suspects starred for the Kangaroos — Jasmine Garner racked up 31 possessions, and fellow midfielder Ash Riddell had a game-high 33.

Key defender Harriet Cordner was mighty for Carlton, especially early, but eventually there was little she could do when the dam wall broke.

Carlton will next host the winner of Sunday's elimination final between Gold Coast and Hawthorn.

World.title: Lehmann says 'everyone' was ball tampering globally, denies Khawaja's sandpaper claims
World.content:
Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann claims ball tampering was once ever-present in international cricket, but denies Usman Khawaja's claim of widespread knowledge of the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Lehmann was the coach of the Test team during the Cape Town controversy, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during the match.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were all suspended in the wake of the incident, while Lehmann stood down from his post.

Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claim Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

In an interview with Nine newspapers on the eve of the release of his new book, Sabr, Khawaja claimed Cape Town was not the first time the Australian side had used sandpaper to tamper with the ball and that the plan had been known by "all of us".

"Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

Speaking to ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand, Lehmann denied personal knowledge of the use of sandpaper and said he does not think all members of the Australian camp would have known about it either.

Lehmann did claim though that up until that day, "everyone around the world" was ball tampering.

Loading...

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case by case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja said he had suggested to the entire playing group after Bancroft had been caught that they take collective responsibility.

Lehmann, who is part of the ABC's cricket commentary team and has recently joined the ABC Cricket Podcast as a co-host, said he could not confirm or deny that discussion took place, as he was not present.

Darren Lehmann stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"I don't remember that. There were two change rooms obviously, and there were meetings going on everywhere. To be perfectly honest I was in meetings with Cricket Australia a lot," Lehmann said.

"That could have been the case, I don't know. I'm not saying yes or no to that one. There will be different points of view everywhere on this whole matter."

Lehmann also said he was not aware of an alleged conversation between Bancroft and a member of the coaching team, which Khawaja said was important in the formation of the sandpaper plan.

Earlier on Saturday, a Cricket Australia (CA) spokesperson said they remained comfortable with the initial findings of their investigation.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Lehmann said the 2018 incident left him in a "really dark place" and said the release of Khawaja's book and its explosive accusations has brought up "bad memories" for him, the players and their families.

"End of the day, Cricket Australia had their findings. It was a really tough week, two weeks, at that time going through the process and talking to all the relevant parties," he said.

"I was in a really dark place for a period of time where for four months I didn't leave my house.

"Eight years after the fact and trying to sell a book is a bit different. That's Usman's choice and that's the way he wants to go.

"For the families and the people involved, I feel for them right now because it's taking them back to a really bad place. It's been eight years. You get to a place where you move on, and I've moved on with my life."

Darren Lehmann said the Cape Town affair left him "in a dark place". (AP: Halden Krog)

Lehmann said Khawaja had not reached out to him in advance of these claims going public.

"For me it's a really touchy one mentally, more than anything else, and I know the boys will be feeling that as well.

"Could he have said this at the time? I suppose that's one of the things in the book. I mean, books are there to sell.

"He's spoken to Pat Cummins apparently and the players. I haven't spoken to Usman, he hasn't texted me or rang me. That's just the way it is."

In 2021, Australia's Test bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon released a statement denying any knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.

Speaking to SA Grandstand on Saturday morning, former Australian fast bowler and current South Australia coach Ryan Harris said he thought it was "a bit disappointing" that it had taken Khawaja "eight years to say that".

"That's probably all I want to say on that. Like most people, I've been interested to hear what the book is going to say."

Jason Gillespie, another former Australian fast bowler, said he had always "found it a challenge to believe" only three players knew of the plan, but would not suggest everybody was across it and backed the testimony of the bowling group.

"This is what was interesting, the umpires at the time studied the ball and said they couldn't see any evidence of ball tampering. That's what I find fascinating.

"And that's what the bowlers have come out and said, the actual umpires looked at the ball and found no evidence … of ball tampering."

World.title: Triumph, tragedy and Alan Jones's drive to survive F1's deadliest era
World.content:
The motor racing world is mourning the death of Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, who died on Thursday aged 80.

The Australian legend, a winner of 12 grands prix, leaves a huge legacy both on and off the track after a life dedicated to the sport.

As tributes flood in for Jones, and reflections of his tremendous career are written, his death has brought into focus the dangerous and deadly era of motorsport he competed in.

Jones raced and won in an era when the safety of drivers, marshals and spectators was not front of mind.

In an already dangerous sport, the period Jones raced in is often remembered much more for its tragedies than its triumphs.

And it was tragedies that had a major impact on Jones's career, right from the very beginning.

Jones begins F1 career at tragic Spanish Grand Prix

Alan Jones made his F1 debut at the 1975 Spanish Grand Prix, one of the darkest and most controversial F1 weekends in history.

Rolf Stommelen suffered serious leg injuries, while five spectators were killed when his car crossed the barrier. (Getty Images: Sutton Images/David Phipps)

There was drama from the start with fears barriers at the Montjuïc Circuit in Barcelona were not bolted in correctly.

Members of the Grand Prix Drivers Association went on strike before practice, but the race went ahead after alleged rumours that the Guardia Civil, Spanish law enforcement, would seize the cars, which were at the Montjuïc stadium.

Jones qualified 21st for Hesketh Racing, but would retire just three laps into the race after a collision.

But the horror of the day was still to come.

Race leader Rolf Stommelen went off the circuit on lap 26 due to a broken rear wing, with his Hill-Ford car crossing the barrier into the crowd.

Five spectators were killed and Stommelen was seriously injured. The race continued for another four laps it was called off.

The 1975 Spanish Grand Prix holds another slice of history, with Lella Lombardi becoming the first, and to this date, only female driver to score F1 world championship points after placing sixth.

Jones gets F1 drive after fatal accident

After falling out with Team Surtees at the end of the 1976 F1 season, Jones was out of the series for the start of 1977.

He would get his chance to return to F1 following a harrowing and tragic accident in South Africa.

Anthem mix-up fed Alan Jones legend Alan Jones's first F1 grand prix victory in 1977 was so out of the blue that he said the band played Happy Birthday to him instead of the national anthem, but is the story true?

Welshman Tom Pryce and a track marshal were killed in an incident that was indicative of the poor and unimaginably lacklustre safety measures of the day.

Renzo Zorzi, who drove for Shadow, suffered a fuel leak and pulled off to the side of the main straight at the Kyalami circuit.

A small fire broke out, leading to a pair of marshals running onto the track to extinguish the flame. One driver was able to swerve and avoid the marshals, but not Pryce, Zorzi's teammate.

Pryce was unsighted and drove at full speed into 19-year-old marshal Frederik Jansen van Vuuren, killing the teenager on impact.

Van Vuuren was carrying a massive fire extinguisher that hit Pryce in the helmet, killing the Welshman instantly.

Race winner Niki Lauda was preparing to celebrate on the podium, until a member of tyre manufacturer Goodyear was able to get to the Austrian and inform him of Pryce's death.

The horrific and needless deaths ultimately led to Jones being called into the Shadow team for the next race in the United States.

Later that year, Jones would claim a stunning maiden win in Austria, the only win Shadow ever achieved, which set him up for future glory in the years to come.

Jones 'turns down' Ferrari after double tragedy

From 1979 to 1981, Jones was at the peak of his powers.

Driving for Williams, he won 11 grands prix in those three years and claimed the 1980 world championship.

But things could have been much different had a potential move to Ferrari eventuated.

Ferrari had met Jones, telling him he was their second option if the famed Italian team could not sign Mario Andretti.

Ferrari missed out on Andretti, who went on to win the 1978 championship with Lotus, but the Scuderia instead signed Canadian Gilles Villeneuve.

Jones went on to sign with Williams, in what proved to be a formidable partnership.

But, as happened so often in motorsport, tragedy struck.

Ferrari suffered a pair of horrors in 1982, a year after Jones first retired from F1.

The remains of Gilles Villeneuve's destroyed Ferrari chassis, after his fatal crash in Belgium in which he was thrown from the car. (Getty Images: LAT Images)

Villeneuve died after a crash during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix, when he ran into the rear of a much slower car. Villeneuve's car launched into the air and he was thrown out as it crashed back to earth.

Didier Pironi suffered a similarly scary incident in Germany, suffering horrific leg fractures after running into the back of Alain Prost's unsighted Renault.

Jones claimed years later that Ferrari reached out to him to fill in for the final rounds of the 1982 season, but he took too long to reply and Ferrari chose another replacement.

F1 safety improves after Jones's retirement

In total, there were five drivers killed on F1 grand prix weekends during Jones's career.

Ayrton Senna, Roland Ratzenberger, and how the San Marino Grand Prix changed Formula 1 While the legendary Ayrton Senna took most of the spotlight, Roland Ratzenberger's legacy lives on through F1's safety innovations.

That does not include two drivers killed in F1 tests, as well as Australian Brian McGuire, who was killed at Brands Hatch in England in 1977 while driving an F1 car.

It was a horrifying era for Formula 1, but one that did improve in the years following Jones's retirement in 1986.

F1 went several years without a fatal incident, until a horrific weekend at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix when Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger died in separate crashes.

There has been just one fatality in F1 since, when Jules Bianchi went off the circuit at Suzuka in 2014 and collided with a crane that was recovering the beached car of Adrian Sutil.

Several safety measures have been put in place, both on the race car and in how marshals and recovery vehicles enter the racing circuit.

The Halo, a curved, wishbone-shaped structure, now sits above the driver and has played its part in protecting drivers in several incidents, including Romain Grosjean's fiery 2020 crash in Bahrain, Lewis Hamilton being trapped underneath the wheel of Max Verstappen's Red Bull during the 2021 Italian Grand Prix, and Guanyu Zhou's frightening crash at Silverstone in 2022.

World.title: Stricter regulation on the cards for controversial combat sports
World.content:
A NSW parliamentary inquiry has heard that controversial emerging combat sports, notorious for head-injury risks, are prepared to accept regulation, despite some medical experts calling for them to be blacklisted entirely.

NSW Sport Minister Steve Kamper referred activities like collision running, bare-knuckle boxing, and competitive slapping to a committee to investigate if they should be brought further under the control of the state's Combat Sport Authority (CSA).

On Friday, CSA chair Darren Kane told a hearing that the sports should be subject to stronger controls.

"These sports are dangerous, there's no way of hiding behind that … but rugby league's dangerous, and cricket's dangerous, thoroughbred racing is dangerous," he said.

"There's a very good reason why an ambulance follows every race around the inside of a racetrack, to make sure that they're on hand if a jockey falls off.

" It's a balancing act. "

Darren Kane says the sports should be subject to stronger controls. (Supplied: NSW parliament)

Under heavy scrutiny at the hearing was collision running — where two athletes run at each other and collide.

Neurologist Rowena Mobbs urged the committee to ban the sports being investigated, due to risks of brain injury like concussion, especially in collision running.

"I cannot see that it's a fundamental activity of a human to run at a brick wall, let alone a brick wall coming at you," Dr Mobbs said.

"I just can't see any sense in that."

Rowena Mobbs told the inquiry that the sports carry the risk of traumatic brain injury. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Organisers from the Run Nation Championship (RNC), a prominent collision running event, did not participate in the inquiry, nor did power slap organisers.

Mr Kane noted in his evidence that RNC had been working collaboratively with the CSA for an upcoming planned event in Sydney.

Boxing offshoot

The organisers of two fight groups gave evidence at the hearing — GTG Fight Club and Bare Knuckle Australia (BKA).

BKA spokesman Michael McConnell said there was reluctance in the community around regulation, but that it would be necessary to continue growing the sport.

"We can do this safely, and everyone can be looked after in the best way possible," he said.

" I think having these regulations is essential for this sport to not just survive but thrive and transcend and elevate to the next level. "

Michael McConnell hopes that any regulations are developed fairly and collaboratively. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

BKA said their bouts included vetted fighters, who were matched up by weight class and had their abilities assessed through gloved-up test fights.

The fighters were then paired up and fought without traditional boxing gloves.

BKA co-founder Randall Rayment said he was hesitant about regulation and wanted governments to "back off".

But he said he wanted the government to understand the positive outlet that bare-knuckle-style boxing could be for men who wanted a controlled environment to express themselves.

Harm minimisation

Organisers of the sports being examined have claimed the presence of medical staff at events was a harm-prevention strategy.

But in her evidence, Dr Mobbs refuted that argument.

"I state that no doctor on the sideline will be able to modify the risk of traumatic brain injury in either collision sports or power slap," she said.

" It is window dressing as far as prevention. "

'Do not try this at home': Controversial contact sport on the rise The Run Nation Championship will see two athletes run at each other, in a sport criticised for its head injury risks. Organisers argue the championship has been professionalised, and will grow to be as big as boxing.

In a written submission, the Australian Medical Association's (AMA) NSW branch said it did not endorse any of the sports in question, but it believed regulations were needed.

"Emerging activities typically magnify the most violent aspects of established sports, and thus present a significant public health concern," the AMA submission said.

"The NSW government should invest in evidence-based public education campaigns to increase awareness of the short-term and long-term health consequences of concussion, repetitive head impacts and traumatic brain injury associated with emerging combat sports and comparable activities."

Dr Mobbs and other medical bodies that made submissions agreed that education was crucial.

Social benefit

Sione Tongia and Stephen Gardiner have faced off in a BKA fight, but consider themselves close mates.

"I feel like at the end of the day, we're boxing; we just don't have gloves on," Mr Gardiner said.

Randall Rayment (centre), with fighters Sione Tongia (left) and Stephen Gardiner. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

Mr Tongia said he felt bare-knuckle events should remain to provide a place for young men to channel aggression and differences.

The fight club concept gaining traction in only unregulated Australian state The organiser of this fight club says it saves lives. But critics say it is putting young men at serious risk.

"I guarantee you that two people who have beef, after they fight each other, they feel good, they feel better," he said.

"When I fight, I don't fight for beef.

" I just fight because I feel like I better myself by doing it. "

The parliamentary committee will hand down its findings in a report by the end of 2026.

World.title: Aussie's heroic Paris Masters run ends at the hands of rising French star
World.content:
Rinky Hijikata has finally been awakened from his dream week at the Paris Masters as a new young French tennis hero ended the Australian's bid to reach his first big-time tennis semi-final.

For the third match running, Hijikata, who came from behind to defeat Novak Djokovic in the second round, battled back from a set down with some scintillating tennis as he quieted the home fans cheering for their new hope, Luca Van Assche.

But it was the 22-year-old Paris-based Van Assche, also playing in his first Masters 1000 quarter-final, who rose to new heights as he came from 2-0 down in the final set to prevail 6-4, 6-7 (4-7), 7-5 after a memorable two-and-three-quarter hour duel.

It meant the end of what felt like a major breakthrough week for the 25-year-old Sydneysider Hijikata, who looked early in that final set as if he was going to win his sixth match in seven days and become the first qualifier to reach the last-four at the Paris Masters in nine years.

Ultimately, he was defeated by a young player who said he felt inspired by the crowd as he struggled physically in the deciding set.

"The crowd were so important for me, supporting me so much in the tough moments, and that's why I played my best tennis," said Belgian-born Van Assche, who becomes the 12th Frenchman to make the semi-finals in Paris and will next tackle American Ben Shelton.

Hijikata's consolation will be to start next week as Australia's number two man behind Alex de Minaur as he enters the world's top-60.

Hijikata certainly continued with that fearless, aggressive streak in the second set tiebreak against Van Assche, maintaining his fine form by then earning an immediate break in the third set.

But Van Assche is one of the most highly regarded young talents in the game, and his defensive prowess helped him turn the tide in the final set with some extraordinary wall-like resilience that kept forcing Hijikata to play one shot too many.

Third seed Shelton, bombing down 19 aces, had earlier prevailed in an all-American match-up to reach the Paris semis for the first time, roaring to a 6-4, 4-6, 6-3 win that ended Tommy Paul's quiet late bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin later in November.

The victory sealed qualification for the end-of-season men's championship for another US star, Frances Tiafoe, alongside world number one Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli and Arthur Fils.
